THE LATE EARL BALDWIN OF BEWDLEY
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO FORMER PRIME MINISTER OF THE UNITED KINGDOM

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE LATE EARL BALDWIN OF BEWDLEY
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO FORMER PRIME MINISTER OF THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it will be the wish of hon. members that before we proceed further with the business of the house some slight tribute should be paid on behalf of our parliament to the name and memory of a former prime minister of the United Kingdom who had over many years close associations with Canada and who, in fact, was a member of the privy council of this country. I refer, of course, to the Right Honourable Earl Baldwin of Bewdley, who passed away at the advanced age of eighty years on Sunday morning.
The unparalleled events of the last few years have more or less overshadowed the careers of not a few of those who in the two previous decades were among the most prominent in public life. That is particularly true of the career of Lord Baldwin, who resigned the premiership of the United Kingdom at the time of the coronation, and who for some years past has been living in semi-retirement. When Earl Baldwin died, there passed from the scene of world politics, one who in his day was pre-eminent among British statesmen.
Baldwin was for some twenty-nine years a member of the British House of Commons. During those years he was outstanding as a parliamentarian. He was three times Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, covering in all a period of some twelve years. In that time he played a foremost part in a solution of the vexed problems which were then before the nation. It was his fate to have been in office and to have occupied the first place in British public life for most of the difficult years between the two great wars.
I shall not attempt in anything I say this afternoon to comment upon either the policies of his administrations or upon specific acts of his government. This would not be the time or place for that. But I should like to say a word in regard to the outstanding place which Stanley Baldwin, as he was known at the time, held at the time and will always
hold in relation to the affairs of the British commonwealth of nations. I believe it to be a fact that no one, at that particular time, had a better understanding of relations between the different nations of the commonwealth and of what was best calculated to further harmony and effective co-operation between them than had the late Earl Baldwin. I think his administration may be credited with having guided the development of the commonwealth along lines which made possible the close co-operation which existed in the testing time of war.
It may not be within the recollection of all present that it was during the conference of 1926, over which Baldwin presided, that the government of the United Kingdom, in combination with the governments of 'the other nations of the British commonwealth, gave formal recognition to what we now speak of as the doctrine of the equality of status of the nations of the commonwealth. That doctrine found expression in legal form in the Statute of Westminster, which will ever remain one of the great documents in British history.
Canadians regardless of party affiliations, retain many cherished memories of Lord Baldwin's visits to our country. Hon. members will remember that it was Stanley Baldwin who was the first prime minister of the United Kingdom to visit Canada while in office. Fortunately it has become a natural thing for us to have visits from prime ministers of the United Kingdom. This parliament and this country has been visited by others who have since held that high office-Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, Mr. Churchill, and Mr. Attlee have all been here as prime ministers of the United Kingdom-but Mr. Baldwin was the first British statesman who while holding the office of Prime Minister felt it a duty to his own country and to the commonwealth to visit this dominion as the oldest and largest of the overseas nations. Hon. members will recollect that Baldwin came out at the time of the diamond jubilee of confederation and was accompanied by the then Prince of Wales. He visited Canada again in 1932 at the time of the economic conference. Wherever he went throughout Canada in 1927 and 1932 he received the warmest of welcomes from the people of this country.
It was also under Baldwin's government that the first high commissioner came to

The Late Earl Baldwin oj Bewdley _
Ottawa to represent the government of the United Kingdom in this country. The example thus set has since been followed in representation of their governments in the other countries of the commonwealth by all the nations of the commonwealth. These are links with Britain and with other parts of the commonwealth which have proved their enduring worth.
I should like to mention one other important matter, with which Stanley Baldwin was immediately concerned and which had an important bearing on our own relations with the crown. I refer to the part he played in what might have resulted in a critical constitutional crisis at the time of the abdication of King Edward VIII. So tactfully and ably did Baldwin act in that very difficult situation that, without lessening the friendship he enjoyed with the Sovereign to whom he had been prime minister, he was able, at the same time, to inform the British House of Commons of the situation that had arisen and advise acceptance of the abdication of the king.
I should perhaps also mention the general strike that took place in Britain in 1926, and w'hat was spared Britain at the time, and possibly other nations since, by the able manner in which that situation was also met by Mr. Baldwin. He possessed unquestionably a unique gift of reconciling differences as they arose in his own country. It was one of the great objectives of his life. In that very critical situation his conduct once more was such as to commend itself not only to Britain but to all parts of the British empire.
While sharp differences of opinion exist as to some of the policies of his administration, Baldwin himself was always highly respected for his whole-hearted and selfless devotion to Britain's welfare and to British interests as he conceived them. Patriotism and public service were the watchwords of his career. He was a great Englishman and a great gentleman. He had a close and personal attachment to the English countryside and country life; a keen appreciation of literature, to which he himself made important contributions. His natural simplicity and sincerity of manner endeared him to his followers, and brought him many friends.
So far as Canada is concerned, I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the name of the late Earl Baldwin of Bewdley will always hold a high place in the minds of our people, and, to those who knew him and were privileged to enjoy his friendship, a place of deep affection in their hearts as well.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE EARL BALDWIN OF BEWDLEY
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO FORMER PRIME MINISTER OF THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate
myself and the party I lead with the tribute paid by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to a former prime minister of Great Britain. Earl Baldwin was a British prime minister well known to Canada. As our own Prime Minister has said, he was one of the first holding that high position in Britain to visit this country during his tenure of office.
I recall very well his first visit to Canada about twenty years ago. When he spoke in the city of Winnipeg it was from my own window in the second storey of the parliament buildings to a vast assemblage on the grounds outside. I can remember still his interest and the sympathetic manner in which he treated the early history of that part of Canada.
I recall, too, very well his second visit to Canada, I think in 1932. This was at the time of the empire trade discussions in this city. At that time he came 'to us not as the prime minister of Great Britain but as president of the executive council in the coaltion government of Ramsay MacDonald. I recall the great hopes he had for further commonwealth and empire co-operation. It is interesting to recall at this time the faith he had in the encouragement of trade between different parts of the commonwealth.
History will say of Baldwin that he was a generous citizen. It is said of him that he turned back to the state all the wealth it had permitted him to make during the first world war. I think too, that history will speak of him also as a great and typical Englishman, an astute and capable parliamentarian and as one of the outstanding public figures in Great Britain in the interwar period.

maintopic: THE LATE EARL BALDWIN OF BEWDLEY
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO FORMER PRIME MINISTER OF THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, death is a great leveller. No matter how high a position a man has held in public life, in the British commonwealth or any other country, he goes the same way as the humblest citizen, and we are reminded of that today.
Like the Prime Minister I do not propose to comment on Mr. Baldwin's record as a ship he enjoyed with the sovereign to whom the time nor the occasion to do so. As to the work that he did, I think it will be appraised in the light of the history of the period through which we are passing. It is difficult to make a correct appraisal of any political leader who has lived over the last number of years and who played a prominent part in the affairs of our respective nations.

House of Commons
With regard to Mr. Baldwin's part and place in the history of world relationships, when all the facts are known of the times in which we have lived the correct appraisal will be made and I propose to leave that to history. But may I say that with the relatives whom he leaves behind we wish to express our sympathy.

speechtext: No knowledge of it. TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947

The house resumed from Friday, December 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for an address to His Excellency the Governor General praying that the Continuation of

Transitional Measures Act
Transitional Measures Act, for 1947, be continued in force until the 31st day of March, 1948.

Last Friday I adjourned the debate on the Transitional Measures Act. It was generally anticipated at that time that the debate would be concluded Friday evening, and this in spite of the fact that we had a rather limited filibuster in one quarter. Were it not for the fact that once again in that debate efforts were made to misrepresent the position that Social Credit-ers have taken with respect to controls and related matters, it would not have been necessary for me to move the adjournment of the debate as I did.
Sir, it is quite obvious that there are still some in this house who, deliberately or otherwise, are endeavouring to create false impressions with respect to Social Crediters, in that they are endeavouring to assert, in the first place, that we favour the return to the laissez faire of irresponsible enterprise of pre-war days. Secondly, they are endeavouring to create the impression that Social Crediters favour the throwing of Canadians completely on the mercy of certain irresponsible private interests who will be free to exploit them; and in the third place I detected that an effort was being made to create the impression that we are quite satisfied to permit the continuance of certain current economic conditions which actually threaten to stimulate revolution within this country.
Let me once again, on behalf of my colleagues here, deny these allegations unequivocally and categorically. Mr. Speaker, the leader of this group stated on several occasions, for those with eyes to see and ears to hear, our reaction to the current economic upheaval in this nation, and also our recommendations with respect to the necessary cures. I must state emphatically that any attempt to emasculate our speeches by the mutilation of paragraphs and sentences for the purpose of creating such false impressions must be relegated to the category of dishonest politics.
Speaking on Friday the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. McKay) asserted that the government must have been stampeded into what he calls its present untenable position by certain groups in this house. Referring specifically to this group, he stated, as reported at page 258 of Hansard :
No doubt they-
-meaning the government-
-were also influenced by the social credit attitude as expressed by their leader on March 21 in this house when he said: "Social Crediters are implacably opposed to planned controls" . . .
That is not the end of his sentence, but the remainder of it has to do entirely with the Conservative party. That group of words, Mr. Speaker, "Social Crediters are implacably opposed to planned controls" is less than one third of the original sentence.
Read it all.

I shall do so. Just prior to the sentence which the hon. member is presumed to have referred to, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) said:
With us it is not a question of the need of controls; it is indeed a question of what kind of controls.
Then he said, and this is the sentence in full to which I referred a moment ago:
Social Crediters are implacably opposed to planned controls, which enhance the power of the state at the expense of the liberties of the individuals of Canada.
Now I say that t'he eight words quoted to give an entirely incorrect picture and the twenty-six words indicate the position which the leader of this group took on our behalf and the position which we take at the present time. The leader of this group went on, after making tihat assertion, to state that we favour the removal of bureaucratic wartime controls as rapidly as possible-and I would underline the words "rapidly as possible". He then also indicated the necessity for safeguarding the whole political economic and moral wel-ware of our Canadian people. He emphasized too the necessity of taking action to protect the political, economic and moral welfare of our people by introducing, concurrently with the removal of bureaucratic wartime controls, certain effective checks and balances which are inherent in a revitalized and reformed financial policy in the first place. He also laid particular emphasis on the necessity for tax reductions. He also stressed electoral reform, and he recommended the re-application of the subsidies and price discount factors as being one of the most effective methods of bringing prices into line.
Again on Friday the member for Weyburn referred to us, and I find it necessary to take issue with the observations made on that occasion. He said, as reported at page 258:
On the other hand, the C.C.F. requested the government on March 20 in this chamber to retain price controls to keep prices down, but were defeated by a combined vote of government, Social Credit and Progressive Conservatives.
This assertion was challenged by the member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) and
Transitional Measures Act

also by the member for Peace River. The member for Peterborough West said, as recorded in Hansard:
Mr. Fraser:	I think the hon. gentleman
would like to be fair. I do not think he will find any place in Hansard where such a vote was taken.
Mr. Low: When was the vote taken?
Mr. McKay:	On March 20.
Mr. Low:	There never was such a vote.
Mr. McKay:	Yes, there was.
Mr. Fraser:	On the retention of price controls?
Mr. McKay:	Look in Hansard.
Mr. Low:	It is not there.
Mr. Fraser:	It was not called for that
purpose.
Mr. McKay:	That was the essence of the
motion. I submit that this group was reflecting public opinion when that motion was presented to this house last March.
An examination of Votes and Proceedings for March 20, 1947, reveals that on that day the C.C.F. leader did move an amendment to a government motion calling for the continuation of certain essential orders and regulations. The amendment did in effect condemn the government for its so-called headlong decontrol policy and it also called for the reimposition of controls. Votes and Proceedings of March 20 reveal this statement, and I wish to underline and emphasize the statement:
Mr. Speaker ruled the amendment out of order on the grounds that it contravened standing order 50 which precludes all amendment to the main question on a motion to refer a resolution to committee of the whole.
From this ruling the leader of the C.C.F. appealed. The next statement from Votes and Proceedings of that day is extremely significant. This is it:
And the question being put:	Shall the ruling
of the chair be sustained?-it was decided in the affirmative on the following division.
And the division is recorded. After very careful consideration of the amendment, after extremely careful consideration of standing order 50, we came to the conclusion that that amendment was not in order and consequently we supported the Speaker's ruling and nothing else.
I think it is most unfair to endeavour to create the impression, either through a speech in this house or elsewhere, that Social Credi-ters did other than vote to sustain the ruling of the Speaker. I say in all kindness to the hon. member that even with the wildest stretch of the imagination no other conclusion could possibly have been arrived at.
I can conceive of this situation, that the Speaker's ruling may have been challenged

in order to put us in a position where a most fantastic deduction could be made and an impression sent abroad that we voted against the amendment.
There are two further references in Votes and Proceedings to which I think I must refer. On Tuesday, March 18, 1947, all Social Crediters with the exception of the member for Pontiac (Mr. Caouette), who was responding to the will of his electors, supported the extension of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act of 1945 until May 15, 1947. Votes and Proceedings of the above date confirms this fact. This position was further confirmed by a vote recorded in Votes and Proceedings of March 25, 1947.
Finally, Votes and Proceedings of April 16, 1947, again reflects the fact that all Social Credit members, with the exception of the hon. member for Pontiac-who, I may interject, responded once again to the will of his electors -did by their vote support the government measure for the continuation of certain orders and regulations for a limited period during the so-called national emergency. By declaration in this house, Mr. Speaker, we have reasserted our opinion-and it is not only my personal opinion; it is the opinion of this group-that because of abnormal conditiops the government would have to exercise certain controls over price structures, foreign exchange, imports and exports, rentals, and so forth. In the second place we have said that certain controls or systems of controls employed by the government should be removed as rapidly as possible and be replaced by automatic controls of a more democratic character than many of those which operated during the war. We also emphasized that the controls as we have known them cannot be permitted to be carried on indefinitely. I say personally that controls in themselves can no more cure the economic disabilities which confront this country than can the mere locking in an asylum of an insane person cure him of his mental disease.
Speaking on Friday evening the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine), at page 265 of Hansard, made this assertion:
As I said, we have tried to amend this resolution-
Meaning, of course, the resolution to continue the transitional powers act until March 31, 1948.
-and the house has voted down our amendment.
It is the next part that I take exception to: That is to say, the three capitalist parties-
You will notice the emphasis he put upon that word "capitalist," but I think it resulted

Transitional Measures Act
in a case of mental intoxication which sent him completely off the deep end as far as the remaining words are concerned-
-in this nation joined together to vote down an amendment to control the prices to the Canadian people of essential commodities in order that their income might be able to purchase the necessities of life.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, it cannot be construed that the amendment which they moved on Friday did have the intent and purpose implied in the statement made by the hon. member for Cariboo. Without the amendment the transitional powers act would continue in operation until March 31, 1948; then, with parliament in session, members and parties in this house, knowing what conditions are, say, by the first of March, are in a position to come to a decision as to whether they are prepared to support the continuance of this measure or not.
The usual socialist drivel.

I say that arriving at a conclusion of that kind, putting it in Hansard and sending it out, is a vicious sort of thing; in fact, I would almost say it is an obnoxious sort of thing. I heard someone say just now that it was diabolical in character, but I would not want to use those words, because I realize that they are possibly not parliamentary. As I have emphasized, that amendment simply asked for the extension of the emergency powers for a twelve-months period rather than a three-months period. I think I have made our position perfectly clear with respect to that matter. Certainly the past record of this group, as I have indicated, with respect to the whole question should satisfy all of our willingness to support such extensions when the government can justify the necessity for such extensions. The hon. member for Cariboo would be the first to admit that the mere granting to the government of an extension for twelve months does not guarantee that the government will do the things necessary for the establishment of a proper price realizationship and thus assure the people of this country that they can buy the essentials of life.
I want to give one other reference to what the hon. member for Cariboo stated. He is reported at page 265 in Hansard as follows:
I would suggest that neither the government nor the opposition that is before me nor the opposition that is behind me-
Meaning us, of course.
-would be prepared to submit the question before us in the form of a plebiscite to the Canadian people and abide by what they said.
The hon. member for Peace River made it abundantly clear right at that moment that
we would be perfectly happy to have the matter submitted to the Canadian people, in proper form, naturally. What I take strongest exception to are these words, "and abide by what they said." I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that there is absolutely no instance on record of the members of this group not having abided by public opinion, where that public opinion was expressed clearly and effectively. I recall that it was not many years ago that a plebiscite was held in this country. We did not approve entirely of the wording of the plebiscite question, but when the Canadian people voted in the affirmative in support of the manpower plebiscite we came into this house and certainly supported the decision as expressed by the people. But I must say at the same time that, if memory serves me correctly, my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party did not do that. Again, if memory serves me correctly, they voted against the National Resources Mobilization Act.
Before proceeding further, Mr. Speaker, I want to re-emphasize what I said a moment ago. We have no fear whatsoever of a plebiscite, and the people can feel assured that we are prepared to carry out the decision which they render, should such a plebiscite be held.
Un Friday we all listened with a good deal of interest, as we always do, to the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). I always try to be in the house when he speaks, because with much that he says I thoroughly agree. I am not taking exception to anything except a possible conclusion he arrived at. I do not believe, for one moment, that my hon. friend should take the results of government bungling on the one hand and of the activities of certain irresponsible private enterprisers within the country on the other, and on the basis of that advocate the nationalization of Canadian industry. Like the hon. member for Cape Breton South, I represent miners, along with others. As has been indicated to me, the miners of my constituency are not favourably disposed towards the nationalization of industry as expounded by some people in this country. I believe they have taken their lead from John L. Lewis, the president of the United Mine Workers of America. Writing in the Canadian Mine Worker, which is the official organ of district 18 of the United Mine Workers of America, on the occasion of the birthday of that publication in 1944, Mr. Lewis said this-and I think his words are most significant; I think
Transitional Measures Act

labour in this country should take note of them and give the most careful consideration to them. Mr. Lewis said:
Labour must guard against the inroads and acceptance of benevolent fascism as a substitute for sanely and honestly regulated free enterprise. A paternalistic bureaucracy, now so widely exercised as part of our war effort, must not be permitted to hold over and become the governmental yardstick and doctrinaire policy of our transition period. Labour must stand united as never before for the maintenance of its social gains and fight on every hand the imposition of regimentation which flows from the altruistic concept of nationalization programmes which shackled the workmen of Europe into fascism and nazism, and which eventually generated economic injustices into a world wide conflagration.
In those words John L. Lewis set forth my view with respect to this matter as well as I could state it myself.
Just before coming into the house my attention was drawn to another matter which I think is tied in with this subject, 'because in connection with controls we have the advo-lacy in some quarters of nationalization, socialism or whatever you wish to call it. I have here a clipping from the Montreal Standard of December 13, 1947. Apparently the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, spoke to the Reform club of that city at luncheon on Saturday, and this is the newspaper report of his remarks-I am not pretending to quote him verbatim:
Tucker declared that the Liberals are enemies of communism-
I doubt that, to start with.
-and other subversive doctrines. They oppose the socialist doctrines of the C.C.F. and social I
Such downright poppycock! What complet dishonesty in reference to social credit!
-but support the individual rights of privat initiative and promoted social legislation whic will take care of the poor and needy.
I say to the hon. member for Rosthern that this comes with mighty ill grace from him, because it is my contention that through certain policies applied by this government in recent years, and supported by him, the soil has been fertilized in which the communists lay the eggs from which they hope their little totalitarian serpents later will hatch. There is no group in this house or this country that has taken a stronger stand against communism than we have. There is not a group in this house or in this country that has taken a stronger stand in support of private enterprise than we have. For the hon. member for Rosthern to make a statement of this kind is pure and sheer political dishonesty.

Just in passing that reminds me of another statement made in Edmonton by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), in which I believe he referred to social credit as a cancer in the body politic, or something like that. All I want to say to the hon. gentleman is that even though he is Minister of National Health and Welfare, and even though he may have the finest body of advisers, he will not 'be able to remove that so-called cancer. I can assure him of that.
Some of the statements made in the west by cabinet ministers are extremely interesting. These hon. gentlemen ought to scout around a bit after it is presumed they have left for Ottawa, and listen to some of the comments and observations made by the people to whom they have spoken. It would' not enhance their prestige at all. Generally speaking these fellows are likeable chaps. Returning for a moment to the hon. member for Rosthern, in this regard I would refer him to his own minister, of whom the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) said at page 191 of Hansard:
You know, sir, that the first move of a socialist in order to bring in a socialist economy-and sometimes as I look at the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) I wonder how he feels at being an instrument for bringing in socialism in our country-
The minister replied:
Very proud of it.
Of course he quickly qualified that remark by saying that if he had to choose between socialism and some kind of Toryism which he mentioned, he would take socialism; nevertheless the following day, though I have not the quotation at the moment, he reaffirmed his position in that respect. I would not take issue with him at all, because I believe he has contributed very substantially toward bringing socialism into this country.
Does his parliamentary assistant help him at all?
I think he is an important contributing factor.

Mr. Speaker, I would ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw something he said, since the hon. member for Rosthern is not in his seat. If I understood the hon. gentleman correctly he said a few moments ago that the hon. member for Rosthern was politically dishonest.
No.

That was how I understood it.

I said the act could be categorized as a politically dishonest act.
What is the difference?
I am perfectly willing to withdraw as far as the record is concerned, but I assure the minister I still have that opinion.
That is all right, but as I understand it a member of this house cannot say that another member is dishonest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think I was derelict in my duty in not rising immediately that remark was made. I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member say something was downright dishonesty, which was as I understood it, and certainly that should be withdrawn.

I have no desire to do anything to offend Your Honour or the house, but I want to get the record perfectly straight. I am sure the minister can realize how I felt on reading the statement reported to have been made by the hon. member for Rosthern. As a matter of fact I am surprised that I kept my language so moderate. However, I am perfectly *willing to withdraw anything that may be offensive to the house.
Withdraw the statement that he was dishonest.
It might throw the whole sentence out of kilter if I withdrew just one word.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's duty is quite clear; it is to withdraw the words "downright dishonesty," or the word "dishonest," because certainly it cannot be used.

I think the record as it was taken down should be examined, because that might result in the complete mutilation of something that should not be mutilated. On the other hand I did not intend to say the hon. member was dishonest but that I thought the statement could be characterized as such.
The hon. gentleman said that this was downright political dishonesty. If he wants to change that to "downright political" it might be all right, but he should not use the word "dishonest."
Well, it may have been.
But you cannot say a member of this house is dishonest.

As I understood the hon. gentleman, he did not directly accuse the hon. member for Rosthern of having been dishonest; if I understood him correctly he said it was an act of political dishonesty. Since it is the duty of the Speaker to protect freedom of speech in this house I did not intervene when the hon. gentleman made the statement to which I have referred, but my attention having been called to it by the Minister of Agriculture, I believe the hon. member should find another expression to use,, because what he has said really constitutes an imputation.

As I indicated earlier, I do not want to say anything that might be considered unpleasant by the house. I shall be glad to withdraw the word, although it is; hard for me to do so. I respect Your Honour and the house, and I shall withdraw it, but I would ask that I not be required to withdraw the whole statement. I believe the ruling should be limited to that word, and it has been suggested that I use the word "skulduggery".
I shall conclude with just a word or two. It is a fact that the people of my constituency are not satisfied with current economic conditions. The farmers are simply furious about the situation which has developed in the livestock industry. We have seen a virtual liquidation of whole herds, and breeding stock is. moving to the market, I was going to say by trainloads, but at least by carloads. In a district like Red Deer, which is such an important mixed farming area, that becomes a serious situation. Farmers have urged me to register the strongest protest, and I do that now.
The consumers back there deplore the ever-increasing cost of living. We say that the government must do something about it. They have our suggestions and we hope that they will take action. There is also a multiplicity of little aggravations which are wrapped up in what I would refer to as Liberalism. Back home they are no longer betting whether the Liberal candidate will win Red Deer constituency the next time; the betting is whether he will beat the communist who got only 600 votes in 1945.

Mr. Speaker, just before coming to Ottawa to attend this session, with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) I attended a meeting of local 514 of the united electrical workers, held at 175 Bathurst street, Toronto, and presided over by John Rowley and addressed by Ellis Blair. I must say that I enjoyed attending this meeting at which there were present 100 to 150 men and women, apparently all of whom were employed in factories in Toronto, many of them in Davenport riding according to the names I saw there.
I think I can compliment them upon their ability to express their opinions and to line
Transitional Measures Act

up an argument to support what they believe to be correct. I doubt if I would have said anything about this had it not been that a local labour paper called the UE News contained what I thought was a fair article dealing with the attendance of both of us at that meeting. The article was headed:
MP's meet with Toronto UE members but won't sign prices petition.
We were both asked to sign a petition. I thought the petition in principle was quite fair, but I told them that I did not believe it was right for a member of parliament to sign a petition. I said that I felt a member should go to the House of Commons with his mind wide open, ready to listen to any argument for or against what came up on the floor of the house. Therefore I declined to sign the petition and so did my colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood. I think that was a fair position to take. I am glad to be able to say that the reaction of most of those present was, in my opinion, in agreement with a member of parliament taking that position.
Much of what I heard there that day I can agree with, and much of it I have heard expressed by hon. members sitting to my left, more particularly by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart). In saying that, I do not want him to think I agree with most of what he says, but I can agree with some of the things that he has said.
In the first place, I wish to say that I am going to support the resolution before the house. I think my leader has given a plain, well spoken and clear statement of the position of this party. I support him in that and I shall vote accordingly.
My whole life has been spent with working people, and I was one myself for many years. I want them and I want the people whom I represent to feel that I believe my duty here is to be fair and square to everyone and to all classes. I do not want to give my support to any one class; I feel that I should support whatever I think is right.
One of the ladies present, a very bright little woman, expressed almost word for word what the hon. member for Winnipeg North said about refrigerator prices, but in her case she was relating her own experience. The hon. member for Winnipeg North referred to someone in Montreal who had this experience, and I have no doubt that many people have had similar experiences, namely, that at the present time there is little stability in refrigerator prices.
The last time I was in England was at the time of the coronation. At that time I
[Mr. MacNicol.1
obtained a copy of an act-unfortunately I have not been able to find it-which had been passed by the government there. I do not know whether this act is still in operation and I cannot recall clearly what was in it. My impression is that it provided some machinery whereby the buyer of any article who felt that he had been overcharged or gypped could apply to a board or a committee to find out if. he had actually been over-charged. If there had been an over-charge, a penalty was provided. If that act is still in force in Great Britain I am sure the authorities here could ascertain what has been its effect. If the effect has been good over there I believe it would be equally good here.
When I was home on Saturday I saw a bill which had been presented to a working man by some repair man who had performed some service in his house. I thought it was a tremendous bill for the small amount of work that had to be done. It may not have been too large because I suppose one would have to have all the facts before he could say whether there was any extortion. On the other hand, I believe the public should be able to ascertain whether they are being overcharged or whether extortion is being practiced. I do not know whether you would call this price control and I do not know what (hey called it in England.
In addition to attending that meeting of union members, I received, just after coming here, many' wires from different unions along the same line as the information given to me at that meeting. One was from local 252, signed by the president, A. P. Burke; another from local 717, signed by the president, E. Kriek; another from local 725, signed by the president, A. Addison; another from local 753, signed by the president, A. Johnston; another from local 870, signed by the president, R. McArthur; another from local 919, signed by the president, W. Burns; and another from local 975, signed by the president, Victor Emby.
I mention those only to show that there is a very widespread feeling over the high prices people have to pay for the necessities of life today. How they are to be controlled I do not know. I am a great believer in free enterprise and I believe that by and by the matter will regulate itself, but at the moment prices are undoubtedly very high.
On Saturday last someone I know well went into a boot store to buy a pair of shoes which he had been in the habit of buying for $11.50. The merchant told him that the price had gone up to $13.50. When the buyer expressed surprise at the price jump the merchant said,

Transitional Measures Act
"The salesman for the firm that supplies me with these shoes was in this morning and told me that after such-and-such a date the price will be SIS." After that conversation I asked the merchant why the big jump from SI 1.50 to $13 50 and the proposed jump from $13.50 to $18? He said, "These are American shoes and they cannot be imported now, and any price can go.'' Whether the government has power to regulate the price of any particular item or not I do not know, but certainly $18 is a very high price to pay for a pair of low shoes. So apparently there is reason for much of tlie uneasiness throughout the country over prices all along the line.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) in his brief remarks, which on the whole I found not unfair, followed his usual line when speaking of business and industry. I would have thought that a man with such a fine name as Alistair Stewart would not intentionally say anything unkind about anybody, but his expressions toward industrialists were certainly not very kind.
I listened with interest to what my leader said a few moments ago when eulogizing the late Lord Baldwin. I was acquainted with the late Lord Baldwin. He was engaged in the iron and steel business in Great Britain on a large scale and we had some acquaintance because I, too, was in that line of business at one time. I like to think of his generous action in turning back to the national treasury of Great Britain all the profits that his great company made during the war from iron and steel, of which they were large producers. They had a plant in Toronto. I would tell the hon. member for Winnipeg North that there are many manufacturers like that, many with whom I am personally acquainted. I know many who refused to accept profits during the war. I do not like to hear all manufacturers branded with the same mark, that they are all bandits and everything they should not be. On the contrary, from my considerable experience I have found most of them to be men of true Christian principles in the main who command the respect of the people they serve and those with whom they work and of the community in which they live. So I would suggest to my hon. friend not to brand everybody as he does.
In my youth I was associated with labour unions and I can say that I have always respected the stand taken by the majority of labour leaders. They should not all be branded as being everything they should not be. The vast majority of labour leaders, I can say from my experience, are against strikes and do what they can to adjust differences so as to prevent strikes, knowing from experience that a strike does not help everybody. They make every effort to protect the men they represent. There may be the odd one who would like to see a row, but they are not all like that by any means. There may be the odd industrialist who does not avoid a row. But in the main both labour leaders and industrial leaders are men of the very finest character and both do a great deal for industry and the unions, building up industry on the one hand and getting better labour conditions for the men on the other. So while I think well of much that the hon. member for Winnipeg North said, when he attacked industry holus-bolus, I could not support him.
I said a few moments ago that I did not sign the papers which were presented to me to sign. This is not the exact paper I have before me. This one was sent out by the Labour Progressive party, which, too, has something worth while in it. I am not going to denounce all it says and does because it has some good points. These are similar to the proposals they asked me to sign:
(a)	Prohibiting any further price increases.
I could not sign that. I would have to have placed before me the arguments for a particular price increase and the arguments against it. Perhaps there are arguments for a price increase on many goods. I could not sign that proposal holus-bolus. The next one is:
(b)	Re-establishing price controls.
I could not sign that. A lot of controls should have been lifted long ago. A lot of controls have been removed and the minister has given reasons why the controls should be off. I am not expressing any opinion at the moment whether controls should be on or off. I am in favour of extending power to the government to continue certain controls up to March 31, and when that time comes along I shall have to make up my mind again if a further extension is asked. I am not against everything. The next one is:
(c)	Restoring governmental subsidies on essen-tal consumer goods where necessary.
There again I would have to have presented to me the reasons in favour of a particular subsidy and the reasons against it. In other words, Mr. Speaker, I know that you, too, have often been asked to sign petitions. Personally I do not take very much stock in petitions. I had brought to my room the other day a pile of petitions containing I do not know how many thousands of names, and later presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. A lot of those signatures would
Transitional Measures Act

be given in good faith but the majority of them would be given without inquiry whatever. The next proposal is:
(d)	Prosecution of those found guilty of profiteering.
I am in favour of that. I will support the prosecution of anyone found guilty of profiteering. I believe that was the real motive behind the bill in Great Britain some years ago. I do not believe that profiteers, men who deliberately and cold-bloodedly raise prices beyond what they should be, should be allowed to go scot-free. No, Mr. Speaker. For years and years I have studied everything I could study and travelled far and wide and discussed with the sanest labour leaders what legislation could be brought into the house to ensure labour receiving an adequate return. And industry should be able to obtain a reasonable profit on their investments, so as to design and promote expansion in building up the country. Surely to goodness there is some way to do it, and I hope when the government bill pertaining to labour comes into parliament after we resume in the new year we shall have some legislation which will ensure to the investor and to labour fair play. They both are entitled to it, and the country will prosper best and fastest when both have it.
I did not rise to make any extended speech but I wish to make two -more comments. I wish to refer, first of all, to what the hon. member for Winnipeg North said about the lack of price control in this country. I find that in Russia they have the same difficulty as we have, and I am not going to blame the Russians for it. I am one of those who have a high regard for the Russians. I have had a lot to do with Russians because many of them made good moulders and good machinists in the business with which I was associated. I always took pleasure in helping them the best I could. I find that the Christian Science Monitor in its Saturday's issue quotes from the July number of "Monthly Labour Review" of the United States department of Labour having to do with matters in Russia. I am not criticizing Russia, but this article quotes Russian prices and compares them with United States prices. It shows that the average working man's wage in Russia is 500 rubles a month. I had an official telephone the Bank of Montreal this morning and ask how much a ruble is worth today, and the banker replied 18-86 cents; therefore anybody can ascertain from that fact how much labour gets in Russia. All he has to do is to multiply 500 rubles by 18-86 cents. The amount is nothing like what labour gets in Canada. I wish they got more, over there; I

hope the time will come when they will get more. Then the worker out of his small return has to pay infinitely higher prices for what he buys than we have in Canada, which goes to show that even under a socialist government-and I am not talking now of socialism or capitalism-prices are away higher than they are in this country under a free enterprise government. This also goes to show that .prices are something which you cannot control as you might like.
The Russian pays a minimum of 800 rubles for a suit of clothes. Judging by the pictures of the Russians I have seen on the street they are not wearing the same type of clothes as we are over here. I do not know what a Canadian suit would be' worth in Russia, but according to this, 800 rubles at 18-86 cents per ruble it would amount to a very high price. And it goes all the way down the line. A pair of men's shoes cost 270 rubles. Well, when I heard on Saturday that in a short time low shoes will be $18 a pair in Toronto I was surprised, but the Russian is paying many many times that when he pays 270 rubles at 18-86 cents a ruble. Women's clothes, men's shoes, coats, radio sets, phonographs and so forth are all at much higher prices than they are here. I am not blaming the Russian government for that. They have problems about which I know nothing; they have costs about which we know nothing. In like manner I wish to say, mostly to my hon. friends on the left, with whom I 'have little fault to find so far, that I should like to see them be not so all-embracing in their denunciation of capitalism and of industry. What would this country be without industry? The city of Toronto, which has a population today of almost a million, would have a population of perhaps ten or fifteen thousand.
Somebody said something the other day about control of goods coming into this country. Before the bill having to do with importations is brought down I hope that a lot of care will be given to it. In Toronto and Ontario we have no fewer than 2,000 businesses large and small, handling mostly United States goods. One gentleman came to see me when I was home a few days ago and told me that if such-and-such a control went through he would be forced to close. He said that he had a small business employing fifty-three men. He had built up that business over the years, and it will be too bad if he is forced to close. He is only one of several men who came to see me with the same story. I want to support the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in a program of trying to conserve United States dollars because it is patriotic to do so. On

Transitional Measures Act
the other hand, I hope that he will listen to arguments so that his program will not wipe out too many of these businesses handling United States goods.
I should like to say a word on controls in connection with old age pensions. The other day there came to see me a neighbour lady who is eighty-four years of age. She is a dear old lady. She lives in a small, humble home. All her lifetime she was thrifty because poverty made tier thrifty and she had nothing to waste. Out of her small earnings she was able to save sufficient to buy a small home. Now she owns it. She has a very small income and has been able to put two or three hundred dollars in the bank. She rents the upper little flat in her home for $16 a month. That is the total on which she has to live. She asked me if there was not some way by which she could receive some return without surrendering the title to her house. I hope, when that subject comes before parliament, that control will be wiped out, the control which obliges an- individual to surrender the title to his home before obtaining the old age pension. That is all I have to say. I hope that, when that bill comes in, that particular control will be wiped out and the old folks will be given the opportunity of obtaining the old age pension without surrendering title to their homes.

Mr. Speaker, the government resolution before the house seeks extension of the emergency powers until March 31, 1948. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has decried the rising cost of living, and in the course of his speech apparently supported some of the things advocated by Tim Buck. I may just say that it seems we are coming to a queer state in Canadian-
Will the hon. member allow me to interrupt?
Certainly.

The hon. member is taking a wholly wrong opinion of what I said. I did not express any opinion on what Tim Buck said, other than that I respect everybody's opinion. I merely read what was in the circular which I was asked to sign and which I refused to sign. I do not want the hon. member to be smart and try to mix me up with Tim Buck.

I had no intention of being smart or clever, but I have been confused with the attitude taken by the hon. members to the right. I do not wish to take any time in discussing it at this
time. The record speaks for itself. The speaker who preceded the hon. member for Davenport did just two things. In the course of his address he devoted almost his full time to attacking members of this group. He said that he was implacably opposed to planned control. I should like him or some other member of his group at some time to tell us, if he does not believe in planned controls, what kind he believes in. In my opinion if the controls are not planned they are unplanned.
We have before us one of the most serious situations in Canadian history. There is no doubt about that. The decontrol policies of this government have led our Canadian economy into a crisis. Before coming here I talked with many people from various walks of life. Our farmers particularly are enraged at the government's decontrol policy, as I have never seen them on any other occasion. They are opposed to putting coarse grains on the Winnipeg grain exchange, for once again we have the grain exchange gambling in our farm products. Moreover, the farmers are greatly disturbed because in many instances, owing to the increased cost of production, they are forced to wring the necks of their chickens or else continue to produce at a loss.
The opening of the grain exchange for coarse grains came at a most inopportune time so far as western farmers are concerned, when half or more of the coarse grains had already been put into the hands of the grain companies and of speculators. A neighbour of mine told me that prior to the opening of the Winnipeg grain exchange he had sold 4,000 bushels of coarse grains.
The policy of the government is striking at the very heart of democracy in this country. This particular man of whom I speak fought in the first great war for democracy in Canada and for our Canadian way of life. He lost his own son in this last war and he has another son who came back and is now trying to make a decent living in Canada. Yet we find this sort of thing happening to him.
Before getting on the train I had a talk with a veteran of the two wars. He is now trying to make a living taking mail from the station to the post office, and he is doing the best he can to augment his income by running a small poultry farm. He tells me however that since the controls on coarse grains have gone off, his cost of production has risen so high that he is forced either to destroy his flocks or to produce at a loss. That is the result of the government's policy.
We cannot simply stand by to wait and see, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has suggested during this debate. It seems that
Transitional Measures Act

the government will not take action, notwithstanding the fight that my colleagues are making for the reimposition of controls in order that something may be done for western farmers, and for the farmers of the east as well. Such is the situation in the west today that the farmer there has no faith in the future of agriculture.
During the war the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) advised the western farmers that in order to keep the British market for hogs, we would have to go into stable production of these animals, and in the latter part of the war many people like myself put in costly electric fences, self-feeders and piggeries, but we found that as a result of the policy with respect to coarse grains, whereby we could not get a drawback, we were forced out of production. Hundreds of farmers in the west abandoned production in this direction and consequently the output of hogs fell. That was a sledge hammer blow to livestock production in the west.
As a result of the recent decontrol we find that, owing to the removal of the coarse grain subsidies the eastern farmers have been placed in the same position so that they are having to slaughter young pigs or to sell them at the ridiculously low price of $1 or $2 per head. Today in consequence of this, the Canadian farm economy is on the brink of ruin, simply because the government stands by and says we must "wait and see", presumably waiting for some word from the United States as to what we should do in this country.
I have great respect for the United States, but when any country will destroy 8,200,000 bags of potatoes, as was done in the United States last year, when the world faces starvation and when such a man as Sir John Boyd Orr, chairman of the agricultural and food committee, is endeavouring to get all the food obtainable for millions of people, it is time that we did something on our own behalf. We can have our own economy planned so that we may play our part in rehabilitating the peoples of Europe.
Today the peoples of Europe are faced, not with a passing hardship; their situation seems just now to be hopeless. Today we are fighting for democracy in Canada, and unless we answer the challenge that faces us, I do not see what hope there is for all classes who are suffering from the policy of the government.
I have dealt with the effect of the government's policy on the farmers. Let me mention the veterans. There are two classes of veterans who are hard hit by the action of this government. Last year when we were discussing these various measures in the house, I pointed out that lumber was being allowed to go out

of the country and that the exporters had made a profit of 90-3 per cent. One of my friends-on that occasion asked "What did they pay in taxes?" As far as I am concerned, it is not what they pay in taxes that counts. I submit that so long as we allow unbridled free enterprise to take precedence of human rights and a decent standard of living for the masses we shall have to urge that something be done to help these people.
What about old age pensioners? This government saw fit last year to add $5 to the old age pension, but that was wiped out by the increase in the cost of living. Today the government has a budget surplus running from $925. million to something like one billion, and out of that surplus it is only fair that the older people of the country should receive some additional allowance. The government is taxing people to such an extent that there is a surplus of nearly $1,000 million. Surely it is time we did something on behalf of the older citizens of Canada.
What about the workers? As soon as I heard about the decontrol policy of the government I wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggesting that- if we had increased industrial unrest in Canada the fault could be laid at the door of the federal government. I repeat that today. If we allow the cost of living to go up as it has done during the past months, and particularly since the decontrol measures of the government have come into force, we are bound to have unrest in the country, and there is no solution except for the workers to go on strike or to ask for higher wages. Profits are soaring, and the cost of living is going up with them.
According to the Labour Gazette of October 19, 1947, the cost of living has been going up 2-8 per cent per month. As of October 1, 1947, the cost of living, as measured by official government sources, was 19 per cent higher than in 1945, and the cost of living rose in the three months prior to October 1 by 5-2 per cent. This is having an adverse effect on the whole Canadian economy.
During the war w-e found that of those who were being inducted into the army over forty per cent were suffering from malnutrition. The government decided to put a subsidy on milk, and last year when we asked that the subsidy be continued they flouted the will of parliament and removed it, and this in spite of a large surplus. We find that in 1945-46 according to government figures, food consumption in Canada had dropped 3-5 per cent, and in fluid milk in Ontario alone it had

Transitional Measures Act
fallen 4-5 per cent from September 1946 to September 1947. Now we have another increase effective December 1.
I do not want to labour the point, but profits have increased 60 per cent in 1946 over 1945, and the first seven months of this year show further increases. While this is going on our people are having to buy less and less, and they are worried as to how they are going to make ends meet. I do not say for one moment that we in this group are the only ones concerned about this matter. I know that on all sides of the house there are those who appreciate the difficulties which our people are going through.
I might just say here that even the Prime Minister knows of the difficulties facing our people. In his book which he wrote eighteen years ago, he has this to say:
Humanity has rights superior to those of industry and nationality. For their ultimate solution, industrial and international problems must await the inspiration of a universally accepted faith in human brotherhood . . .
Industry must be thought of not primarily as an arena of competition for material rewards, but as a form of social service . . . Industry must be made to serve humanity; humanity must no longer be sacrificed to the demands of industry.
I can only say to him that to some of us it would appear that is what is going on today, namely, that humanity is suffering in order that profits can be made. During the war and after the war we decried the fact that this government did not have a planned economy. We said that if we were going to swing our war economy into a peacetime economy so that we could have a. rising standard of living for our people, it would be necessary to plan that. But in spite of all our pleadings and admonitions to the contrary, this government saw fit to sell our plants down the river and because of that we find we have rising costs of living. To give just one example, there is the matter of fertilizer. I am not going to speak very long on that matter, but I want to bring it to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture. The farmers' costs are going up, even in the maritimes, where they have to buy a good deal of fertilizer. The cost of ammonium nitrate has gone up from S60 to $91 per ton f.o.b. their stations. The whole difficulty is that today we have an economy predicated on profit and not on human values. I want to appeal to hon. members on all sides of the house. The issue is quite clear. To the political democracy we have we must add some of those things which we fought for, among which are social and economic justice.
If no one interrupts me, Mr. Speaker, I shall be only about fifteen minutes.
Tell us what you are going to say.
That is not a threat.
But if someone should break in, I might take my full forty minutes.

Under this resolution the government is asking for the extension of emergency powers for another three months, until March 31, 1948. That is the only question before the house at the present time. In other words, after the resolution carries, as I believe it will, the government will neither be committed to controls nor pledged to abolishing them, except as was indicated in the blunt statement which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made in another debate. However, our C.C.F. friends seem to have such great confidence in what the government will do that they offer to give the government an extension of emergency powers for the whole year-that is, until December 31, 1948. Such confidence seemed to surprise even the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), but it did not surprise any one in the Social Credit group. To us the reasons are obvious. The leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Low), the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) have, I believe, placed on the record the position of the Social Credit members of parliament on the question of the extension of the emergency powers of the governor in council. I need touch on only a few additional points and perhaps stress several of those that have already been mentioned.
But before dealing with these matters I should like to say, as has already been pointed out, that this group supported the granting of the emergency powers to the government last year and also supported essential controls. We did not support abusive controls, but rather maintained that controls should be exercised over some controllers. On this occasion we take the same stand and favour essential controls. We now have before us the resolution to extend the emergency powers of the government for another three months. I will support the resolution, but may I ask this question: extension of emergency powers to do what? To allow a twelve and half per cent increase in the price of farm machinery? To allow a thirty per cent increase in the already unfair scale of freight rates? To discontinue subsidies on coarse grains, and to lift without
Transitional Measures Act

warning the ceiling on the price of coarse grains? To discontinue subsidies on certain essential foodstuffs? Or, by way of agreements, to keep down the price of everything which the farmer has to sell and to allow the sky to be the limit on the price of articles which the manufacturer has to sell? In a word, what does the government intend to do with these emergency powers? These are questions which the government should answer before the vote is taken.
I should like to say two things with regard to the price of wheat. First, the government's wheat agreement may be adjusted if need be. But what is unfair about the agreement is that the farming population alone stands to lose the difference between the agreement price and the world price, whereas this difference should be borne by the entire nation and not by the wheat grower alone. In the second place I wish to point out that the Canadian wheat grower would not mind receiving for his wheat a price lower than the world market price if he were guaranteed a parity price for farm products in the future. But so far the government has failed to indicate what the farmer may expect in future years. For that reason it is unfair to expect the Canadian farmer to sell his wheat below the world market price.
On Thursday last the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) gave his reasons for lifting the ceilings on coarse grains on October 21 instead of on September 21 as might have been expected. The minister gave us, as an -excuse, the meat strike. But why should the farmers be the losers because of any meat strike? In regard to the lifting of the ceiling on coarse grain, I might also say that the greater number of farmers who were hailed out, or dried out, turned to hog raising. They bought grain, fed it to hogs and had hoped to make ends meet until the next crop year. The government's action has now placed them in bankruptcy. The government should make up this loss to those who suffered by reason of the government's move.
I have two telegrams which I should like to read, indicating the present mood of the farmers. The first is as follows:
Farmers this district strongly protest inadequate returns to livestock producers. Urge increase in prices by subsidies to livestock producers, opening of United States markets and re-negotiation of British contracts.
That is signed by R. Henning, president of the Josephsburg local, United Farmers of

Alberta. The next telegram I want to read, making the same request, is as follows:
Immediate action urged on government to adjust price of livestock in relation to feed grain returns.
That telegram is signed by M. W. Cassidy, of Vegreville. I also have a few newspaper clippings, one of them containing a quotation from the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to the dominion-provincial conference on agriculture, as follows:
I am authorized to state that some action will be taken which will result in prices rising on products fed from grain which will take care in future of the increase brought about in feed costs through the removal of ceilings and withdrawal or drawback of subsidies.
The same newspaper report goes on to say:
It is expected the British contracts will provide for reduced shipments of meats, partly because of an anticipated decline in Canadian production of livestock next year and partly because of Britain's shortage of dollars.
I want you, Mr. Speaker, to keep in mind the phrase "because of Britain's shortage of dollars." Then the article goes on:
This suggestion received support yesterday in London dispatches which quoted informed sources as saying that a complete cut-off in bacon imports from Canada appears in prospect unless new financial arrangements are made with the dominion.
That clipping was from the Edmonton Bulletin of December 3, 1947, and was a Canadian Press dispatch by George Kitchen. The next clipping I should like to quote is taken from the Toronto Evening Telegram of December 12, 1947, and is a Canadian Press dispatch from London:
Canada and Canadian farmers need a gesture from us-
That is, from Britain.
-to convince them that there is something stronger than merely commercial considerations linking the dominion and the mother country.
The final clipping to which I want to refer is from the Ottawa Journal of December 11, 1947. The headline is, "Russia agrees ship grain to Britain." The dispatch states:
Russia has agreed to ship Britain a "substantial quantity" of coarse grains from the 1947 harvest, Harold Wilson, president of the board of trade, announced today.
Then the article goes on to say :
We also agreed that in May next there should be further discussions to prepare long term supply arrangements over a wide range of goods providing for balances in the program of trade between the two countries.

Our aim was to secure a long term balance in trade and financial transactions, and there was no question of payment by either side in hard currency.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that the article I quoted from the Edmonton Bulletin contained the suggestion that the trade agreement as between the United Kingdom and Canada presented a difficulty as far as money was concerned. Now we are told that in the agreements which have been reached and which are likely to be reached in future between the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, money is not an immediate problem. That just goes to prove that if Canada does not keep her head and does not do some serious thinking we are going to lose the best market we ever had. Surely if the people of the United Kingdom need the farm commodities we produce and want to sell, we should be able to find ways and means of reaching an agreement as between the two countries, because some of the other nations are going to take advantage of the present situation. We know that Canada and the United States have been assisting various European countries. We intend to go on giving that assistance, but if we should ever seem to get a little tired of helping these people the Soviet Union may jump into the game and take over that assistance; and of course psychologically that move would appeal to some of the devastated countries of western Europe. That is the thing on which we must keep our eye. Canada can produce large quantities of foodstuffs, and certainly Canada should be able to find ways and means of making this assistance available to other countries.
As was urged in the telegrams I read, prices of farm products should be increased, or subsidized if you wish, in order to spread the load over the entire nation, so that the farmer would not be asked to bear the burden alone.
I might mention briefly another weakness in the policy of the government, and that is in regard to freight rates, a matter which is still before the board of transport commissioners. If the application of the railways is approved it will mean an addition of thirty per cent to present costs. As far as I can judge, the application is not merely for an increase which will apply only for a limited period; I believe it will be extremely difficult, when prices of farm produce fall, to bring freight rates back to any lower level. In that case the farmers will take up the matter again. They will discuss it at their meetings; they will ask members of parliament to speak on it; the whole thing will drag out and it may be years before the freight rates are adjusted.
So much for that point. Another important matter is the price of farm machinery; and here again, when the prices of farm products fall, it will be extremely difficult to convince the machinery companies and the government that prices of farm implements should be reduced so that farmers would be able to buy them.
Then I would say the policy of the government today appears to be to discourage production, though we all know production is perhaps the only solution of the problem of inflation. In my opinion, production is the answer, so should we not do everything within our power to see that production is increased? By the present policies of the government, however, and its agricultural policy in particular, production all across western Canada is being reduced. The objective of the government should be a fair relationship between the prices which the farmer receives for his products and the prices which he has to pay for the things the manufacturer sells to him. That is parity prices; that is what the farmers of western Canada and all over Canada want. The present agricultural policy of the government will result in the liquidation of our agricultural industry.
In closing, I should like to refer to two clippings from the Edmonton Bulletin. The first one reports a convention of the Alberta Farmers' Union which was held in Edmonton during the first week of December. The Edmonton Bulletin of December, 5, 1947, contains this:
The A.F.U. board of directors has been authorized to consider taking the necessary steps to call a grain non-delivery strike if and when necessary, unless certain demands are met.
The resolution also sets up the following five demands be met:
1.	Initial price of wheat be raised to $2 per bushel basis Fort William and Vancouver.
2.	The payment on participation certificates, to be made at the end of each years' operations, and the participation payments for the crop year 1945-46 be made immediately.
3.	If the dominion government wishes to sell cheap grain to the domestic market or the international field, pending the setting up of the fact-finding board and the establishment of parity price, that they subsidize from the dominion treasury, the difference in price between the British wheat agreement and the price paid on the export market.
4.	The Canadian farmers should be paid the market price on domestic sale of wheat and any necessary subsidy paid by the dominion government.
5.	The dominion government set up a national grain board to market all grains, and such a board to have adequate farm representation.
I quote that report in order to point out the dissatisfaction of organized agriculture -with the present trend of affairs.
