I thank the minister for interrupting me, but I think what I am going to say from now on will prove helpful to him. No member wants to see a grain strike, particularly in his own constituency. I would not quarrel so much with a strike instigated in the constituency of the minister, but it so happens that last year a strike was started in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. The result was that the farmers got worked up. There was a lot of dissatisfaction. Neighbour began to hate neighbour and all the rest of. The men who had initiated the whole thing slipped out from under it quite easily, and the feud finally subsided.
I do not want to see a strike. It would not be good for the country. It would not be good for the agricultural industry. It would not be good for the farmers. I urge the government, and particularly the Minister of Agriculture, to do everything possible to find the best possible solution to the problems faced by our farmers at the moment.
In conclusion, I should like to quote a report which appeared in the Edmonton Bulletin of December 2, 1947, referring to a speech by the president of the Alberta farmers' union. I want to put. this on record because I think it expresses the sentiments of organized farmers. The report reads:
Non-delivery strike on grain only, if proposed adjustments in farm produce prices are not affected, was urged Monday at the Alberta farmers' union convention in the Masonic temple.
The price of wheat should be $2 a bushel, basis Fort William, for the 1918 crop, according to C. J. Stimpfle, AFU president, who delivered his official report to the convention.
The AFU head further said, "I maintain we cannot sit idly by and allow producing costs to increase without a corresponding increase in the produce we sell. Therefore I would suggest that this convention set a price for our production and service, and failing to achieve that price, after all other methods have failed, nondelivery of all grain be instituted.
Remember, grain only; I do not think nondelivery of all farm produce can be as effective as on one commodity such as grain, because of its shortage in the world supply.
We are living in an organized society and organized people in this society use this method. That being so, we must use this method too, when all other means fail, whether we like it or not."
I want to leave that statement for the consideration of hon. members and the government. We know that when strikes occur they are not always planned for the benefit of the farmers or of labour. We know that there are individuals who want to foment strikes and

they usually are found among those who lead strikes. I do not say that all those who lead strikes, whether of farmers or of labour, have ulterior motives, but there are those who want to paralyse this country. They want to paralyse the United States; they want to paralyse France; they want to paralyse Italy; they want to paralyse every country in western Europe and on this continent so that their objectives may be achieved. We as a nation are capable of producing all the foodstuffs that are required; we are capable of increasing our production in order to assist Europe in her recovery. It is our duty to see that Great Britain suffers less. It is up to us to do everything we can to see that Great Britain is again placed on her feet.

Mr. Speaker, probably the major part of my remarks would have been more appropriately made on the resolution having to do with the Agricultural Products Act than on this measure, but I am compelled to make them now by representations received from farmers in my constituency and by the fact that the discussion on this resolution has had to do largely with agricultural problems and particularly with the impossible situation in which our livestock producers and feeders now find themselves.
However much the Minister of xigriculture (Mr. Gardiner) may talk around the problem, he and everyone else who is familiar with the livestock industry know that an impossible situation does exist. Subsidies and controls on the prices of coarse grains were removed, resulting in a sharp increase in prices. At the same time the embargo against the export of beef cattle and hogs to the United States markets has been retained. As a result of that and of the price levels of the British meat contracts, the returns to the producer have been held down actually to what the British contracts call- for. That is the practical effect and the situation at the present time. The minister has recognized that things are bad by making a statement to the federation of agriculture that something would be done about the matter, and the farmers of the country, I think, were led to believe that that statement of the minister would be followed' very shortly by another one saying just what would be done. That belief was reinforced by the statement made last week by the minister's parliamentary assistant. The time is long overdue when the anxiety of the livestock producers of this country should be ended. They have been kept in a state of uncertainty too long. The minister should forthwith make a statement on what is to be done to alleviate the situation.

It is futile for the minister to argue, as he did in this house last Thursday, that the price in the British contracts for cattle and hogs is the floor price and not the ceiling price. That is just not so, in my opinion. It is quite true that these contracts give a floor price, but it is mere quibbling on the part of the minister to say that the floor price is not, for all practical purposes, at the same time the ceiling price.
Half a cent a pound.

The minister said something about half a cent a pound. But the fact is that, as long as we are producing more cattle and hogs than we can consume ourselves, and the only buyer for our surplus is the government, the price it pays is, in effect, the ceiling price. There may be half a cent a pound difference between the ceiling and the floor price. The packers are willing to pay a small amount over the ceiling price in order to induce supplies to come on to the market so as to keep their plants in operation. But it is mere quibbling on the part of the minister to say that it is a floor price only for any increase over that price that is paid by the packers is insignificant.
One thing further I would say. The policy of the government and the situation it has produced will rapidly convert the price into a floor price absolutely through the rapid killing off of breeding stock and young animals. Next year, unless the situation is corrected rapidly, we shall see very much higher prices for livestock because of the destruction of a large part of our livestock industry.
The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), myself and several other members of this party have repeatedly urged the government to help the situation to some extent by removing the embargo on beef cattle shipments to the United States. We have urged that ever since we have been in this house. We urge it to a large extent from the point of view of retaining for the producers of this country what the minister himself has admitted in this house is the natural market for Canadian beef over the years, when the present more or less unnatural situation disappears and Great Britain can again secure her beef supplies from the Argentine or elsewhere.
There is at the moment an added and urgent reason why the embargo should be lifted. Livestock returns must be increased if the ndustry is to be preserved in a healthy condition. What have the farmers themselves to say on this question? I should like to read a telegram which was handed to me on Friday 5849-19
evening as I was sitting here. It is from Okotoks, the largest town in the rural part of my constituency:
Okotoks U.F.A. unanimously request lifting embargo on cattle to U.S. market. We request immediate action.
Okotoks U.F.A.
So much for the U.F.A. I have also had sent to me, and it arrived on Friday last, the program of the sixth annual convention of the Alberta farmers' union which was held at Edmonton, December 1 to 5, 1947. Reference was made to that a few moments ago by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka). One of the resolutions which was carried at that convention reads:
Whereas livestock yards here are glutted, and an adverse relationship to feed costs exists, and
Whereas there is a shortage of U.S. currency which can only be met by the sale of Canadian goods to the U.S.A., and
Whereas dominion goverment policy has tended to decrease the production of livestock, and
Whereas the manufacturers of lumber, nails, and wire, etc. have been allowed to avail themselves of higher market conditions in the U.S.A. regardless of domestic requirements.
Therefore be it resolved that we ask the dominion government to immediately lift the embargo on the shipment of livestock to the U.S.A.
There are several other resolutions on the program along the same line, so the minister can no longer maintain that the farmers and livestock producers do not want this embargo lifted, or that they are not very anxious to have access to the United States market.
During the past two years the Minister of Agriculture has always contended in this house and throughout the country that everything was rosy in the agriculture picture, that the policies followed by this government were aimed at producing a stable and prosperous agriculture, and, furthermore, that the farmers and their organizations were behind these policies and supported them, and so forth. But the representations I have just referred to and everything said in this house in the last few days regarding the livestock situation is conclusive evidence that the farmers of this country no longer have confidence in the livestock and agriculture policies of this government.
The fact that the farmers have not confidence in the government's policy on wheat is also quite apparent. The hon. member for Vegreville read to the house the resolution passed by the Alberta farmers' union in connection with a threatened strike unless grain prices were increased. I shall not read that again but I would just comment that the program of the convention of the Alberta

farmers' union is endorsed by twelve districts and over 200 locals. There are only twelve districts in the union, so that it is endorsed by them all. I think the last thing we want in this country is another non-delivery strike. I do not want to go into the 1946 strike except to say that in my opinion it was ill-advised and a mistake. But certainly it was a disturbing event, and it should have served as a warning to the government and to the urban population of Canada of what the effect is likely to be if the farmers are pushed too far in the matter of prices. If the farmers of this country got together and called a non-delivery strike I do not need to elaborate on what the results would be. By the strike in Alberta they demonstrated that they are capable of doing it if they are pushed too far, if they are made too angry -and they certainly have been made angry at the present time. They are getting angrier all the time. I would suggest that the government take immediate steps to alleviate that anger so that we do not get on our hands a delivery strike by the farmers. That would really be a strike to end all strikes.
The statements of the Minister of Agriculture in connection with all these matters have always sounded very well. I am a great admirer of his ability to make a good-sounding case out of very poor material. However, the more I listen to him, the more I am reminded of a story of an old rancher in our part of the country. He had a ranch away out west of Calgary where the big hills sort of merge gradually into the small mountains, and he conceived the idea that the best type of cattle for that country would be some of the Highland cattle, long haired and so forth, which originated in the same spot as the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie). He imported some of these cattle and had them running out there. Not so very long afterwards a livestock dealer from Calgary called on him. The temperature was about thirty degrees below zero. It was an extremely bitter day. In the course of the conversation he said, "Well, Mr. S. how are your Highland cattle getting along?" The reply was, "Oh, they are getting along all right." The dealer said, "I understand that they are very hardy cattle, and that they can stand the cold much better than anything else." The rancher said, "Yes, they are hardy. Look, there is one of them up on that hill right now cooling off." That is an example of the minister's statements. In fact, when I hear one of them I always think, "There is another of those 'bull on the hill statements' ". He should bring this type of thing to an end and,

as I said a while ago, make a definite statement as to what is to be done to put the livestock industry back on its feet.
They usually make you warm up instead of cooling down.
You know, cattle can't swim.

For a few moments I should like to turn to the statements that have been made here in regard to prices and the high cost of living. I agree that the cost of living is too high for a considerable number of our people. It is too high in relation to their income. The people to whom I refer particularly are those on fixed incomes, the disability pensioners, and more especially the people on the so-called burnt-out pension. It is within this government's power to correct that situation, and they should exercise that power by increasing these pensions or by granting a cost of living bonus to these pensioners, and it should be done forthwith. There are other people who are sufferers from the high prices. There are the old age pensioners, in fact pensioners of any kind. There are many pensioners who receive their pensions from private sources. Many of them are just as hard hit as anybody else, and together with the so-called white-collar workers, store clerks, and people of that kind, they are the people who are suffering most.
A more realistic approach than that of the C.C.F. is necessary to this problem. I can see no use whatever in presenting, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) did, a neat little theorem in connection with this problem along these lines; that the rate of wages has not risen as much as the cost of living has increased, and that therefore wages must be increased. Presenting this little theorem, supported by a large number of statistics, many of which could be used to prove the opposite if you put them on a little different basis, is not going to get us anywhere. I suggest, first of all, that real wages can be increased only if production per man hour is increased. That is the only way in which real wages can be improved. I suggest that it would be much more helpful, if you are going to make calculations along these lines, to make them on this basis,-how much have wages increased per unit of production as compared with the cost of living? In other words, what is now the labour cost for laying 100 bricks, for turning out a ton of steel, for producing an automobile or anything else that one might mention? If you relate labour costs to any article which is produced

and the increase which has taken place in the labour cost to the increase in the cost of living, I suggest that you will find a very different picture from the one presented by the C.C.F. I suggest, further, that that essentially is the difficulty which we see in England at the present time. The production per man hour is not sufficiently great-I am not going to go into what the reasons may be-and therefore a great many of their economic difficulties stem from that. Similarly I am convinced that a great deal of the outcry over the cost of living in Canada and the fact that it is out of proportion to the wages of our people stems from the same fact, that the labour cost per article produced has been too great. The greatest complaint at the present time along this line is over the increase in food prices.
I should like to say right now that a great deal of the outcry is due to the fact that the urban population has become accustomed, through the depression years and since, to relatively low food prices, and naturally they would like to see these low food prices retained. Who would not? The C.C.F. party, of course, have been trying to make political capital out of that fact and, as usual, have been trying to stand on both sides of the fence, with the constantly reiterated cry that food prices and cost of living must come down, at the same time saying to the farmers that the price for their products must go up. Well, you just cannot have it both ways. What they are doing is trying to propagate the old unreasonable view that you can have your cake and eat it too. It is impossible. Still, that idea fools a lot of people. I suggest that we look at the thing. Are agricultural prices too high? Would any hon. member rise in his place and say that prices received for agricultural products by their producers are too high? I do not think a single hon. member would say it. I am sure that he would not. In fact nearly everyone here would say that prices of farm products are too low. If they are too low-and I think they are, as shown by the low average income received by farmers across the country-then the food price is too low in relation to the cost of production rather than too high, and food prices should go higher rather than lower, if you look at it from that point of view. I am not saying that they should go higher; but, as I say, to relate the thing to the cost of production, then they should be higher The only way in which you can bring these two opposite things together, to give the farmer a high price for hi? ?;oods, his food 5849-19J
products, and to supply them to the consumer at a low price, is by way of subsidies or something of that nature. There is just no other way it can be done. Somebody has to pay the difference between the two.
I should like to point out that there is a great fallacy in subsidies and it is this. They must be paid for, plus the cost of administering, which is always very great. There may be situations in which a subsidy on food prices is justified as a temporary measure. I think there are situations of that kind, but I should like to point out the fact that any subsidy which you pay means in the long run a higher cost for food or anything else for the people of Canada as a whole, because they must pay the extra cost of administration which enters into it; in addition to which there result many inequities to both consumers and producers. One of the greatest complaints with regard to the high cost of living and the rise in food prices has to do with the price of milk. We have heard that brought out by many members of the C.C.F. particularly, who refer to starving children and so forth. I should like to discuss the subsidy on milk by way of illustration of what it would cost to subsidize all food products and other items entering into the cost of living.
May I suggest a neat little scheme which the government could put into effect to alleviate the worst of the cries about the high cost of living-the price of milk. As a palliative, and an immediate means of helping people with low incomes, and having families to support, the government might issue, with the family allowance cheque, a monthly allowance of thirty milk tickets, or thirty-one as the case might be per child, each of them worth, say, five cents. [DOT] If the recipient wanted a quart of milk, supposing the price to be, let us say, fifteen cents, he would put in one ticket with ten cents into his bottle. The only expense in connection with this scheme would be the cost of printing the tickets and issuing cheques to milk distributors. The family allowance cheques are sent out anyway, and that would be all that would be required. The milk distributor would send in his tickets. If he sent in 1,000, he would get a cheque representing five cents per ticket or whatever amount might be decided upon by way of subsidy. Furthermore, as regards those who pay income tax, the whole thing could be collected back from them. They merely pay it back with their income tax. This would be a means of subsidizing the really low-income class of people who have children, and it would be a useful scheme whereby the

I do not intend to take up much time this afternoon. I shall simply deal with two problems that have come to my attention over the week end, both having to do with the matter of price control. The government has taken a definite stand with respect to its future policy on price control. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) advised us that it could oe only by means of a completely controlled and completely directed economy that we jould re-institute price control.
Over the week end I received a telegram from local 695 of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers at Sheridan, Man., and its 284 members to go on record as being entirely in favour of re-establishing price controls on the basic necessities of life. Before coming to Ottawa, the matter of rising prices was discussed with a number of dairy managers who operate throughout my constituency. These men reminded me that, since the abolition of the producer subsidy on milk, and with the great increases which have taken place in the cost of living since midsummer, the consumption of milk has gone down noticeably. They advise that families who in the past consumed between three and four quarts of milk a day now buy from two to three quarts. They expressed the opinion that the reason for the reduction in the consumption of milk is that their purchasing power is not sufficient to enable them to make further purchases.
The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), who spoke a few moments ago,

stated that one of the reasons for not increasing wages in this country was that production per man hour had not gone up. The Minister of Finance, in his budget address last year, informed the House of Commons that over half the workers in Canada received wages which were insufficient to bring them within any income tax bracket. It is these people who find the increasing cost of living a very difficult problem with which to cope.
The increases we have experienced in the cost of living over the past six months are something which greatly concerns the people of the country, and that is why I am taking a few minutes now to bring the opinions of my c-onsituents before the house.
There is one other matter with which I wish to deal, and that is coarse grains. In the fall of this year the government placed coarse grains on the open market and within a very short time the market price for these grains increased approximately thirty cents a bushel. Prior to this, many farm organizations in the west had requested the government to state its policy with respect to coarse grains for the present crop year. When no statement was forthcoming many farmers took it for granted that the policy then in effect would continue for the rest of the crop year. The result was that many of them marketed coarse grains one or two days before the new policy was announced. They lost as much as thirty cents a bushel. Farmers in my area alone lost as much as from SSOO to $1,800 each, and it is needless to say that they were not very well satisfied with the policy of the government.
But there is another matter in that connection that should be brought to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and also to the attention of the cabinet, because I believe the cabinet was interviewed with regard to it. A large number of farmers in Saskatchewan were adversely affected and the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan, the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), flew to Ottawa to have the situation looked into. On his return to Saskatchewan he reported to the Western Producer that action would be taken by the government which would reimburse these fanners for at least a part of the losses they suffered because of the government's new coarse grain policy. I am sure the farmers of western Canada are interested to know if it is still the intention of the government to remunerate them for the losses they suffered because of the sudden reversal of policy by the government with respect to the marketing of coarse grains.

Mr. Speaker, keeping in mind the limited amount of time we have before Christmas, I will endeavour to make my remarks short.
Speaking as a representative of the farmers in my constituency-and I say we have the right to consider ourselves among the best farmers in the west-I wish to emphasize here that in the constituency I represent we have never had to lean on the shoulders of anyone.
There is one aspect of the emergency powers as to which I wish to say a few words. It is the considered view of my constituents that the trading in coarse grains should be taken over by the wheat board; and, should a fluctuating market prevail, the western farmers are of the opinion that it should be carried on under the wheat board with a stabilized initial price; and profits, if any, distributed at the end of the year among those who have marketed their grain.
I feel sure that the official opposition will concur in this, for their leader (Mr. Bracken), speaking in this house on February 24, 1917, as reported at page 758 of Hansard said, "I do not oppose the board taking over coarse grains"; although at the time he was very careful to guard himself and his party against the definite closing of the Winnipeg grain exchange.
I am not a lawyer and I do not propose to say how this marketing should be achieved, but my impression is that it requires only a few strokes of a pen by a good legal draftsman to amend the existing legislation; and perhaps the deletion of the words "wheat or wheat products" wherever these words are used, in part 4 of chapter 15 of the statutes of 1947, would have the necessary results, these deleted words to be replaced by the word "grain" as defined in the 1947 legislation referred to. It could even be done in other ways, such as by an order in council, but in any event it should be done immediately. I am sure that there will be agreement from all members of western Canada, and I am sure the results from such marketing would certainly help our farmer neighbours in eastern Canada. By this action we would definitely close the Winnipeg grain exchange.
According to Sir John Boyd Orr, the present food shortage will continue for many years. We must not deceive ourselves that it will end with the 1948 harvest. The reason for that is the anticipated increase of the population of the world, which will be forty million from May 8, 1945. Therefore food production will have to be increased by 110 per cent in the next twenty-five years.
The marketing of wheat by the wheat board and the marketing of coarse grains under the same board, if permitted-and it must be so- must continue long after August 1, 1950, when the present legislation expires. It is unfair and unjust to permit the trading of any grain or foodstuffs by any group who can rig the world food market.
I therefore repeat that if the government has the power under the present resolution to continue the present control over the trading in wheat, it may as well have it with respect to coarse grains; and if the amendments I advocate can be instituted in the present statute, if the government has not the control at the present time it should take the necessary steps to do it now.
Speaking in the house on December 11 last, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said, as reported in Hansard at page 214:
The fact is that on October 21 and down to the present the government has had no authority to place oats and barley under the control of the wheat board.
I would therefore strongly and firmly suggest that, in the best interests of the Canadian farmer and of Canada as a whole, the authority should be taken as soon as possible and steps taken at the same time to prohibit the trading in grain by any Canadian grain exchange.

At this time. Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with some of the remarks made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) the other night. Before doing that, however, I wish to say a few words about the whole question of price control. It seems to me that the government has failed in its price control policy in at least two ways.	First of all, I
believe it has failed to listen to the voice of the Canadian people. There can be no argument as to the fact that the people of Canada desire price control at this time; and there eannoc be any argument either, as to the fact that, because there has not been price control, we have seen the sad spectacle of run-away prices. The other way in which I believe the government has failed is with respect to carrying out what it said was its declared policy, namely, the removal of price controls in such a manner as not to cause a drastic increase in the cost of living. Because of this failure, we see the spectacle of increasing prices from one day to the next.
There can be no argument as to the fact that the policy of decontrol has not helped the average Canadian. On the contrary, the
Transitional Measures Act

policy of decontrol has helped big business. I say that it is the duty of any democratic government to listen to the people whom it represents. It seems to me that at this time the administration is not running the country as much as big business is running it. That can be seen easily by the results of the policies the government has undertaken. In a period of inflation people suffer because they cannot buy the necessities of life in the way and in the quantity they should be able to buy them. At this time many people cannot afford an adequate diet. They cannot afford to wear proper clothing. They have not sufficient money to provide themselves with proper shelter. But of those three things, I believe the fact that so many people cannot afford a proper diet is the most appalling. In a country such as Canada, a country which produces such huge quantities and varieties of food, the government, at least in the field of food, should have kept prices down.
Out of the Department of National Health and Welfare there came a bulletin which stated that the people of Canada should be drinking twenty-five per cent more milk. I am sure the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) would agree with that statement; but while his department is saying the people of Canada need twenty-five per cent more milk, the Department of Finance, through its decontrol policy, is making certain that the people do not get even as much milk as in the last few j'ears. According to a report in the press, when milk prices increased in Toronto dealers in that city admitted that their sales had dropped by from twenty to twenty-five per cent.
The same thing is true in regard to the price of butter, which went up from fifty to seventy cents a pound when the government discontinued the subsidies on coarse grain. The farmer who produced the cream that went into the production of the butter did not get all the benefits of that price increase. The business organizations which manufacture butter were able to reap a profit of twenty cents on each pound of butter they had in storage. The same thing happened when the government implemented its so-called austerity program; prices of vetgetables increased by from twenty to 120 per cent, but the farmer did not get the benefit of that price increase. He had marketed his vegetables long before, and it was only the great wholesale houses and the dealers who stood to make that profit.
I think we can all agree that during the war years the government's price control policy

was pretty successful. From 1944 to 1945 the cost of living, according to the official index, went up less than one point. I believe one reason for that small increase was the policy then followed by the government of paying subsidies and carrying on over-all price control. During the war people of Canada were asked to invest in victory bonds. The people rallied to their government in time of need and invested in those bonds. In the advertisements published during those campaigns the people were asked to invest in this way in order to prevent inflation, and were told that if they did so they could be sure there would be no inflation in this country. In 1945 the Liberal party went to the people on a program of no inflation. An article sent out by the Liberal party under date of May 15, 1945, appeared in the press under the heading, "Liberal policy will create post-war opportunities for all." That was part of the program of the Liberal party at the last general election, and this is what the article had to say:
Jobs! Jobs with bright futures for the young men and women coming out of the armed services with the best part of their lives before them. Jobs for all. Jobs with big prospects and good reliable money that will keep its buying power. After all the hard work, sacrifice, and self-discipline which has brought us through the war, the people of this country have earned a brighter future in a better, juster, grander Canada than we have ever known.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the government has not kept faith with the people of Canada; that it has not implemented its election program which promised jobs with big prospects and good reliable money that would keep its purchasing power. So far this year the cost of living has gone up some fifteen points, and has increased by twenty-three points since 1945. Truly today inflation is with us, and I submit that it is time the government obeyed the will of the majority of our people. It is time it implemented its own election program; it is time controls were reimposed, so that the people who invested in victory bonds will not find the purchasing power of that investment dwindling from day to day.

Only the other day I saw a forecast in the Financial Post that gasoline is to take another jump of from one and a half to two and a half cents a gallon.
The farmer believes, and rightly so, that when his costs go up that increase is permanent. When there is a slump in the prices he receives he finds that his costs do not go down at the same rate. A number of tariff reductions were announced recently. I believe any tariff reduction is a step in the right direction. The tariff on tea was reduced from eight to two cents a pound and on coffee from three to two cents a pound. However, those reductions in tariff were not reflected in reduced prices. The distributors absorbed the tariff reductions as increased profits.
All increases in the cost of production to the farmer and all increases in his cost of living should lead to necessary changes in the government's wheat policy. The leader of this party, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), when speaking the other day referred to the statement that had been made when we were discussing the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement, namely, that the C.C.F. advocated the payment to the farmer, out of the public treasury, of any increase in production costs that had taken place since the signing of that contract.
I shall now turn to the government's coarse grain policy. The head of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Mr. Hannam, is reported in the Rural Co-operator of November 11, as having said:
Nothing that has happened in Canadian agriculture in many years has stirred farmers throughout the dominion to such a high pitch of resentment as has the recent action of the dominion government in removing ceilings and subsidies from coarse grains at this particular time. i
I was pleased to note that apparently the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) felt that this issue was important enough to warrant the major speech which he made in the
house the other night. When I commenced my remarks before six o'clock the minister was in his seat and I stated that I was going to deal with some of the things he had said. I believe he left two veiy important questions unanswered. First, where does the minister stand with respect to the Winnipeg grain exchange? Does he or does he not believe in the speculative sale of farm products through the grain exchange? He did not say. I am forced to the conclusion that he supports the Winnipeg grain exchange method of handling coarse grain because he said nothing at all with reference to the action taken on October 21.
He did not state to what extent, if any, farmers who had sold grain prior to October 21 and thus had lost a good deal of money would be compensated. He did take some time to attempt to show that prices of coarse grains were properly in line with the price of wheat, but in making that argument he assumed that the correct price for wheat at this time is $1.55 a bushel. I do not think that assumption is altogether fair. When one considers the price of wheat going into domestic consumption, the price of wheat going to Great Britain under the contract and the price of No. 2 wheat, one will realize that the average price which will be received by the wheat board for the 1947-48 crop is more likely to be closer to $2 a bushel than to $1.55. If that is true, then, if we take the minister's own argument, prices of oats and barley are still too low.
If we assume that the price of wheat is $2 a bushel, then the ceiling price of barley should not be $1.25, as the minister stated, but rather $1.61. The ceiling price of oats should not be ninety-two cents, but rather $1.19. It seems to me that, in making his statement, the minister forget one important relationship. It is not good enough to relate oats and barley only to the price of wheat; there should be a fair relationship between prices of oats and barley and prices of hogs and beef. If there was some semblance of a fair relationship before October 21, then there is no fair relationship today. The proof that there is no fair relationship is shown by the fact that farmers who raised hogs for years are now going out of hog production as rapidly as possible.
It is time that the government gave producers of livestock a price that was fair in relation to the price of coarse grains. The present price of coarse grains represents a serious blow to the livestock industry. If immediate steps are not taken either to

increase prices or to reinstate the subsidy on coarse grains the livestock industry of this country will dwindle to an insignificant point.
I should like to deal with the situation which prevailed in western Canada this fall before the government's policy on coarse grains was announced on October 21. The argument was made by the Minister of Agriculture that the farmers of Canada had a reasonably good idea of what the government was going to do. The fact is that the farmers delivered more oats and barley from August 1 to October 21 in this crop year than they did during the same period in the previous crop year.
If these farmers had known they were going to lose thirty cents a bushel on their barley they certainly would not have marketed their grain. But this was the situation. There was no quota against oats and barley at the elevator delivery points, but there was a quota on wheat of about ten bushels per seeded acre at most delivery points. Barley is always harvested before the wheat crop, and the farmer knew he would have to save his storage space on the farm for wheat on which there was a quota, so he delivered his oats and barley to his local elevator. The fact that there was no quota on oats and barley was directly part of government policy. The government was saying to the farmer, "Come on, boys; deliver your oats and barley so that you will have room on your farm to store your wheat". And, as a colleague beside me says, the Winnipeg grain exchange made a handsome gain on that account.
The Minister of Agriculture, in the course of his remarks on Thursday last, said at page 212 of Hansard:
During the last session provision was only made for continuing these drawbacks until August 1, and everyone surmised from this that the controls would probably be taken off on August 1.
He is saying there that everyone knew that the government was going to take these controls off on August 1. But in the next paragraph he has changed his mind and the farmers no longer know the government's policy, for he says:
It was only the uncertainty as to whether or not prices would be changed on August 1 that caused the grain to be delivered, together with the fact that throughout the whole period of control, both before and after the act, farmers had been treated ill a way which those who might desire to do so could justify as being reasonable.
"As being reasonable"; what does that mean?

I do not know, I am sure. In the third paragraph the minister again changed his mind. He has decided once again that the farmers do know the government's policy. He says:
An intimation was given to the people of Canada at that time-
Namely, August 1:
-that, in addition to what had been voted during last session, sufficient funds would be provided to take care of any drawbacks for a two months' period; and the statement was also made at that time that the controls ought .to be taken off at the same time.

I also say I do not believe a member of the government party outside of the cabinet knew what the government policy was going to be. It was a deviating, vacillating policy which changed from day to day and month to month, and certainly the farmers could not be expected to follow a policy of that kind. The farmers all this time believed, and they had good reason to believe, that should the subsidies be taken off and the controls removed, they would be compensated wholly for any change in price.
On March 17. in the House of Commons, the Minister of Agriculture said at page 1408 of Hansard, in what he deemed to call a statement in regard to the production of coarse grains in 1947:
In order to avoid discrimination against producers who have already delivered barley during the present crop year an adjustment payment will be made of ten cents per bushel in respect of deliveries between August 1,	1946, and

There are four general principles that should be laid down to express the will of the federal riding of Lethbridge. First, the cost of living must come diown. Second, prices of feed and of livestock and of livestock products must be established and maintained at such relationship that producers will be encouraged to produce buoyantly and abundantly. Third, farmers as a class must not be obliged to bear more than a fair share of the burdens resulting from national policy. Fourth, there must be introduced into Canada's agricultural policy such a degree of consistency and stability as will give farmers confidence in agriculture.
Farmers throughout my constituency feel that in the case of the British-Canadian wheat agreement they were required to pay out of their pockets what the whole Dominion of Canada ought to have paid in order to guar-

antee the British consumer wheat at a reasonable price. They do not believe that kind of thing should continue.
The removal of the ceilings on coarse grains was obnoxious to the people in my constituency. It injured our hog raisers, our dairymen and our poultry producers beyond measure. The sugar policy of Canada must be revised. This is the first time in this debate the beet sugar industry has been mentioned, but inasmuch as sugar control comes under the act now being discussed, it seems appropriate that I say a few words with respect to that industry on this occasion.

So much depends upon the answers to three questions: First, how much non-empire cane raws has been or will be purchased by Canada for 1948, and at what prices, and at what average price?
It is reported that already Canada has bought the Dominican crop at 85 per hundred weight. At the same time it is reported that Holland has bought 10,000 tons from Mexico at 84 per hundredweight. This tends to indicate how uncertain the sugar market is even now, and consequently how uncertain, according to these words I am discussing, the situation may be for producers of sugar beets in 1948.
Second, how much empire cane raws has been or will be purchased by Canada for 1948, and at what prices, and at what average price?
And, third, does the Canadian government propose during 1948 to buy all cane raws through a government agency or will certain Canadian private enterprises be permitted to buy on the world market where prices of sugar might seriously fall?
To indicate how serious the fall might be, may I point out that the evidence which is coming to hand, or which has already come to hand, indicates that for the year 1947-48 there will be more sugar produced by those areas supplying the peoples of North America than those peoples will be able to use. I quote from "Sugar Facts Extra" of December 9, 1947, one sentence:
Making allowance for the natural increase in consumption, it can be seen that, with over 13 million tons in the offing, there is more than enough sugar available for North America during the coming year.
Such being the case, it is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that there could be a rapid fall in the price of cane sugar. From the results of this fall our beet sugar producers must have protection. Empire producers of cane raws must receive their $1 preference. If not, then the importer of empire cane raws will be getting his sugar with a duty of twenty-nine cents, whereas the importer from non-empire sources will be having to pay $1.29 for his sugar. It is quite obvious that the refinery importing empire sugar and paying only twenty-nine cents is going to have a distinct advantage over others in the country and is going to have a particular advantage over the beet producers. This fact is likely to deprive the beet producers of fifty cents per hundred of their normal protection. This would be the minimum. If a very much larger percentage of sugar is imported from empire countries than is imported from non-empire countries, then the beet producer will be deprived of more and more, perhaps up to seventy cents

per hundred, of his normal protection against cane sugar from outside. If normal protection is denied the beet-grower he must be compensated by subsidy.
I ask the minister to answer at an early day, the questions which I have asked so that the house may have in its possession information upon which to base its judgment concerning the way in which the dominion, government proposes to manage the sugar industry of Canada during the year 1948. When the minister answers those questions, I shall have some further observations to make.

Hymie Margolis,

There is also to be considered the matter of the development of the milk business. If you go back to conditions twenty-eight or thirty years ago, you will remember that you heard the rattle of the milk wagon, went out with your container and obtained what milk you wanted. At that time distributors' costs were not very great. But, later on, bottles were introduced, and then wax containers, all of which has gradually added to the expense>
of the distributor. We now find five or six different wagons going down the same street, all selling 3-5 or 3-6 milk, depending on the province you are in. Some of the creameries are owned by the one outfit, but they still have different wagons on the street selling milk in competition with one another. Then also there are different kinds of milk. All this has added to the cost of distribution. Then there is advertising that we did not need in the old days. All that has to be paid for. Somebody must pay for it. The distributor does not want to pay for it; the milk producer does not want to pay for it, and the consumer wants cheap milk. So we are caught in a vise. The farmer cannot produce milk unless he gets paid for it, nor can a man distribute it unless he is paid for it. Therefore some other way must be found of dealing with this situation. It will be necessary to have the distribution of milk dealt with municipally or provincially. But the people cannot pay any more for milk than they are paying today. What has aggravated the milk situation is that during the war people bought milk for ten cents a quart.
It is now eighteen cents a quart in Toronto.

It is unfortunate that such a valuable commodity and such a balanced food as milk should have reached such a price. But

The Minister of National Health and Welfare says that everyone should have a quart of milk a day, but people cannot buy that much milk on the wages they are being paid. If you have a small family like mine you may be able to do it, but if you have a good-sized Scotch or French family you just cannot buy enough quarts of milk with the wages you make. However, personally I am very glad to have come three thousand miles, if only to say two things. One is to assure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that I am waiting for his announcement on feed grains. The other announcement I should like to hear before we leave is as to what steps the government intend to take in regard to increasing the allowances to the various classes of war pensioners in Canada. I sincerely hope that before we go home for Christmas we shall have a statement in that regard. I am quite sure that all the members of the government are kindly men, and that they will feel much better when they sit down to their Christmas dinners if they feel they have done the right thing in this very important instance.
1 imagine, too, that other hon. members are receiving a great many telegrams and letters, as I am, in regard to price control. I know we are all very much concerned with the drastic increase in living costs here in Canada, particularly as it affects those in the fixed income groups. I am inclined to agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), however, that any over-all reimposition of price controls would be most difficult to carry out at the present time. Looking around the government departments here, I for one cannot imagine where on earth you would find room for one more desk to put one extra stenographer at work if we set up such an organization. I also agree that it would be most difficult for a trading nation like Canada, which has to import and export so much, to keep prices of commodities in this country very much below world prices. Just for the minister's consideration, however, I was wondering if it might be possible for us to control undue or unwarranted price increases by setting up a price spreads board. Such a board would require to have power to present a report to the minister, and then there should be some teeth in the legislation, which would permit the minister to take action in the courts in any case in which undue profits were working against the public interest. Actually I do not think the threats we have heard from the government in this regard are sufficient to deter certain unscrupulous operators who may move into our commodity fields.

The statements made so far by the minister would indicate that the government is trying hard to get away entirely from the payment of subsidies. I have not convinced myself that that is entirely wise. I was of the opinion that for many reasons the government should not have abandoned its subsidies on milk, flour and bread products. The government is committed to the payment of family allowances and it is prepared to go certain lengths in redistributing wealth in Canada. I was wondering if it would not be possible to include a few milk and bread tickets with the family allowance, veterans payments and old age pensions cheques that are sent out. They would go to the right people and in that way the subsidy would be selective. It might be an excellent thing to slip in a couple of extra tickets with the old age pension cheques that go out in Saskatchewan. They probably need them.

remote part of the riding and was unable personally to welcome him. I always felt that the hon. member had a great intellect and I think it most unfortunate that his outlook is somewhat circumscribed, possibly due to a too long residence in Saskatchewan and recently here in Ottawa.
The Albernis are perhaps the most advanced industrial towns in Canada and I am sure that the hon. member must have been impressed with the prosperity that was visible there. And the biggest strike.

It was
probably a humbling experience for him, as well as educational, to compare that mill to the little box factory he lelt in Saskatchewan. I realize that things are not perfect and that there are still certain injustices under our social system. There seems to be tendency on their part to try to gain political prestige by preaching a class struggle or something like that. That is entirely wrong. Probably I have been in Canada too long, but I have never seen evidence of the existence of a class or caste system in this country. It has always appeared to me that that is a form of mental escape for those who have not the vision and courage which one must have to get ahead under our system of society.
I am extremely sorry that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was not able to stay longer

in Alberni. I should have liked to take him along the west coast where there is probably the greatest undeveloped and richest frontier still remaining in Canada. You are invited.

I am not referring to propaganda machines because all political parties have those. There must be a socialist calculating machine down there. It is really amazing how they will take concrete facts from the Financial Post, put them through the machine and turn out the greatest bunch of political hamburgers you have ever seen to feed to the boys in the back concessions. They are so astute in so many ways that I am amazed they do not save the facts and figures that they get from this machine for the back concessions. I was very much interested in the figures which the

leader of the C.C.F. party put on Hansard by unanimous consent, showing the increased profits different companies had made. I think he tried to leave the impression with the house that a certain percentage of those increased profits necessarily was the answer to the percentage increase in the cost of the goods. I think the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar is far too intelligent and far too honest to try to make such an approach, particularly to the House of Commons. Most people have not an analytical mind such as he has, and probably many people will draw a wrong conclusion. If he was really trying to convey information to the house I could not help wondering how much more helpful it would have been if, in taking the profits of a bread company, for instance, which had shown increased profits, probably due to legitimate reasons such as an increased volume of sales, he had divided those profits by the number of loaves of bread which the company had distributed during the year and, instead of leaving the impression with uninformed people in the back concessions that the three or five cents increase in the price of a loaf of bread was due to inordinate profits that the company had made, he had shown the increased volume of sales and that the increased profits represented undoubtedly a very small fraction of a cent of increase in the price of a loaf of bread.
I hold no brief for big business. I have never been associated with it myself. But I am particularly grateful for the prosperity we have in my riding, which in very large measure is due to the fact that large capital has come in and invested its money and created jobs at high wages for the people I have the honour to represent.
I noticed among the figures which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar put on Hansard he listed the profits of British Columbia Packers. That happens to be a company with which I am very familiar. With most of the senior executives I was associated as a fisherman twenty years ago on the British Columbia coast. They have all come up the hard way themselves, and they are very able men in the fish business and very decent men. I just could not imagine them trying to grind down the faces of the poor or trying to make inordinate profits out of their misfortunes. I do not believe it is in their character to do it.
I managed this m-orning to get hold of the company's 1946 balance sheet. Keta salmon is the cheapest kind of salmon we pack in British Columbia. I have sold it myself for one-half cent a pound, and in those days the

The profit represents only 2'2 per cent of the value of the total net sales for the year. This profit of one dollar for each forty-six dollars of production at sale value is insufficient having regard to the large amount of capital invested and the risks incurred in a business wherein millions of dollars must be expended in preparation for a fish run which in volume may prove to be far below expectations, and in which a year's production normally acquired within a short season and subject to decline, must be carried for comparatively long periods.
It is interesting to note that there was an increase between 1945 and 1946 of $9,637,000 in sales value. The company sold that much more product in 1946 than in 1945. Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of dwelling at length on this matter, important though it be. I merely wish to present to the house, and more particularly to the government and to the honourable minister of agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) a specific request on behalf of eastern farmers, and more specifically on behalf of the constituency I am privileged to represent in the house.
We have learned from previous speeches and from the press, of the demands being voiced all over the country. It is my belief that the eastern farmers also expect their demands to be voiced in this bouse, so that the government may act as soon as possible, as they hope it will, in adjusting the price of feed grains.
I know that in requesting that subsidies be restored or that controls become once more a part of our policy, we touch upon a very difficult subject, and one that arouses great enthusiasm in a large number of politicians. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that even if it were necessary, in order to meet the needs of the farmers in my district as regards mill feed, to restore some controls, I would heartily support such action, as I have always done, and I have clearly indicated my stand in that connection. I shall support whatever control is necessary or any control which may help farmers in the raising of cattle.
I have had the opportunity of meeting many delegations from the county of Portneuf, especially those associations representing l'Union Catholique des Cultivateurs. Almost all parishes in my constituency have sent delegations to meet me, and I communicated at that time-that was about two months ago -with the Right Hon. the Minister of Agri-

culture with a view to obtaining a price readjustment whereby our people could follow the cattle-raising policy which formerly gave splendid results.
I asked the delegates whether they could supply me with the prices they were paying for certain foodstuffs, certain feeds or other products required for breeding purposes. They provided the following figures which I wish to place on record: ordinary feeds: $3.50; chicken-feed, $4.35; hog-feed, $4; oats, $3.75; wheat, $3.25; flour, $5; linseed^bread, $5, which is very scarce, almost impossible to secure; corn, $5, which six months ago sold for $3.75.
I do not wish to paint too dark a picture of the situation, but the farmers I represent in this house do not expect me to create a literary masterpiece upon bringing their legitimate claims to the attention of the government. I shall be very brief and content myself with placing before this house the reasons they gave me, which are found in the Guide, a publication representing our Union Catholique des Cultivateurs (Catholic Union of Farmers). I quote:
First, the dominion goverment should entrust the wheat board, or any other organization established for that purpose, with the sale and distribution of feed grain to farmers of eastern Canada, in order to eliminate any speculation which might have the effect of making prices soar and creating inequality of distribution;
In the second place, the dominion government should immediately negotiate with the British Ministry of Food in order to readjust the prices of all agricultural products which we have agreed, under contract, to supply Great Britain;
In the third place, the Agricultural Prices Support Board, or the Department of Agriculture acting on its behalf, should establish minimum prices for agricultural products, the prices of which are too low or tend to go down, or take any other step capable of creating a satisfactory balance between the costs of production and the sale price on the Canadian and British markets, and
Finally, the dominion Department of Agriculture should consult with Canadian agricultural organizations before taking any new step with a view to ensuring the economic stability of our agricultural production.
Such are the grounds for these claims. They reflect quite accurately the views of farmers in my district and, I am sure, in the whole of Quebec province.
It is rather unusual, sir, for Quebec members to air grievances and inveigh against certain

measures of the dominion government aimed at bestowing greater favours on farmers of the west and other provinces. I mention the west because I recall that hon. members from Quebec province have always been prepared to support the government in expediting the adoption of measures likely to lend greater help to western farmers.

Figures given in this house on December 9, I think, by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) have not been denied as yet, to my knowledge; and to complement those figures may I state that during the year 1946 chartered Canadian companies increased their profits by about 350 per cent over those for the year 1938, realizing SI,400 million; while during the year 1947, which will end in a few weeks, the profits realized by these companies will probably reach the 82,000 million mark, or about 500 per cent greater than the profits cashed in by the same companies in 1938.

In 1946 the total cost of living index had increased to 126-8 and the food index to 148-5, while at November 1 of this year the total index stood at 143-6 and the food index at 173-6, an increase of seventeen per cent for the whole index and fifteen per cent for the food index in a single year. I do not like to mention these things, but they have to be said. The situation cannot continue indefinitely. The people of Canada are not prepared to accept this kind of squeeze much longer. We all know this is not an agreeable task to have to perform; it is a most difficult one, indeed, but inflation such as we are experiencing in Canada today is one of the most crucial problems to face this country since the war. We did not need conscription to get production of agricultural products, and there is no need to have conscription of manpower now if we can get a decision from the government, and if we can get some co-operation from the people on this side of the house to face up to the facts that Canadian citizens are now living in a state of insecurity with a rising cost of living. They do not know whether next year they will be able to maintain food, clothing and shelter for their families.

Mr. Speaker, this debate has taken the form of a debate on the usefulness or otherwise of controls, and a rather simple motion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) to extend the emergency powers bill under the statutory clauses in the bill has developed into a wide-open discussion that has wandered all over the world with regard to the advocacy of a completely controlled economy for Canada.
There is one country in the world that has a completely controlled economy. The previous speaker mentioned it in rather laudatory terms as being the saviour of Europe. I refer, of course, to the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, which have been such a help to us in the recent four power minister's conference which has just broken up today, thereby destroying the hope of any secure peace in Europe for an indefinite period.
Let us see what this great utopia has done this very day. There is a current joke going around in the Soviet republic which is repeated by those who are able to travel, and it is this. One Russian asks the other, "what is the jolliest money in the world?" and the other Russian answers, "The Soviet ruble, because the foreigners laugh so much when they see it." Let us look at what has happened in Russia in the last two days. The currency of that country has been cut by the ratio of ten to one; that is, if you had a thousand-ruble bill it is no longer of any value unless you exchange it in the bank for a hundred-ruble bill. I think that is a fairly drastic deflation in currency, the wealth of the people, and I hate to think what any government in any democratic country would be up against if they adopted any such measures as that.

Agricultural Products Act
Let us go to the next question, bank credits. Bank savings accounts are cut anywhere from a third to a half, depending on the size of the bank account. Government bonds are cut by two-thirds. That is, for every government bond, every victory bond you have there is a drastic reduction. You would take three 100 ruble victory bonds to the bank and the bank would say, "Thank you very much; we will give you one new 100 ruble bond in exchange." That is what complete control of currency, complete control of the life of the people, complete, control of production, complete control of every going in and coming out of the citizen means. That is inflation; that is chaotic conditions. I ask this house whether any government in this country, in the United States or in any country that calls itself a democracy, could withstand the wrath of the people for one five-minute period if it took steps such as these?
Let us see what happens to the Russian worker. We have tremendous demands for controls, tremendous demands for the imposition and increase of controls over the entire economy of Canada. Every day spokesmen for unions wire members of this house to reimpose controls, saying, "Let us go back to the controlled economy of the war." What happens to the Russian worker in a completely controlled economy? His salary remains the same. His bank account is cut by a half to two-thirds, if he has one. The currency in his pocket is devalued by ten times. He can buy food or clothes or anything that he has money to pay for, only in the new currency. The worker, office or factory-and I am quoting from an Associated Press dispatch from Moscow-offers to continue his salary at the new rate for the generous period of one-half of a month. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is an example of an agricultural and industrial country that was held up by hon. members to the left as being the saviour of Europe, as being the economy, the ideology of the nation that is prepared to step in if the Marshall plan fails, to prevent starvation in western Europe. In fairness, I think some examination of what conditions are actually like in Russia should be made. When you get across this country a wave of pressure groups demanding a completely controlled economy, I wonder how far they would be prepared really to put up with it if they got it.

If this government cannot tell the farmers of Canada that over a period of years they will have stability in their industry and will get cost of production out of their efforts, the

Now, Mr. Speaker-

I do say, however, in view of the tremendous job which the farmers have done across the country, that it ill becomes any member, and least of all the hon. member for Vancouver East, to call the farmers criminals because they have slowed down in production after continuing for five years the effort they made during the war.

Mr. Speaker, I object to the hon. member taking up the subject now. He should have taken it up when I made the statement. Moreover, I did not say what the hon. member says I said; I was saying it in an altogether different sense. The Agricultural Products Act, Mr. Speaker, which was passed in this house on March 21 last, does not need further debate. In view of the fact that we met in December instead of January, this debate cannot be avoided. My remarks regarding the act can be found in Hansard, and they would be exactly the same today if I were to repeat them.
Agricidture today faces the most serious situation with which we have been confronted in many years. Almost irreparable damage has been done, regardless of what the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture said in London on Tuesday last, and I quote:
Robert McCubbin, parliamentary assistant to agriculture minister Gardiner, today forecast to the Middlesex federation of agriculture an announcement from the federal cabinet within "two or three hours" or at the latest two or three days which would solve all their farming problems.
Regardless of that fact, even though that statement were to be made now, the truth is that the result will be lowered production and that ultimately the cost to the consumer will be raised either through straight cost to him or through taxation. This is definitely the responsibility of the government through the

Agricultural Products Act
side-stepping tactics of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I do not think the excuses voiced by the parliamentary assistant will make the farmers of Ontario believe other than that. At least as far back as March 31 last year, as the record will show,
I warned the government of impending danger; I did so from that time until the last day of the session on July 17, and I endeavoured to get an answer to my question from the government through the Minister of Agriculture. But I did not get it. There was no answer forthcoming and that was the situation even up until the last night, on July 17. Being a farmer myself, I would liken the attitude of the government to a situation which is, I believe, quite commonly known to Ontario farmers. It is one which I remember particularly, as a boy, namely, that of being asked to go for the cows on a day when a severe electrical storm is pending. Invariably those cows would be found in the farthest corner of the field lying there quite contentedly chewing their cuds and paying no attention whatever to the impending storm. By this time the rain is pouring down, but they are still lying there, in spite of all the prodding that is done. They are content not to be disturbed; they are quite reluctant to move and are indignant at being driven to the shelter of the barn or stable. By this time, the herder of the cows is getting a good soaking, just as the public is getting a good soaking today.
Last Thursday evening the Minister of Agriculture made a good attempt to justify the government's action on this feed grain policy; but even then he did not answer the question which was asked as far back as last March. Apparently the government has no policy; it had no policy then and it has not one today. The promise which the parliamentary assistant gave to the people of London means very little, because the three days are long since gone. But three days mean very little after waiting for eight months and suffering the uncertainty which the farmers of Canada have suffered, and after the loss of breeding stock which has already occurred far across this country. The answer to our criticism has only been given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself in the form of a threat of a general election. I believe it was quite evident to all members of the house what our answer to that threat was. Personally, I would welcome it, and I would also welcome a visit by the Prime Minister to the town of Paris in the county of Brant for the purpose, not only of buying more dress shirts which he required
to go to the wedding in London, but to explain to the people how he proposes to extricate them from this mess that his government has got us into.
One question I have been asked by many of the farmers of my riding is this:	Even if
the price increase was announced today, will the farmers get it? Where is the 84 increase they were supposed to get for their bacon last year after the 84 increase was brought about by an increase in the British food agreement? I have here two statements with regard to hogs delivered in the city of Brantford. One is for January 17, 1947, for grade B-l carcasses and the price is given as $21.95 per hundred. The other statement is for November 17, 1947. again for grade B-l carcasses, and the price now is only $22.60 per hundred after the $4 increase. As I say, during that period there was supposed to have been a $4 increase in the price of bacon to the farmers.

In any event, the statement is there on Hansard for anyone who wants to check up on it. I must say to the Minister of Finance that the farmers are at least intelligent enough to run their own business if they were not hampered by a bunch of armchair theorists who tell them what they should do, and who profess to know more about what they should do than the farmers do themselves. Regardless of how long I talk, Mr. Speaker, the government's attitude is apparently not going to change. Their attitude has been and will apparently continue to be, "We will tell you when we get good and ready to tell you."
In closing, the only thing I can say is -that the farmers of Canada want a statement from the Minister of Agriculture and they want it now. They are sick and tired of being pushed around in the dark.

The hon. member
should have been down in Prince Edward Island last week. The people there are all farmers.

That is the trouble,
Mr. Speaker. These statements can be made outside the house, but they cannot be made inside it where all hon. members can hear them. This selling of breeding stock is not something which occurred just recently since the increase in feed prices. The selling of breeding stock has been taking place since last spring. I warned the minister of it on that occasion, so that it cannot have been caused just from the fact that the price of feed has gone up. It has been greatly accentuated since that happened, it is true; but it cannot be blamed solely on that fact. It is purely and simply a case of the farmers not knowing what the policy of this government was or what it is going to be. The damage has been done, but further panic selling can be avoided if the minister makes his statement. On behalf of the farmers of this country, I am asking once more that the Minister of Agriculture tell them what he is going to do and that he tell them before it is too late.
