speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Before this motion is put, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word. I was going to inform the

house tonight that the government intends tomorrow to proceed with the second reading of Bill No. 3, an act respecting emergency measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources. It is quite true that on Wednesday of last week I said we would go on with these two resolutions until they were completed, but at the time I was speaking I had in mind what hon. gentlemen opposite had represented, that they were matters which would not likely take very long. I do not think anyone in the house dreamed we would spend three days on one resolution. If we are going to spend another three days on the next one it is quite obvious that little will be accomplished before an adjournment on Friday for the Christmas recess.
It is important, I think, that the house and the country should have full particulars in regard to the emergency measures for the conservation of Canada's foreign exchange resources, and that the minister should have an opportunity to make his statement without further delay. I would hope, therefore, that everyone would agree to this measure getting precedence over any others tomorrow. If hon. members wish to debate the matter on second reading tomorrow might be reserved for that purpose. Later we could go on with the resolution being discussed tonight. But I would remind the house that there are one or two other measures, particularly the one having to do with assistance to the gold mining industry, which the minister will wish to introduce before the house adjourns and on which hon. members doubtless will wish to have some discussion. To make sure these measures are before the house and the country before we adjourn over the Christmas season, I shall have to hold in reserve the possibility of an adjournment on Friday night. I believe we can get through by seeking to accommodate each other, but it will require some measure of accommodation.

May I make an observation at this time? If I interpret the Prime Minister's remarks correctly, they are to the effect that the debate in which we are now engaged will not be proceeded with tomorrow, but that in its place we shall proceed with the second reading of Bill No. 3, respecting emergency measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is right.

Then with all respect may I ask the Prime Minister whether he would be willing, provided that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is ready, to

Agricultural Products Act
have the minister make a statement on the resolution with which we are now dealing. I think the house and the Canadian people would welcome such a statement by the minister. It may be that he is not ready to make it; but, speaking for many in this house and outside, we would like that to be done if the government are willing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the minister is in the position to do so, that could be done when we return to this resolution.
Of course it could, but we do not know when that is going to be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly we will return to the resolution we are now debating before the house adjourns. We must get that resolution through before the year is out; otherwise the legislation to which it relates will terminate. I have no doubt the minister, if he is in a position to do so, will be glad to make a statement before the debate is concluded.
I agree with the leader of the opposition on this; I think the country is waiting for the statement of the Minister of Agriculture.

Just on the point which has been raised, and not speaking on the resolution at the moment, I do not think it is possible to make the sort of statement for which the leaders are asking. That statement cannot be made until the negotiations with Britain have gone further. I presume what is wanted is a statement that we are going to do so-and-so in regard to prices of certain commodities. That statement cannot be made until we have completed our discussions with London, and there is no way of giving a statement of that kind at this stage. It may not be possible even to give it by Friday evening; so if hon. members are just talking until that statement is given, I do not know how it can be made on that basis.
I presume that is one reason for not proceeding with the debate on the agricultural matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. This measure respecting the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources is very important. It w-as one of the measures which, in our opinion, required the house to be called together before the Christmas season. I think it ought to be brought forward without further delay. That is the reason.

If I might ask one other question: the Prime Minister has indicated that the motion now before us will have to be dealt with finally before we adjourn this
month. I do not mean my next question to be embarrassing, and I hope it will not be; but does the government consider that Bill No. 3 should be finally dealt with before the adjournment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, no; not finally dealt with, but certainly progress made; if possible, through second reading. The-debate can be adjourned at any time.
Can the Prime Minister say how much time he will allow on that before returning to the discussion of the measure now before us?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen wish it, we might devote tomorrow to Bill No. 3 and return to the resolution respecting agricultural products on a following day.
Did the Prime Minister say Bill No. 3 did not have to be finally dealt with before we adjourn?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
Then under what authority will the taxes involved in that measure be imposed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That has nothing to do with taxes. Bill No. 3 relates simply to the import restrictions; it has nothing to do with taxes.
May I ask the Minister of Finance when the bold bill, by whatever name it may be called, will be printed and ready for distribution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it may be ready tomorrow. I have given to the Clerk tonight the text of the resolution which must precede the introduction of that bill. It will appear either in Votes and Proceedings or on the order paper tomorrow, and I intended to ask, perhaps with the unanimous consent of the house, to be allowed to advance the resolution one stage by simply making the statement about the legislation having received the approval of the governor general. It should be on the order paper tomorrow.
If I understand the position correctly, it is a money bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
And concurrence of this house will have to be given before it can be enacted and go into operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is a money bill, and of course it cannot become law until it is passed by this house and the other place. But I am not sufficiently optimistic to think we can get it through both houses between now and Friday, so that I am afraid it will have to go over until later.
Agricultural Products Act

Mr. tOW: May I ask the minister when it will be his intention to introduce the resolutions authorizing the change in the excise tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Those could be introduced at any time. I intend to introduce the resolutions before the house adjourns, but I have not discussed with the Prime Minister or my colleagues the matter of just what day that will be done.
And will it be necessary for the minister to have those resolutions adopted by the house before we adjourn?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid it would not be possible. I think all we can hope for is to get all those measures before the house before we adjourn. They could be discussed briefly, perhaps, for whatever time is available, but I do want to have all those measures introduced before we adjourn, so that at any rate hon. members may study them during the recess.

I should like to know, then, why this is called an emergency measure for t'he conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources. Apparently there are really only two emergency measures before us. One is the resolution we dealt- with tonight ; the other is the resolution it is suggested we should not deal with tomorrow; and those would not be matters of emergency if we had not been called in this session. Under present conditions there are only two emergency measures now before the house. While I think there is merit in what the Prime Minister just suggested, though less merit now than when he made the suggestion, in my opinion we have only the two emergency measures and otherwise we are asked to deal with matters which are not matters of emergency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They are emergencies in the largest sense of the word.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The whole situation has arisen out of the international condition. If it had not been for the international situation being what it is, these measures would, never have had to be brought forward. In the real sense they are emergency measures. The resolutions just referred to are relatively trifling things. The Minister of Finance has a
long standing obligation to speak in New York on Thursday of this week. He will not be in the house on that day.
We have an emergency here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was going to suggest that, as the first order of business tomorrow, we take the second reading of Bill No. 3, respecting emergency measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources and then adjourn that debate after the minister has made his statement.
No.
We cannot accept that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Just a moment; hon. members have not heard what I have to say. Then if it is desired, the whole of Thursday might be devoted to the continuation of the debate on the second reading of that measure. Rather than continue the debate on the second reading tomorrow, we could have the minister make his speech and then adjourn the debate until Thursday. We would follow the second reading of this measure tomorrow with a continuation of the debate we have been having tonight.

I do not know what powers the Prime Minister or the government may have to determine the course of procedure in that way, but as leader of this party I must object to the Minister of Finance making his speech on this matter without any time being allowed for anybody else to speak. We object to that procedure. After the Minister of Finance speaks, there ought to be time for someone from each party to follow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am perfectly agreeable to that.
I think the Prime Minister might have allowed two days for this debate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon. friend would rather follow immediately after the Minister of Finance makes his speech, well and good. We can take all of tomorrow for the debate on this second reading, but we shall have to make some adjustments for Thursday.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS, AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

speechtext:
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, respecting emergency measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving second reading of this bill, I wish to give the house a broad outline of the comprehensive program which the government has worked out to deal with our United States dollar problem, and to discuss in somewhat greater detail the special part of that program with which this bill deals, namely, the restriction of imports. The details of other parts of the program-the new excise taxes and the assistance to the gold mining industry-will be dealt with when the appropriate measures are before the house. In regard to the import restriction program, I shall leave to my colleague, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), the task of discussing those aspects of it with which he is primarily concerned.
I apologize to the house for the length of my statement but it has seemed to me necessary to present the facts with which the government was faced, and to state the considerations and objectives by which it was guided in seeking and in determining an appropriate policy.
Canada's Exchange and Balance of Payments Position
The necessity for vigorous action to correct our United States dollar difficulties is shown by the sharp reduction in the official holdings of gold and United States dollars this year. From the end of 1946 to the middle of November, these exchange reserves fell by almost S750 million. IV hen the program to improve our exchange position was announced, the official reserves were down to $500 million as

Foreign Exchange Conservation
compared with S1,245 million at the end of 1946 and SI,500 million at the end of 1945.
As I said in introducing the budget last spring, the government expected a very substantial reduction in our exchange reserves during the post-war transition. It was quite clear that recovery in Europe and Asia could occur only gradually and that, during the period of reconstruction, the maintenance of our exports to many overseas countries would depend in part upon the provision of credits. It was also clear that our imports from the United States would be very large. It was hoped, however, that as recovery abroad gained momentum we should receive payment for a growing proportion of our overseas exports in the form of a return flow of goods and in convertible exchange. It was also hoped that imports from the United States would gradually level off as stocks were replenished, as more goods became available from other countries and as improved production checked the sharply rising trend in world prices.
Hon. members will be familiar with the developments that have postponed the realization of these hopes-the extreme winter in western Europe with its fuel crisis and resulting poor crops, the growing political unrest in a number of countries induced in large measure by the uncooperative attitude of Russia, the breakdown in the attempt to make sterling convertible, and the spread of the "dollar" crisis to almost the entire world. Aid from the United States, large though it has been, has not been sufficient for the task. For the time being the ability of most overseas countries to pay for their purchases from us with convertible exchange or with a return flow of goods is very limited. At the same time, the level of investment and consumption here in Canada has risen beyond the most optimistic predictions and this in conjunction with the further marked rise in external prices has involved an extraordinary increase in our imports from the United States. The deficiency in our current transactions with that country, which because of other countries' difficulties had to be met to a large extent by drawing on our exchange reserves, became so large as to threaten the efficient working of our economy.
There is of course nothing new for Canada in running a deficit in her current transactions with the United States. For many years, it has been customary for this country to spend more in the United States than that country spends in Canada. Before the war the surplus in our transactions with Great Britain, western Europe and other overseas countries had for

some years been sufficient, and indeed usually more than sufficient, to meet the deficit with the United States. Since the surplus was convertible into United States dollars we were able, in addition to meeting the United States trading deficit, to achieve' a considerable reduction in our foreign indebtedness.
Canada's import requirements, especially from the United States, were greatly increased by the war. Our expanding industrial effort was heavily dependent on access to materials and components from the United States. Great Britain and our other allies were in no position to pay for our growing shipments of war supplies on a cash basis and early in the war we began to run short of United States dollars. Measures were taken to restrict the use of United States dollars to essential purposes mainly through severe import restrictions and special excise taxes. Such restrictions, however, could not have provided an adequate solution. We needed and looked for a constructive and far-reaching approach which would release our war effort from the limitations imposed by the United States dollar shortage and we found such a solution with the helpful co-operation of the United States in what was known as the Hyde Park agreement. The main point of this was to pool North American production so as to achieve the largest total of war output. In the process the United States government purchased large quantities of war supplies in this country, thus helping to overcome our United States dollar shortage and putting us in a position where we could carry out a very large war program of our own and also provide large-scale assistance to overseas allies.
As a result of these policies and arrangements we were able to pay cash for all our purchases from the United States. Some liquidation of Canadian holdings of United States investments and a substantial inflow of capital from the United States later in the war further strengthened our liquid position. The net result was that we emerged from the war with large exchange reserves amounting to no less than $1,500 million at the close of 1945.
We were thus in a favourable position to proceed with our own reconstruction program and at the same time to provide a substantial contribution to relief and reconstruction in the war-torn areas of the world. Total credits, contributions to UNRRA and other assistance were approved to the extent of $2,000 million to be expended over a period of several years. Britain and our other major customers in Europe were not able to make full payment in cash or in goods for the large quantities of food, materials and equipment which they needed from this country. From our point of

Foreign Exchange Conservation
view, we wished to sustain our exports in the transition period, particularly in view of the rapid curtailment in war expenditures. Moreover, we wanted to help our friends and customers to meet their very difficult problems of reconstruction, looking toward the rebuilding of soundly based and mutually beneficial trade.
In 1946, our balance of payments position was not far out of line with expectations. We were able to permit the use of a large amount of the credits extended to other countries without any undue reduction in our exchange reserves. Recovery abroad seemed to be making headway and the new organizations for international co-operation were coming into being. While our trading deficit with the United States was increasing substantially, our total transactions with the world still showed a favourable balance.
To give the essential figures, our position in 1946 may be summarized as follows:	we
had a favourable balance in our current transactions with the world of about 8460 million. In addition, there was a net inflow of capital, mainly from the United States, amounting to approximately $100 million. We also received a net amount of about $40 million in convertible currency as a result of certain other capital transactions. If all transactions had been on a cash basis, our exchange reserves would have increased in 1946 by the total of these three items, that is, by $600 million.
Needless to say, all these transactions were not, nor could they have been, on a cash basis. The United Kingdom and other countries utilized a total of $750 million out of the credits which had been authorized to them. In addition, through UNRRA and mutual aid we gave away exports to the value of $110 million. There were therefore exports of $860 million which did not produce foreign exchange in 1946. So instead of adding $600 million to our exchange reserves, there was a reduction of about $260 million, the official holdings falling to $1,245 million at the end of the year.
We could have faced reductions of this magnitude in our exchange reserves without undue concern for two or three years, provided of course that there was a gradual and sustained recovery in Europe and elsewhere. During the present year, however, the situation became steadily more unfavourable. On the one hand, we found it necessary to aid our overseas customers by permitting them to make large further drawings on their credits. On the other, our imports increased very rapidly, to such an extent that the surplus in our total current- transactions with all countries disappeared. Whereas in 1946 we were shipping substantially more goods and
services out of the country than we were bringing in, in 1947 our purchases were as large as our shipments.
The picture for 1947, that is, for the ten and a half months up to the middle of November, was approximately as follows:	Our
current transactions with the rest of the world were pretty well in balance-actually the tentative estimate puts imports and other current payments at a figure about $15 million in excess of exports and other current receipts. However, there were also capital payments mainly of an unusual or non-recurring nature of $220 million which consisted of our gold contribution to the international monetary fund of $75 million and of a net retirement of Canadian debt in the United States of 3145 million. Thus if all our transactions with other countries had been on a cash basis our exchange reserves would have decreased by about $235 million-the sum of the net capital movements I have mentioned and the very small deficit in our current accounts.
But part of our exports were financed on credit, though not as much as in 1946, since some countries had already used up most of their credits and since Canada was not in a position to allow as rapid a use of the remaining credits. The net credits utilized during the ten and a half months up to the middle of November were approximately $480 million and in addition we gave away, through UNRRA. exports to the value of about $35 million. Thus our current transactions with the world, though approximately in balance, resulted in a drain on our exchange reserves of about $515 million. When you add to this the decrease of $235 million which would have occurred if all our trade had been on a cash basis, you have the approximate measure of the loss of reserves since the beginning of the year, which left them in the middle of November at approximately $500 million.
Another way of presenting the developments of this year is to start with our United States dollar deficit. During the ten and a half months up to the middle of November the deficiency in our current transactions with the United States was approximately 81,100 million. From the countries to which we were extending credits we received cash payments for part of our heavy surplus of exports to them and we also had a small current surplus with other dollar countries than the United States. These cash payments reduced our over-all dollar deficit on current account to around $530 million, to which should be added the capital movement mentioned above of $220 million in order to obtain the loss in our
Foreign Exchange Conservation

exchange reserves this year. It must be recognized that the balance of payments estimates which I have given for ten and a half months are necessarily very approximate, but I believe they give a reasonable picture of the nature of the changes.
The High Level of Imports from the United States
In the ten months up to October, Canada's mports from the United States have been running at the rate of nearly $2,000 million per annum, an increase of almost fifty per cent as compared with 1946 and four times as much as just before the war. In October, they reached the highest monthly figure on record, $190 million.
There' are several reasons why our imports from the United States have risen to such heights.
The marked increase in United States prices has of course been an important factor in swelling the dollar value of imports. Wholesale prices in the United States during the first ten months of this year averaged twenty-eight per cent higher than in the like period of 1946 and were eighty-six per cent over the pr.e-war average. But the really significant point is that the actual quantity of imports continued to rise substantially in 1947, despite the notable increase in United States prices and despite the fact that the Canadian price level was relatively lower than that of the United States.
The reasons for the much increased purchase of United States goods are to be found in the high level of production and income in Canada and in the accumulated needs and requirements of industry and consumers alike. The great program of capital expansion and improvement born of requirements long deferred by depression and war, and nourished by high demand and by developing opportunities, added heavily to our imports of machinery and equipment, of parts for incorporation into Canadian-made capital goods, and of steel and other materials. Judging by a tentative estimate by the Department of Recoustruction and Supply, investment in plant, equipment and housing this year will run to about $1,800 million compared with $1,240 million in 1946 and a pre-war figure of less than a third as much. As an illustration of the effects of high capital expenditures on our imports, our purchases of machinery from the United States at around $300 million in the first nine months of this year were sixty-eight per cent higher than in the like period of 1946 and nearly six times the corresponding 1939 value. Our imports of primary iron and

steel at $81 million were up fifty-nine per cent over the previous year and were about five times pre-war.
High consumer purchases have also contributed substantially to raising our imports from the United States. Long deferred demand for such things as automobiles backed by accumulated wartime savings has made itself strikingly apparent. Imports of finished passenger automobiles from that country, for example, amounted to $37 million in the nine months up to September, more than three times the amount in the corresponding period of 1946. Moreover, sharply rising domestic production of automobiles and household appliances has involved heavy imports of parts and materials. High expenditures on less durable goods are also clearly reflected in our dollar imports. For example, our purchases of cotton goods (not including raw cotton or cotton yarns) from the United States were $75 million up to the end of September this year, as compared with $37 million a year earlier and less than $5 million in the corresponding period of 1939. More and more citrus fruits, out of season vegetables, as well as a variety of luxury and semi luxury goods have been flowing into this country and there seemed to be no end to the increase.
The large volume of our exports has also contributed to raising our imports from the United States. This is notably the case in respect of exports of such goods as automobiles and electrical goods where there is frequently a substantial United States content in Canadian production.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS, AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Yes. I think they could probably be made available from the bureau of statistics. I will see that those figures are made available to the house before we conclude the committee stage. To continue my statement: Normally, this would not produce

Foreign Exchange Conservation
any exchange difficulty, but today when the bulk of such exports are going to countries which find it difficult or impracticable to settle in convertible exchange it is a factor that cannot be ignored.
Finally, replenishment of business inventories has swelled imports of many articles and materials. Inventories of most of the goods which we normally obtain from the United States were very low and in some cases non-existent at the end of war. This year, however, there has been a considerable increase in such stocks toward more usual levels.
Even if Europe and Asia had experienced a full recovery from the effects of the war, the bulk of the great expansion in our imports would have come from the United States. Actually, most of the countries outside of this hemisphere had not been able to re-establish a satisfactory volume of exports and we therefore had to rely even more than usual on United States sources of supply. In the first ten months of this year seventy-seven per cent of our total imports came from the United States, whereas in the five years prior to the war the proportion was sixty-one per cent.
This analysis of the reasons for our extremely high imports from the United States indicates that there are certain temporary elements in the increase. Overseas countries will in time be able to ship us more and we shall return to usual sources of supply for goods which we can now only obtain in quantity from the United States. Great Britain, for example, has every intention of increasing her sales to us to the greatest possible degree. There is also, as I have noted, a considerable element of inventory replenishment by business and restocking by consumers in the present import totals, and this of course will not continue indefinitely. Moreover, the great program of capital expansion now under way reflects to a substantial degree deferred needs for replacement and improvement and as progress is made in catching up with this backlog of demand, the rate of capital investment and its associated requirements for imports can be expected to decline. In addition, the prices of some imports from the United States have risen to an exceptional degree in relation to other prices and as world production expands some reduction may be expected in their cost.
However, even when due allowance is made for the temporary factors which have been swelling our imports from the United States, it is not possible to escape the conclusion that our propensity to import from that country is very great. Under conditions of high employment, it is natural to expect a continued heavy flow of imports from the United
States. In 1929, the most active pre-war year, imports from that country were nearly as large as they are today in relation to our national income and production. High employment, rising consumption, and heavy investment in physical capital inevitably produce a great demand for the sort of goods that the United States can most readily supply, in addition to the essential fuels and materials which we require at all times. The use of the same methods of production, the close trading and financial connections, the ready access to United States materials and techniques are among the factors which produce this result. The similarity in habits of consumption, supported by continuous contacts between Canadians and Americans, work in the same direction. Most important of all is our proximity to the greatest concentration of industry and natural wealth in the world today.
The Question of Convertibility
-If Canada could rely on soon being able to convert into dollars a large surplus in her trade with Britain and other European and sterling countries, our dollar problem might still be regarded as purely temporary. The facts of the present position, however, suggest that it would not be wise to depend too heavily on converting overseas surpluses to meet our United States deficit.
In saying this, I am not taking a pessimistic view of the outlook for European recovery. I am confident that Britain will surmount her great present difficulties. I also believe that there are good reasons for expecting substantial further recovery in other western European countries. At the same time, we cannot ignore the fact that western Europe is not as favourably situated as before the war. It has suffered very heavy economic losses both in the form of destruction and dislocation and in the liquidation of foreign investments. It will be years before a full recovery has been achieved. The plans drawn up at Paris do not envisage that the pre-war standard of living will be fully regained even in 1951. For some time western Europe's purchases from this continent will be restricted and, even when the special trade restrictions which prevail today are removed, the ability of this region to purchase from us will have its limitations. We must therefore guard against optimistic assumptions as to the size of the convertible trade surplus which we may have with western Europe in future, and we should not forget that there have been occasions in the past when our dependence on converting an overseas surplus to pay a United States trading deficit has caused us considerable difficulty.
Foreign Exchange Conservation

The Basis of Government Policy
These were the facts and considerations which the government had before it. They indicate that we have an urgent and serious United States dollar problem. They suggest that it is in part temporary and in part of a more lasting nature.
In determining a policy, the government had the following considerations and objectives before it:
1.	The measures taken had to be sufficient to bring our United States dollar problem under control. At the recent rate of depletion, our remaining exchange reserves could have lasted for only a limited period and their disappearance would have clearly involved extreme difficulty and drastic restrictions. A country, like a business, without liquid resources is in a highly vulnerable position no matter how favourable the other items in its balance sheet may be. Its freedom of action, its trading position, and its very welfare would be gravely prejudiced. The program had to be big enough and broad enough to do the job even if that involved the use of restrictive measures.
2.	It was essential to find a lasting solution to the United States dollar problem through a constructive approach designed to increase -and to re-direct our trade and production. Canada's interest lies in freer and expanding trade and our approach to the problem has been one of constructive co-operation with other countries. We have demonstrated our intentions in this respect by our contribution in establishing the new machinery of international order and by our policy of assisting war-torn countries in reconstruction. We do not wish to use restrictive measures to any greater extent or for any longer time than can be avoided, and we do not believe that any satisfactory and lasting solution to our problems, and indeed to the problems of others, can be found within the limitations of a restrictive approach. In working out constructive and expansive measures, it is essential for us to enlist the fullest co-operation of the United States with the dual aim of achieving a better balance in our mutual trading relationships and of making the fullest practicable contribution to world recovery.
3.	It is much in Canada's interests to assist and facilitate recovery in western Europe. Given economic recovery, this region can provide markets for certain basic Canadian products which it would be difficult to sell elsewhere on a permanent basis. More than that, our freedom of action as a trading nation depends in large measure on the recovery of Britain and the other European democracies.
I say this in no spirit of criticism of our good
[Mr. Abbott. 1	'
neighbours to the south, for there are no two peoples that get along better and trust and understand each other so well as Canadians and Americans. But it is none the less a fact that Canadians value their independence, and I believe that' our American friends respect us the more for it.
4.	The measures to correct our exchange difficulties should be designed-with a view to minimizing dislocation to our economy. Restrictions which would affect our basic production should be avoided and every effort should be made to apply the required measures in a manner that will not create unemployment. The government is also conscious of the necessity of avoiding measures that would raise prices and costs indiscriminately. While some price increases are unavoidable, or even necessary to check the demand for imports from the United States, it is clearly undesirable to add any more to inflationary tendencies than can be helped. It is most desirable to interfere with individual initiative as little as possible.
The emphasis of the program is on constructive measures which we hope and believe will bring about a solution to our United States dollar difficulties in the reasonably near future, and bring it about in a manner that will enable us to maintain a high standard of living and a high degree of freedom in our economic life. We cannot, however, expect to achieve a sufficient expansion and readjustment in our production and trade to correct overnight a United States dollar deficiency of the present magnitude. The constructive side of the program must, therefore be supplemented by restrictive measures. We are in a serious situation and we must make some prompt adjustments in our consumption and in our investment programs.
The restrictions will save substantial amounts of United States dollars. While it is difficult to make precise estimates, the prohibitions and quotas if they had been in effect during the twelve months ended June, 1947. would have excluded imports from United States dollar countries to the value of something like $300 million. The travel restrictions would have reduced our United States dollar expenditures by from $30 to $40 million. A substantial saving will result from the control of imports of capital goods but it is hard to say how much and in this case the saving will increase as arrangements are worked cut in particular industries, and as capital expansion plans are reviewed. As time goes on, the constructive measures will steadily bring about a better balance in our United States dollar transactions, and

Foreign Exchange Conservation
meanwhile as an extra margin of safety we have at our disposal a United States credit of $300 million.
The Longer-Range Constructive Policy
I have heard it suggested that the constructive part of the program lacks content, that it is too general and too vague. That is a mistaken view. There is nothing vague about the reductions in the United States tariff which resulted from the negotiations at Geneva. And if the statement that the governments of Canada and the United States are consulting on measures designed to achieve the maximum degree of economic co-operation between the two countries is a general one, let me assure the house that it is far more than a mere statement of good intentions. If the United States congress decides to authorize the use of Marshall plan funds in making purchases outside the United States, as we hope and expect it will, that will be a decision of great importance to Canada. It is true that the program to develop and re-direct our resources and industry in a manner that will permanently reduce the undue lack of balance in our trade with the United States is just beginning. But as the Minister of Reconstruction will confirm it is a serious program which the government will pursue with determination and vigour.
Referring for a moment to the Geneva trade agreements which are now before the house, I would direct particular attention to the reduction in the United States tariff as it affects this country. Substantially better terms of entry have been accorded to farm products, lumber and wood products, and base metals, to mention some of the more important categories. Note should be taken of the fact that tariffs have been reduced on articles processed from our primary production as well as on the primary products themselves. This enlarges the opportunities for further development of fabrication and processing of our primary output and for increasing the proportion of our exports to the United States in the more valuable processed and manufactured forms.
Important as these new tariff reductions are, the government believes that steps should be taken to reduce further trade barriers and to promote closer and more advantageous economic co-operation between the two countries. It is the desire of the government to reach a further trade agreement with the United States. This proposal has been made informally to United States officials who are studying this and other methods of promoting mutually beneficial economic co-operation. The government has been investigating the possibilities of shipping additional supplies to the United
States and there is a good deal that can be done in the near future. While it will take time to increase to desired levels our production of the sort of goods which have a ready market in the United States, output of some such commodities is still expanding and new capacity is coming into operation. Considerable further expansion in our United States dollar exports can be achieved by diverting exports away from other countries and by reducing Canadian consumption. Action along these lines is necessary and practicable to a substantial extent. It is expected that deferment of some capital projects and reduced consumption of some goods in this country will make available larger supplies for export. It is well to remember that expansion projects and production of durable goods involve the use of large quantities of Canadian-produced goods, such as base metals and wood, which might otherwise be exported, as well as the use of very substantial imports.
So far as diverting exports to the United States is concerned, the exchange difficulties of Britain and other countries have led them to restrict their imports from Canada with increasing severity and to confine their purchases to only the most essential items. Fortunately, there is a market in the United States for many of the exports which are being restricted by these countries and to that extent diversion will take place rapidly. Canada naturally does not wish to divert supplies which are urgently needed overseas.
The extent to which we can continue to assist Britain and other countries will depend in large measure on the implementation of the Marshall plan. The prospects for the approval of this plan by the United States congress are, I believe, encouraging. Such a constructive and imaginative step by the United States could make the difference between a healthy world recovery and the indefinite continuance of economic dislocation and distress over much of the world.
The form in which the Marshall plan is implemented is also very important to us. We have pointed out to the United States how our difficulties in buying from that country arise very largely from our inability to sell to Europe for cash, and we have expressed our concern that dollars made available by congress for aid to Europe will be used in part to purchase supplies in Canada and elsewhere that are not readily available in the United States. The United States government has recommended to congress that it should authorize the use of funds voted for aid to Europe in making purchases outside the United States, and this principle has alieady been accepted by the United
Foreign Exchange Conservation

States senate in regard to the interim aid program. We expect that this policy will be implemented in regard to Marshall plan funds and if it is, we shall be better able to continue our own program of aid to Europe. If it is not, we shall have no alternative but to divert further exports from overseas to the United States.
It will be appreciated that our ability to contribute to world recovery depends very largely on overcoming our exchange difficulties in a manner that will not restrict our total production. A greater integration of the efforts of the United States and Canada to assist world recovery would add considerably to the capacity of this continent to provide urgently needed assistance just as it did during the war. We are making every effort to achieve the needed integration and we have encountered a most co-operative and helpful reception in our discussions with the United States government.
I do not propose to deal at length with that part of the policy which is the particular responsibility of the Minister of Reconstruction, since he will shortly be outlining his plans to the house. The aim is to achieve a better balance in branch plant operations, to encourage expansion of production for export to dollar markets, and to facilitate the development of production and resources in a manner that will ease our United States dollar deficiency. The government has no intention of embarking on a program of building up uneconomic production in this country. It is convinced, however, that there are great possibilities for expanding and re-directing our production in an efficient manner so as to improve permanently our exchange position.
The government will endeavour to centre the attention of industry on this question and in some cases it may be necessary to take specific action to facilitate the kind of readjustment and increases in production which are required. We expect that Canadian industry will realize its interest in and responsibility for the success of this program and there has already been an encouraging response. We want to maintain and expand our industrial structure, but we must find methods of doing so which will not involve the present-excessive drain of United States dollars.
In the statement which I made to the house on December 11, I have already explained the government's plans for assistance to gold mining. I need not repeat them now.

The Import Restriction Program
I now come to an explanation of the import restrictions covered by the bill. As the Prime Minister (Mr.	Mackenzie	King)	has
emphasized, the	government believed it
unwise to impose any such restrictions before the Geneva agreements were concluded. At the same time, we could not postpone action until early in the new year when the new session of parliament would normally have met. Parliament was therefore called at the earliest practicable date. As we feared it might, the calling of an early session was widely interpreted as an indication that imports were to be restricted. The rush to buy goods in the United States which had already assumed large proportions was aggravated. The government had therefore to watch an accelerated additional loss of United States dollars which could be ill afforded or to find some means by which the special measures could be put into effect before the program could be placed before parliament. As I said in announcing the program, the government had not believed that powers to restrict imports were contained in the Foreign Exchange Control Act, but was advised by the law officers of the crown that the act did provide a legal basis for such action. In view of the dangerously mounting losses of United States dollars, the government decided that the right course was to use these powers until parliament had the opportunity to pass special legislation. Hon. members will appreciate that, even if the program had been delayed until parliament met, it would have been necessary to introduce the import restrictions in the same way. By that I mean that they would have had to go into effect immediately on their announcement to avoid widespread evasion, windfall profits, and a heavy further increase in United States dollar expenditures.
It has been suggested in some quarters that in connection with this matter certain bureaucrats decided they needed power and believed that if they could twist certain sections of the Foreign Exchange Control Act they could obtain that power. Certain senior civil servants have been mentioned by name, and it has been suggested that they should be brought before a committee of parliament to give evidence as to the advice they gave and as to whether they did advise that the Foreign Exchange Control Act should be used for that purpose. That suggestion was made in the house. I was not in the house at the time, but let me say this, that so far as the reference to the so-called bureaucrats deciding that they needed extra power is concerned

Foreign Exchange Conservation
and that if they could twist the provisions of the Foreign Exchange Control Act they could obtain that power, that is nonsense and completely without foundation. So far as the use of the Foreign Exchange Control Act is concerned, the government takes the entire responsibility and I as Minister of Finance must take the largest share of responsibility in that connection.
When I came to the conclusion that import restrictions were inevitable I at once gave personal consideration as to how they could be brought into effect. I consulted the law officers of the crown, the deputy minister of justice, and I was advised that under the Foreign Exchange Control Act the governor in council had power to designate the currencies which could be used for imports and that that act was available for the purpose of imposing such restrictions. As I said a moment ago, it was never believed that the act contained those powers, and certainly the foreign exchange control board never had those powers and never wanted to have them.
I wish to add but one remark. I deprecate more than I can say this practice of suggesting that permanent civil servants should be brought before a committee of the house to state the advice they have given, to the government, because that strikes at the very foundation of the British parliamentary system of responsible government. The policy which the government announces is the government's policy and it must stand or fall by that policy. It takes its advice from the permanent civil servants and in some cases accepts that advice and in others rejects it, for reasons. The government itself must take the decision. But to suggest that permanent civil servants should be subject to questioning as to what advice they have given the government would, if followed, be completely destructive of our parliamentary system of responsible government. I know of no case in which any such suggestion has been made before this one to which I am referring. It has never been made in the British House of Commons. To my knowledge it has never been made before here and I hope this is the last time it will be made.
One of the strengths of any British parliamentary government is the permanent civil service which goes on from government to government. The government may change but the permanent civil service is always there, ready to advise and carry on the functions of government. If we are going to expose the permanent civil service to personal attack and innuendoes and call them to account for 5849-221
the advice they have given to their political superiors, I say that we shall not be able to get any sort of first-class men in our civil service.
Some concern has been expressed as to the severity of the specific restrictions which were imposed. In the spheres where it was feasible to impose specific restrictions, they are admittedly quite severe. They had to be, if we were to save any substantial amount of United States dollars. The point is that a large proportion of our imports cannot be much restricted without very serious effects on our economic life. We cannot readily cut our imports of fuel or raw materials; coal, oil, cotton and iron ore, for example, are basic necessities in our economy. Nor could we suddenly cut down the import of many components and parts without most serious effects on a variety of major industries. In regard to capital goods, some are urgently needed to expand our production and while a considerable reduction in such imports is practicable, it is largely a question of screening these imports in terms of the uses to which they will be put. More than three-quarters of our total imports from the United States are comprised of fuels, raw materials, components and parts and capital goods. This means that the direct restrictions had to be concentrated primarily on finished goods, mostly of a type used by consumers.
In working out the prohibitions and quotas we could not consult with industry nor could we carry out exhaustive inquiries with respect to each item. Absolute secrecy was essential. We were also under the necessity of specifying the restrictions in terms of tariff items since the tariff classification is the machinery with which our customs officers are familiar and can work effectively. This created some difficulty in getting suitable definitions and specifications. We recognized that an ironing-out job would have to be done as soon as the restrictions were announced. As a result of representations received and more detailed information acquired since the announcement, appropriate adjustments and improvements have been made in the original schedules.
There is one further general point about the restrictions that I wish to emphasize. It is that we have imposed them in a manner broadly consistent with the principle of nondiscrimination. That is to say, the same restrictions calculated on the same basis have generally been applied to all countries. When the import of an article has been prohibited, the prohibition applies to all countries. Similarly, the import quotas are based on
Foreign Exchange Conservation

pre-war trade and are applied in the same manner to the two groups of countries which have been listed. This principle of nondiscrimination has caused some confusion and misunderstanding. Why, we have been asked, when it is generally desirable to increase our imports from Great Britain do you prohibit the import of any goods from that country? Why, when the whole program of restrictions is frankly designed to save United States dollars do you not confine them entirely to dollar countries? There is a very strong reason for applying this non-discriminatory principle. It checks the possible abuse of restrictive practices in that it does not permit the country concerned to treat the import of a particular product in differing ways for different countries. It is a sound principle of international trade which it is most important to us to have generally accepted and which is included in the draft charter for the international trade organization. It is a principle which our neighbours in the United States also regard as very important. The restrictive program is of course designed to cut our imports from that country and is anything but welcome to many of- their exporters. The longer-term constructive program depends greatly on co-operation with the United States. Knowing their views and subscribing to the same principle ourselves, it was only reasonable that we should make a special effort to avoid direct discriminatory practices.
I have heard it suggested that because of their non-discriminatory character the restrictions are likely to have serious effects on our imports from certain non-dollar countries. This is a quite mistaken view. The prohibitions affect only a very minor portion of these imports and the quota restrictions leave wide latitude for expansion of imports subject to quota from the non-scheduled countries, which include Great Britain, France and Australia, among others. Indeed, because of the incentive which the quota system provides to importers to increase their purchases from non-scheduled countries, it is likely that the restrictive program will on balance tend to enlarge our imports from such sources.
The Import Prohibitions
The prohibited list-schedule I of the bill-covers a wide variety of consumer goods and certain other articles which the government has decided can no longer be permitted to draw on Canada's reserves of foreign exchange. The list includes a number of items of a luxury or non-essential character. It also includes a good many things which are important in themselves but which are pro-

duced in Canada in substantial quantities and which are frequently of such a nature that their purchase may be postponed.
All the items on the list have been selected with a view to saving United States dollar exchange; in other words they are goods which are imported entirely or largely from the United States. Since the principle of nondiscrimination involved application of the prohibitions to all countries, the list naturally does not include items which are of considerable importance to countries to which we have been extending credits. Thus there are no restrictions on the import of some luxury goods, as for example, sterling silverware and certain classes of perfumes.
There are a large number of non-essential and luxury items on the prohibited list. These include such things as cut flowers, some fancy foods, novelties, comic and "pulp" periodicals, pleasure boats, fur coats, jewelry, paintings, and various amusement devices.
The greater part of the list, however, is comprised of items that could not be described as luxuries. These are largely goods which are produced in substantial quantities in Canada or for which adequate Canadian substitutes are available. In respect of foods, for example, the import of meat, poultry and eggs is prohibited. Imports of fresh fruits, except citrus fruits, bananas, and apples, of fresh vegetables, except potatoes and onions, and of dried fruits, except pitted dates, figs, prunes and raisins, are no longer permitted. Hon. members will note that the exceptions are very important. The prohibitions mean, however, that we shall have to go without the usual supplies of out of season vegetables and put up with a less varied but still adequate vegetable diet. The fact is that we cannot now afford to spend scarce United States dollars on these additional amenities. Cigars, cigarettes, toilet soaps, and cosmetics are also prohibited because we produce a sufficient supply of these things in Canada.
The prohibitions also extend to most household electrical appliances, including refrigerators, washing machines, stoves, sewing machines and toasters. Canadian production of these articles is large and has been increasing sharply. For example, our production of domestic electrical refrigerators was more than three times as great as our imports in the twelve months ended in June of this year. Our output of electric washing machines at 133,000 was four times our imports, and in the case of stoves the domestic production accounted for 95 per cent or more of the total supply. The ban on imports of radios would

Foreign Exchange Conservation
have kept out less than 50,000 sets in the twelve months ending in June when our domestic production was 720,000 sets.
The other significant items on the prohibited list include a number of paper products, furniture, certain building materials and household supplies, passenger automobile tires, cameras, typewriters and certain other business machines. In most of these cases there is a large Canadian production. Imports of automobiles have been temporarily banned, but a restrictive quota is being worked out and its detailed provisions will be announced as soon as possible.
There have been some cases of hardship resulting from the suddenness with which the prohibitions came into effect. Hon. members may recollect that the prohibitions applied to all goods which were not actually in transit at the time of the announcement. We simply could not afford to permit all goods on order to enter the country, and the difficulties of defining "goods on order" as well as the fact that some purchasers had been over-ordering made this standard an unsatisfactory one in any case. In a few extreme cases special permits have been issued; for example, where goods have been completed and ready to ship which were made to the particular specifications of the buyer and which were not resaleable in the country of origin.
The Quota Restrictions
There are other types of imports which, though significant and desirable, had grown to excessive proportions in relation to our capacity to pay out hard currency. We wanted and in many cases needed to bring in these imported goods but we could not afford to pay United States dollars for the very large quantities of them that were coming into the country. A disproportionate quantity of these imports was coming from the United States as compared with pre-war conditions.
The method adopted to meet this problem was to set quotas based on the pre-war pattern of trade and to divide the quotas into two parts, one being applicable to imports from certain countries which we must pay in United States dollars and which do not appear to be suffering from a serious shortage of dollars, and the other being applicable to imports from all other countries. Our problem is one of reducing United States dollar outlays rather than of restricting our imports generally. We have been purchasing goods now subject to these quotas from the United States, the principal country in the first or scheduled group, on a scale many times in excess of pre-war. At the same time the value of our purchases from the
second group described as the non-scheduled countries is not greatly above the pre-war level. We can afford to increase our imports from these non-scheduled countries, which include Britain, the British dominions and the western European countries among others, and we do not wish to add to their problems by seriously restricting their sales to us.
The imports subject to quota are listed in schedule II of the bill and are classified into five quota groups. A description of each of these quota groups will give a much better idea of what the system is and how it works than any explanation in general terms. The first group includes the following fruits and vegetables: oranges, grapefruit, lemons, limes, fruit juices, apples, potatoes and onions. As I noted earlier most other fruits and vegetables are on the prohibited list except for bananas, raisins, figs, prunes and pitted dates, which are left unrestricted. Imports of the fruits and vegetables listed in this group amounted to $10 million per year for scheduled countries and $11 million for non-scheduled countries in the pre-war period of 1937-39. The quota which has been set for this group is 200 per cent of pre-war which means that about $20 million of these goods can be imported from scheduled countries in the next twelve months, and about S2i million from non-scheduled countries. During the twelve months ended June 30, 1947, such imports from scheduled countries were not far from $40 million while those from non-scheduled countries were less than $700,000. This means that such imports from the United States and other scheduled countries will be cut to about 50 per cent of the actual imports in the twelve months ended last June. On the other hand, imports from non-scheduled countries could be increased three and a half times without exceeding the quota.
Any individual importer shares in the group quota in accordance with his share of the trade during the twelve months from July, 1946, to June, 1947 inclusive. In other words. ' an importer simply reports to the government the total of his actual imports of the goods in the particular quota group from the scheduled countries for this period' and his permitted imports for the next twelve months are calculated' by applying the appropriate percentage.

Provision is made for that, and particularly for veterans. There is a gap left in the total quota to allow quotas for new businesses, particularly those which have been established by veterans who have no quota basis. The base period, as my hon.

friend will appreciate, is 1946-47, ending June, 1947, so that we believe that most of the veterans will have been established in that period.
In the case of the fruit and vegetable quota, this percentage, as noted above, is 50 per cent of the actual imports from scheduled countries in the twelve months ended June 1947. For the time being, open permits are being issued for imports from non-scheduled countries since actual imports are so far below the amounts permitted under the quota system. The annual quotas will normally be administered on a quarterly basis.
The quota on fruits and vegetables will mean some reduction in our imports of citrus fruits. I am advised, however, that prices for oranges in the United States are considerably below those prevailing a year ago and the total quantity that may ;be imported with half last year's dollar expenditure is likely to be very much more than half last year's physical volume, and certainly more than before the war.
The second, and! largest quota group, relates to textiles. It includes almost all textile products advanced beyond the yarn stage -fabrics, knitted goods, clothing and other finished goods. It does not include textile fibres and yarns on which no restrictions have been placed. Because of the shift in sources of supply, our heavy dependence on imports of cotton goods, and the much increased level of textile prices, it was necessary to set the quota at 400 per cent of prewar. Even at this figure the quota system will sharply restrict imports from scheduled countries though it will give wide latitude for increasing our purchases from non-scheduled countries.
In the pre-war period, imports from scheduled countries of the textile products now subject to quota averaged only about $10 million. However, during the twelve months ended June, 1947, imports from these same countries were nearly $130 million. With the total quota at $40 million, that is 400 per cent of pre-war, this means that importers are now only permitted to purchase up to 32 per cent of the amounts which they imported from scheduled countries in the period from July, 1946, to June, 1947.
The position in regard to non-scheduled countries is almost the complete reverse. In the pre-war period, imports of the textiles now under this quota from Britain and the other non-scheduled countries amounted to $30 million. The quota is thus $120 million. Actual imports during the twelve months ended June, 1947 were only $52 million and

the result is that we could more than double our purchases from non-scheduled countries before reaching the quota limit.
Since most of our imports of woollen goods come from the United Kingdom and since we have a large and generally adequate rayon production of our own, hon. members will appreciate that the main effects of this textile quota will be felt in the sphere of cotton goods. There will be a sharp reduction in our purchases of cotton fabrics from the United States and we hope a substantial and continuing increase in our purchases from Great Britain. In 1946 we imported more than 200 million yards of broad-woven cotton fabrics from the United States and only 5 million yards from the United Kingdom. This is a complete reversal of the pre-war trade pattern, when our average imports from the United States were less than 25,000.000 yards and those from the United Kingdom were
70,000,000 yards. Since the quota from scheduled countries is only 32 per cent of the recent rate of import, our imports of cotton fabrics from the United States are likely to be reduced by from 125,000,000 to 150,000.000 yards during the next twelve months.
The adequacy of the total supply of cotton fabrics will therefore depend on obtaining much larger supplies from the United Kingdom and to a lesser degree on increasing our domestic production. From the discussions we have had recently with British government officials, we are confident that a pronounced increase in imports from that source can be expected. If actual shipments approach expectations, our total supply of cotton fabrics will be quite sufficient for our needs. Taking our estimated domestic production, the much expanded imports from the United Kingdom which we expect, and the sharply reduced imports from the United States, our total supply in 1948 should work out to somewhere in the neighbourhood of 450,000,000 yards. This is somewhat less than the very high figure of 1946-about 490 million yards-but much more than our average pre-war supply which was around 350,000,000 yards. While there will be difficulties in this readjustment of sources of supply and while the total supply will be somewhat less plentiful than in the last year or two, the Canadian people are still going to have a sufficient supply of cotton goods.
The third quota group includes leather, footwear, gloves and mitts, leather garments, luggage and purses. The quota is 200 per cent of pre-war and as in the other quotas this restricts imports from scheduled countries and leaves considerable room for expansion

Foreign Exchange Conservation
in regard to non-scheduled countries. The quota works out to slightly less than $7 million for scheduled countries which is 70 per cent of the actual imports in the twelve months ended June, 1947.
The fourth quota group includes clocks and watches, cutlery, sporting goods, toys, smokers' supplies and certain types of glassware. The quota in this case also is 200 per cent and this involves a cut of nearly 60 per cent in the recent rate of imports from scheduled countries.
A fifth quota group to come into effect on January 1 was announced on December 12. It includes a wide range of prepared foods of a kind for which the United Kingdom, Australia and France were normally our principal suppliers. Included in this new group are such items as pickles and sauces, meat and fish pastes, cheese, pickled and preserved fruits, canned fruits and chocolate and confectionery products. The national quota will be 200 per cent of pre-war and the individual importer's quota from scheduled countries will be 28 per cent of his imports during the twelve months ending June 30, 1947.
As administrative experience is gained it may be possible to develop further quota categories in order to meet the special problems of some of our importers and some of our supplying countries. There are, however, narrow limits to such further adjustments, at least until our basic dollar position has substantially improved.
It will be observed that the whole quota system has been made as flexible as possible. Importers are not tied down to particular items or particular countries but are permitted to use their quotas to purchase any goods in a given quota category from any of the countries in the applicable schedule. The government believed it desirable to permit freedom of action to the largest feasible degree and wished to avoid undue administrative complications which might have retarded the efficient working of the system.
Import Controls on Capital Goods
As I mentioned earlier, prohibitions and quota restrictions are applicable only to a limited portion of our total imports. These methods would not be suitable to check the heavy flow of imports of capital equipment, and materials and parts for use in construction and in the manufacture of durable goods. The significance of such imports' depends mainly on the use to which they are put. The same imported material or machine may be highly essential when used for one purpose and much less essential when used for another.
The control of such imports must therefore be flexible and related to the use of the imports concerned.
The system adopted therefore is to make imports of the kinds of capital goods, components and materials listed in schedule III of the bill subject to control, and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply has been charged with the administration of this phase of the program. He will be in a position to review with industry proposed expenditures involving the import of such goods with the aim of reducing the drain on our dollar resources. Industries with capital expansion programs should check their import requirements with him and where feasible postpone such projects, as a number of firms have already done. This control also involves examination of methods to reduce the net dollar deficiency resulting from many of our industrial operations. Hon. members will appreciate that it is closely related to the plans for developing and re-directing Canadian production which are also the particular responsibility of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply.
While this completes my outline of the main features of the bill, I wish now with the indulgence of the house to refer briefly to the remaining parts of the dollar-saving program since they are so closely related to the restrictions contained in the bill.

The Travel Restrictions
A necessary corollary of the restriction of imports was the limitation of the amounts that could be spent for travel in United States dollar areas. We had to ration the use of dollars for pleasure travel or else make the import restrictions even more severe. The travel restrictions now in effect are approximately the same as those which prevailed immediately after the war. They allow an annual ration of funds for pleasure travel not to exceed $150 per person for those who desire to travel in a United States dollar area.
Mr. MaeNICOL: Per month?

Per year. That was the regulation in effect at the end or me war and for some time after. We were each allowed $150 once a year for pleasure travel in the United States.
Applications for travel funds in excess of this annual ration, when required for genuine

reasons of business, health or education, will be dealt with on their merits by the foreign exchange control board.
The Special Excise Taxes
The remaining part of the restrictive side of the program consists of the special excise taxes on a wide range of durable consumer goods. This is not the time to discuss these taxes in detail but I wish to explain why they were imposed and how they fit into the general program as an essential supplement to the import restrictions. Their first and primary purpose is to discourage the sort of expenditure which adds to our imports from the United States. Most of the goods subject to these taxes are produced in Canada in substantial volume and most of them have a significant United States dollar import content. The import of practically all these goods in finished form has been prohibited or placed under quota restrictions and substantial savings in United States dollars are expected to result from this action. The savings, however, would be considerably reduced if domestic production of the same type of articles were to expand to fill the gap in the supply, since this would involve further substantial imports of parts and components.
It could be argued that a more effective way to check expenditures that involve a considerable import of parts and materials would be to relate the tax directly to the import content of the article concerned. But the objections to this type of action are conclusive. Taxes directly related to import content would be tantamount to sharp increases in the tariff and under the Geneva agreements as well as in our own longer-range interests we would not consider such a course. In addition, taxes of that kind would involve levying different rates of tax on substantially the same articles, and hon. members can readily imagine the complications that would result. Moreover, such action would represent an extreme form of discrimination against businesses which are in the early stages of developing their operations in Canada.
A second reason for these taxes was to limit so far as practicable the degree of discrimination against regular suppliers in the United States and their dealer organizations in Canada. For the time being, many of these suppliers and dealers are losing a part of their business because of the unavoidable necessity of restricting imports from the United States. Regrettable as it is, we cannot help that. But by imposing these excise taxes we are doing something to protect the legitimate longer-range interests of these businesses. While the Canadian manufacturers are temporarily relieved of competition from
IMr. Abbott.]
the United States, their unexpected advantage is being at least partly offset by the effects of the special taxes. Without these taxes, prices of many of the articles affected could have risen a good deal, to the benefit of the manufacturers and distributors. As a result of the taxes, it is the public treasury that benefits.
Now I have emphasized that the main purpose of the new excise taxes is to save United States dollar exchange rather than to produce more revenue. At the same time, additional revenue will not be unwelcome for two good reasons. The first is that the new taxes will undoubtedly withdraw some purchasing power even if, as we hope, they lead to some reduction in purchases. As the trend of prices indicates, spending is still outrunning production over a wide area of our economy. The second is that our budget position, though good, is not as good as many popular reports would have it. We do have a large surplus this year, so far-larger than we had expected But we have been making large advances to overseas countries as I have already indicated. While these outlays are advances rather than expenditures, the government has to raise and pay out the funds. On a cash basis, including these outlays, our income is only moderately in excess of our outgo. And there are good grounds for the view that we should be running a substantial surplus in times of high activity like these.
The Credit from the United States Export-Import Bank
As I stated earlier, our official reserves were about $500 million at the middle of November. In addition to this liquid reserve we have the rights conveyed by the articles of agreement of the international monetary fund to draw upon our quota in the fund. As an extra margin of safety we have 'believed it prudent to add to our exchange resources by arranging for temporary financing in the United States.
A foreign loan is not of course a solution to our dollar problem. It merely provides a supplement to our exchange reserves to take care of a temporary deficit until the constructive, longer-run measures which are going into effect get into full operation and produce a more reasonable balance in our commercial and financial relations with the dollar area. Not only does it give more time for the constructive solutions, but it also permits the adopting of a program less upsetting to business than would otherwise be necessary. Without the additional latitude which a loan provides, the program of restrictions would

have to be much more severe which would cause undue dislocations to the Canadian economy and to many of our suppliers in the United States.
