speechtext:
To continue:
The Question of Currency Depreciation
Before closing, I wish to make it quite clear that currency depreciation was considered neither a desirable nor effective alternative to the measures which the government has adopted. In formulating its program, the government has followed the course which will have the least tendency to raise prices and which will work. No program could be devised which would not increase the upward pressure on prices to some extent since we have to reduce the inflow of goods from dollar countries and, so far as practicable, increase the outflow to them. While it has been necessary to raise the prices to consumers of certain durable goods by imposing special excise taxes, we have tried to avoid measures which would increase the pressure on the prices of day-to-day necessities. We have taken very special care to avoid actions which would increase prices unnecessarily and indiscriminately.
This is one of the reasons that the government rejected the course of depreciating the currency. Make no mistake about it. Depreciation, or devaluation as some people prefer to call it, would raise the whole price level, necessities and non-essentials alike, over and above whatever increases might otherwise occur. Not only does depreciation increase the cost of imports, such as coal, oil, cotton textiles and steel products, but it also raises the Canadian dollar prices of most exports and thus increases the cost of food, wood and paper, and metals to give some of the main examples. In present circumstances, depreciation would have prompt repercussions on our living costs: many items would be raised immediately and others would follow without much delay. Anyone who suggests that depreciation is not an inflationary measure in times like these is living in a world of fantasy.
Strong as are the objections to depreciation from the standpoint of its effect on prices, they are not the most conclusive argument against it. As I said the other day, if a moderate reduction in the exchange value of our currency would really solve our dollar problem, it might be well worth considering. But there is nothing to suggest that depreciation would begin to solve our dollar problem. Currency depreciation may be helpful to a country which is in balance of payments difficulties because its costs and prices are too high to enable it to compete effectively in world markets. That is certainly not our position. Our costs and prices are generally
Foreign Exchange Conservation

lower than those of other countries with whom we compete in export trade. Price competition is certainly not restricting our exports. On the contrary, we have kept our costs relatively low and at current rates of exchange our staple exports can be sold in the markets of the world in competition with any country. The fact is that our difficulty in obtaining United States dollars for our exports arises from the international financial difficulties in which some of our best customers find themselves, and it is apparent that these difficulties would not be eased by depreciating the Canadian dollar.
So far as imports are concerned, it seems most unlikely that exchange depreciation of moderate proportions would exercise a major restricting influence on our United States dollar purchases. It would be far more likely to restrict our imports from European countries which have relatively high costs and are having difficulty in producing and in making available adequate supplies for export. With regard to our purchases from the United States, it must be remembered that prices in that country have risen by about 40 per cent since the middle of 1946 and despite this increase we have steadily enlarged the volume of our imports from that source. It is difficult to imagine that a further moderate increase in the cost of these imports would result in their sharp restriction. The demand for imports from the United States is much too broadly based to be greatly or quickly affected by a moderate change in their prices.
Now some of the advocates of depreciation say that the government made a mistake in returning the Canadian dollar to par with the United States dollar in July, 1946. They say that the government's unwillingness to admit this alleged mistake is the cause of our dollar difficulties. I would certainly not argue that the government is infallible. These are very difficult times and we are doing our best to plot a course through waters which are pretty largely uncharted. Nevertheless, I want to emphasize that we believe as strongly today as we did in July, 1946, that the action then taken was in the best interests of this country. It brought our price and cost structure into betier alignment with those of other countries and it limited the increase in our price level and living costs. It helped in the readjustment to high peacetime production, and it did not in any way create difficulties for our customers abroad.
But quite apart from the validity of our decision, it is pretty far-fetched to suggest that the 10 per cent change in our exchange rate is the cause of our present dollar difficulties. That would be to claim that the

difference between a forty and a fifty odd per cent increase in the cost of imports from the United States would have reduced our purchases from that country by something of the order of $500 million. It certainly could not be maintained that a change in the rate on the Canadian dollar would have in any way relieved Europe's difficulties and thus provided us with more United States dollar exchange.

speechtext: Surely it is not as simple as that, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS, AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
It is just about as simple as that. The truth is that we should still be faced with an acute United States dollar problem today even if the rate had not been changed in 1946.
It should be stated that some of the advocates of depreciation argue that we should have continued to experience an inflow of United States capital had we not returned the dollar to parity. While there may be something in this view, it can be very easily overemphasized. Perhaps some types of capital, particularly capital seeking a speculative profit, might have more readily entered Canada with the dollar at a moderate discount, but not in a quantity to make any major difference in our exchange position. As I said the other day, that is not the sort of borrowing we want to do in the United States. If United States capital has been deterred from coming into Canada, it has, I believe, been because of the unfounded rumours which have been circulated as to possible depreciation of the Canadian dollar, coupled with a complete misunderstanding of the nature of the unofficial rate for the Canadian dollar in New York, rather than because of any real doubt as to Canada's ability to solve her current United States dollar problem. United States investors who have placed their confidence in Canada have had a remarkable record of safety and satisfaction with their Canadian investments and while during the war and at other times Canada has faced temporary difficulties, these investors have always seen Canada take the steps necessary to correct the situation. They are confident that Canada will again solve her current problems, and that confidence is soundly based. Those who spread false rumours about possible devaluation of the Canadian dollar are rendering a great disservice to this country and to those who have made and will make investments here.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS, AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS, AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Not guaranteeing the world anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS, AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
No.
There is another point which is important in regard to this oft-discussed question of currency depreciation. If we go in for depreciation when our competitive position is strong and our exports high, is there any logical end to this business of reducing the value of our currency? Much stronger reasons for depreciation could be advanced when exports are more difficult to sell. Do the advocates of depreciation suggest that we reduce the value of our currency whenever we have difficulties in our United States balance of payments, pushing our price level up farther and farther and continuously reducing the value of our money? It seems to me that is not the sort of policy that would appeal to the Canadian people. It is not the sort of policy that would be conducive to stabilization of currencies and to economic co-operation among nations.
I have not discussed the theoretical alternative of depreciating our currency to a point where it would achieve a sufficient reduction in our imports to correct our dollar position. This is not consistent with our international commitments and, even if it were, it is not the sort of alternative to which the government could give serious consideration. The drastic devaluation that would bo required would produce the kind of inflation that all of us have read about but fortunately have never experienced, and I hope never will experience, in this country. It would produce gross distortions in our economic structure and, through the friction and unrest which it would generate, it would reduce our productive capacity and our ability to compete abroad. If it severely restricted our imports from the United States, it would even more severely cut our purchases from other countries and further reduce their ability to buy from us. It might produce a substantial inflow of United States capital but that would mean in fact that we were selling Canadian assets to United States investors at bargain prices. That would involve in turn a further substantial increase in our annual dollar payments of interest and dividends to United States investors. In short, the course of drastic depreciation is one which no responsible government would choose.
In conclusion, I believe that the approach we have adopted to meet our dollar problem is the only sound and sensible one. Given time, the constructive aspects of the program should be sufficient to do the job. Meanwhile, we
have to put up with restrictions if we are to retain control of our own affairs. The government believes that the restrictive side of the program will involve comparatively little dislocation of our economy. I sincerely hope that hon. members will try to see the program as an integrated whole. It is easy enough to criticize and find objections to any particular aspect of the restrictions. None of them are welcome. But let us remember that we must save dollar exchange and that if we do not like one method of doing it we must find another. The program must be sufficient to do the job and it must be flexible enough to meet contingencies. The maladjustment in our dollar position is much too large to be corrected without a good deal of inconvenience and some difficulty.
The speed with which the constructive program achieves the needed results will depend in no small measure on our own efforts. But it must be recognized that it will also depend on external factors, namely the rate and extent of recovery in overseas countries and continuance of a high degree of co-operation with the United States.
The program is designed to overcome a national problem and it depends on a national response. The more that businessmen and the public generally support it and adopt it in their individual thinking, the quicker and the better will the program achieve the desired results. We must make a national effort to increase our dollar exports and to readjust our industry so as to reduce our dollar deficit. We must make a national effort to curtail our spending, particularly on durable goods, and to postpone new capital investment of a less essential nature. It is a program which calls for intelligent understanding and co-operation. It is the sort of program which Canadians can take in their stride and make work. We live in very troubled and uncertain times. But the Canadian people have shown a remarkable capacity to adapt themselves within the framework of their democratic institutions and traditions to changing conditions. We faced and met the challenge of the war in a manner which surprised even ourselves. We can meet this present challenge with less difficulty if we will only recognize and accept it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding
with a discussion of the question before the house, perhaps I might be allowed a word with respect to the interjection of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) with regard to the reference made to civil servants. I agree fully with the principle he laid down, but there is a corollary to that, and that is that higher civil servants let themselves get thrust into positions where they seem to be making announcements, as they did during wartime from time to time, which we all thought should have been made by the ministers. I suggest that it is a two-way street, and on that basis I agree fully with what the minister said.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think any of us envy, or indeed could envy the task of the Minister of Finance this afternoon. I wonder if he thought sadly of the budget speech of last April, of the "surplus which was greater than all surpluses", and of the "unlimited prosperity" which we had at that time. I was glad to observe a note of caution in what he said today, and I am not surprised that after these last months there is a note of caution, because I think the Canadian people are surprised, indignant - almost incredulous - after the talk of surpluses and prosperity to find that they are having austerity-I noticed the minister did not use that word today; but it is his word-they are having austerity, embargoes, under the act, new taxes, and all the things which go with it. And I suggest that the people have not even yet realized the full significance of all this, and that the government may hear a good deal more from them, when they do.
I do not wish to make too good a case, and I do not wish to be in the position of not recognizing the difficulties. So I just wish to say this, here and now: that we recognize the difficulty of getting money from Europe, we recognize the growth of purchases in the United States, we recognize the assistance we have given to others. But we say we are here today in this session, this somewhat abortive

session, not for those reasons, but because of mismanagement by the government, to which I shall now refer.
During the short time it has been my privilege to be in the House of Commons I have tried, and I hope with some success, to use moderate language. This I find it difficult to do today, because I think this bill must be one of the most preposterous bills ever presented in a free parliament.
I say that for this reason; it is not so much because of what the minister said today, but rather because of what he did not say. Listening to what he said today, one would think there was nothing really unusual in it; that we were in trouble, and that we had to impose taxes and embargoes. What I complain about, and what I believe many people are complaining about, is that this bill gives powers which have never been given before in peacetime, perhaps never even approached in wartime. It gives arbitrary powers to one man to control the industry of this country, to an extent that I would never have believed any party, and still less any party led by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), would have come to. We who have been free, moderately, are asked to put shackles on ourselves. We who have struggled for generations to achieve the position of living under the rule of law are now to live, so far as business is concerned, to a very large extent under the arbitrary powers of one man. This is control-complete, final and absolute. And I shall prove that in a minute, at least to my satisfaction, by reading certain sections of the bill.
Let me give an illustration of the fantastic lengths to which this goes. It came to my attention yesterday that an American living near the border, and who spends his summer holidays in Canada, wanted-in his own truck as I understand it-to bring some lumber across to improve his own premises in Canada. It did not involve any United States money at all, because it was his own. But he could not do it. That shows the extent to which this goes; and this is only the beginning of it.
I now wish to read one or two sections of the bill. Section 3 states:
No person shall import or attempt to import into Canada any goods listed or of the classes described in schedules I, II or III except in accordance with a permit . . .
And so on. And section 4:
No permit shall be issued for the import of goods listed in schedule I-
And that refers to luxury goods.
-unless, in the opinion of the minister, exceptional hardship would result if a permit were not issued.

Foreign Exchange Conservation
I would not object to that so much, but in section 6 we have the final pay-off. I refer particularly to paragraphs (c) and (d). But before turning to that section, let me refer to section 5 which states:
The governor in council may make regulations, etc.
That is only by order in council, of course; we are getting used to that. But when we come to section 6 we deal with administration and we find that it states:
6.	(1) Subject to this act and the regulations, the minister may
(a)	prescribe the procedure to be followed in applying for and issuing permits;
(b)	prescribe forms necessary for the administration of this act;
(c)	in particular cases or classes of cases, from time to time, prescribe terms of, and conditions to a permit or the permission granted in a permit additional to those prescribed by regulation.
In other words, the minister's judgment is absolute and final. And-and perhaps this is even worse:
(d)	authorize any person, under his control and direction, to act on his behalf under this act.
In other words, under this act, the minister is going to have these astounding powers.
It may well be asked how people who call themselves Liberals-and I think there are some real Liberals across the way-were ever brought to agree to this. The only way I can imagine is that they were told it would not last long. There has been added to Liberal principles the new Liberal principle of arbitrary powers, the application of arbitrary powers.
That is what it is. I must say I was surprised; I thought the minister did not quite do justice to the bill in that respect. It seems to me that he was not at great pains to underline to us the full extent of those arbitrary powers.
You may say, What do we want? We want law, known to all, the same for all and fair for all, such as the tariff act, which will have provisions written into it and which will not be left to the discretion of one man, and, as my colleague beside me points out, we want this law to be subject to the interpretation of the courts.
I suggest to the house that this bill is an offspring of the order-in-council mind and legislative bankruptcy, or lethargy-I do not know which it is-of the government. In any event it is a refusal to try to write a law which will be the same for all, known to all and fair for all.
I need not delay the house by arguing as
to the reason for this legislation, which is
the currency mess we have got into, and which the minister himself described at some length. How serious it is we all know. It includes not only such important things as coal and oil, as the minister pointed out, but many of the products used in manufacturing in the factories of Canada. Indeed I suppose if we managed to get into the position where we actually did run out of United States funds, it would mean widespread unemployment in Canada.
There are many people in this country who know how serious that is. They are those who have had their businesses ruined already, and who have been told that they have to come to a full stop. I shall now read a paragraph from a letter sent by the assistant deputy minister of finance to a man who is advised with regret-it was a nice letter- that.:
. . . under the regulations of the order in council the articles which you have on order may not be imported into Canada at the present time.
Then there is this paragraph which I ask the house to consider:
It is unfortunate that these necessary emergency import control regulations cut across long-established trade connections such as yours, but as the Minister of Finance has stated, the urgency of Canada's foreign exchange position forces the government to adopt these restrictions to correct it.
There you have it. Those people, and there are many of them, will understand very fully what this bill means.
I digress for a moment to refer to a point the minister brought up again today. He brought it up in his speech last November. I refer to the use of the Foreign Exchange Control Act. I would like to read from evidence given by the governor of the Bank of Canada to the senate committee on banking and commerce in August of 1946. The governor was being questioned by the Hon. Mr. Crerar as to the powers of the foreign exchange control board under the act:
Hon. Mr. Crerar:	Let me put it this way.
Supposing Eaton's, which is a large retailing establishment in Canada, wanted to buy a half a million dollars' worth of goods in the United States for sale through its stores, there might come a time in your judgment when the foreign exchange control board would say to Eaton's, "No, you cannot do that."
Mr. Towers: God forbid! sir. We have never done that, and I hope we never shall under this proposed legislation.

speechtext:
I quite realize that. I think the law officers of the crown should never have been approached on that question because, if an assurance of this kind is not valid there is no assurance of any kind, it seems to me, that is valid. I do not think the government should ever have asked the law officers of the crown that question. It was what the lawyers call an ex parte motion. The people of Canada were not represented at all when that was done. It was done simply between the government and the lay officers of the crown.
I return now to the reason which brings us here this afternoon, and that is the currency mess. The minister has dealt with it, and I shall not detain the house long on it, but I draw attention to a few things that happened.
It certainly is unfortunate that this large fund which the governor of the Bank of Canada said in August, 1946, he thought would last at least two years and perhaps longer has gone practically within one year, that it has so rapidly, so unfortunately, and so tragically been dissipated.
I want to remind the house of one or two things. In 1939 when the war began we had 3ome $400 million in the fund. As the minister pointed out, they got pretty near the bottom of the barrel in the early years of the war, but the Hyde Park agreement came to our rescue and the fund was built up, so that oy the end of 1943 there was in it $649 million; by the end of 1944, $902 million; by the end of 1945, $1,508 million, and in June of 1946. $1,624 million.

I draw attention particularly to one thing. That fund was growing steadily. It was a fund, as the governor of the bank pointed out to the senate committee, which resulted from capital movements, to a very considerable extent LTnited States investments and other capital. We did not earn it but it came in in that way, as the governor said. In June, 1946. with our dollar at 90 and the United States dollar at 100, we had achieved a rough and ready balance. Our securities in the United States at that time were quoted at 93; in other words, above the official rate. We had, as I say, achieved a kind of balance. The fund was continuing to increase up to that moment and there was, so far as I am aware, and I have heard nothing to the contrary suggested, no reason for alarm that it might not go on increasing. That was the very moment when the government, for reasons to which I shall refer later, reasons having to do with price control, which actually was a foreign principle introduced into a currency matter, pulled the plug and our United States resources cataracted down the drain. I want to explain what was in the mind of the government. They had a hope which might have been realized but it was not, but at any rate at that time the fund began to disappear, and I want to draw attention briefly to the way it went. *
In the first six months of 1946 .it had increased by $116 million. During the whole j-ear of 1946 there was a loss of $264 million. In other words, in the last six months there was a loss of $264 million plus $116 million, or a total of $380 million. But that is not the whole story.
If it is fair-and I do not know anything unfair about it-to project the conditions of the first six months of the year through the last six months, assuming that the dollar had been left where it was and where it was pretty comfortable, we would have reached a situation where we would have had $116 million in the second half of 1946, subject to this, that we would have had to make an adjustment for an increase in our United States imports in the second half. They did increase. The excess of United States imports over our exports in the second half of the year was $71 million more than in the first half. So the increase we would have had would not have been the whole $232 million, $116 million multiplied by two, but $232 million less $71 million. In other words, it would have been $161 million. If you had that $161 million and compare that $161 million with the actual loss of $264 million, you would reach the conclusion that at the end of the year we would have been $425 million better off.

Foreign Exchange Conservation
Now we come to a longer period, from July, 1946 to November, 1947. During that period we lost roughly SI,150,000,000. Can we blame the government for that? Let us examine it.
First of all, we must admit that the United States imports were up, but I shall suggest to the house that there were two very strong reasons why they were up, for both of which the government were responsible. The Minister of Finance claimed in a recent speech that going to parity had saved us $200 million, namely, ten per cent on S2 billion of purchases. There may be something in that, but it overlooks the offsets. If the dollar had been at 90 it would have deterred Canadian purchases in the United States, stimulated American purchases in Canada and operated to draw here United States investments which have practically dwindled to nothing. This is a point which has been grossly ignored by the government and was ignored at the time this action was taken. We would have had that great difference.
As I said a moment ago, United States imports had increased but the government was to a very considerable degree to blame for that and there are two reasons I shall give for that. In the first place, the government's conscious, calculated, continuing policy during that year was to go on inflating, to go on increasing the money supply, which inevitably operated as a stimulus to further purchases. And finally this: for months there were kites being flown to suggest that there would be restrictions, and so on. Indeed, it was almost as if the president of a bank said to the depositors, "Now, I am going to warn you that six months from now we shall probably not be able to pay." What do you think the depositors would do? That is what happened here. The government practically occasioned a run on American dollars.
The minister also told us that there has been a great uprising, an increase of United States imports. As a matter of fact I think a great many people rushed in to anticipate their demands. I think it is perfectly clear that it is proper for us to say that, on the basis of what I put before you, the government, by their action in June, 1946, which in retrospect seems to me to have been wholly a mistake, did lose several hundred million dollars of our exchange.
In one way it might seem almost incredible that this action was taken, and yet when one looks at the actual situation, one can realize just what it was that led ministers to this conclusion. In the speech made by the Minister of Finance in July, 1946, when the announcement was made of return to parity, to me it is a most extraordinary thing but after reading the speech very carefully, I find
no reference in it whatever to the movement of United States capital. What clearly happened is this. The government were troubled because United States prices were going up, and they hoped that we might escape that and meet United States prices coming down later on. They were going to let the people of the United States take the high road and us take the low road. It would not be a "detour over rough and difficult ground," to use the Prime Minister's words of November 17. No, this was not going to be any "detour over rough and difficult ground." We were going to go very comfortably, as I say, on the low road while the people of the United States went on over the side of the hill and came down to meet us. That was what was hoped, and I think, in the light of that, it is very interesting to read from the speech of the governor of the Bank of Canada at the annual meeting of the bank which took place last February.
I should like to say right here it seems to me that what the governor said in his speech contained notes of warning which should have been taken at that time. This is what he said in his speech of February 11:
United States prices are substantially higher than Canadian ones at the present time. Obviously this spread could not be maintained indefinitely, even if controls were retained in Canada. The return of the Canadian dollar to parity with the United States dollar last July reduced but did not remove the upward pressure on Canadian prices arising out of the rapid increase in the United States price level. However, many observers in the United States are expecting a considerable reduction in the case of some of the more extravagant price increases which took place during 1946.
You see, there was still some hope, though there was much misgiving in the mind of the governor when he made this speech. Then he goes on, and this, I think, is very important. This is the crux of the whole matter. This shows what they hoped for, the pleasant hope that they had which, unfortunately-and I think we can say unfortunately with great genuineness-did not come off. This is what he said:
If this occurs and Canadian and United States prices in general come together at a less inflated level, Canada's effort to make an orderly transition from war to peace will have borne fruit.
What does that mean? It means, as I said a few moments ago, that this was a gamble. This was a gamble that United States prices would come down. If it had succeeded it would have been a very pleasant gamble; it would have looked very clever, but it did not succeed and we are all paying the price. It did not succeed, and we lost our exchange, we failed to meet United States prices on the low level and we dried up United States
Foreign Exchange Conservation

investment in this country. That is the reason for the trouble we are in now.
Were there any warnings of any kind? Oh, yes, there were warnings. I have referred to the speech of the governor in February, which I think was a warning. There was a much stronger warning given by a well-known international banker, which appeared in the financial press some time in March, I believe. But apparently nothing could be done. I understand from the Prime Minister's speech of December 8 that they were troubled about the matter and had thought about it, but they could not do anything about it. This is what the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 66 of Hansard'.
I can say to this house quite honestly-
I do not think the Prime Minister needed to put in the words "quite honestly". I am quite sure there are not two kinds of statements which the Prime Minister makes, one which is honest and the other which is not. But I continue:
I can say to this house quite honestly, knowing the situation as I have from the beginning, that we were deeply concerned about the loss of United States dollars over quite a period, hut we were informed by those who were concerned with the Geneva negotiations that that conference had a great possibility of succeeding; and that it would be unfortunate if anything were done in Canada which would prejudice the success of the discussions that were taking place there. That was the reason we waited until we knew definitely that the final agreement had been reached before we took the step to call parliament and to have those great questions discussed here.
Well, now, that sounds grand, but I have one or two things to say about it. In the first place, it seems to me that if that was the real reason, and if we did actually refrain from giving any inkling of this to the people who were negotiating busily at Geneva, then we played a terrible trick on them. Apparently the implication of it, if I understand it, is that we could not tell them just what we were going to do here, that we would have to wait until the agreements were made; yet I suppose the measures that we are being asked to enact now will be the greatest blow to the success of these trade treaties, of which we must all desire the success. I suppose there could not be any greater blow than this, and therefore I suggest that reason is a bad one. I suggest also that other countries did take steps to meet their situation during that period because they were under pressure as we were.
I think I know the real reason, and I think the Minister of Finance told us the reason this afternoon, why they delayed. They were in the Micawber business; they were hoping for something to turn up.

I now want to read another interesting extract, and I would ask hon. members to observe that when the minister is given power he uses it. He is a realist and when he is given power he will use it. Do not let anyone be fooled on that; he has not got it just to play with. This is what he said:

Perhaps I might say of it what Churchill said of a certain speech. "Parts of it were true and parts of it were trite; the parts that were true were trite and the parts that were not trite were not true."
I should like to say just a word or two about these restrictions because they will be there in a big way. I never thought I should live to see the time when industry would have to operate, shackled as it is at the present time. These proposals will raise costs too. But what I wanted to talk about particularly at the moment is the embarrassment to business. The minister seems to me to talk about the businessmen of the country as if they were a lot of Rip van Winkles who have been asleep all the time, and as if all the minister has to do is to wave a magic wand and they will rouse up and do things they never did before. May I point out that many of these very men were here during the war helping to do the job?
The minister talks in an airy way about Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies and he suggests that they will have to change their whole way of business. There is no mystery or want of knowledge as to what brought them here. They came here for two reasons, first of all for the Canadian market, and, secondly, because they could export from here more readily to other empire countries. That was the chief reason for their coming here; and for the minister to say to them that they will have to change their whole way of doing things-well, he might as well go and bay the moon as do that. He cannot suddenly get people to change in that way. Let us try to imagine the position of a man endeavouring to set up in a new business now, a

Foreign Exchange Conservation
man of energy and initiative. What has he to do? He cannot see the minister when he comes here. The minister is too busy. Therefore such a man must see someone else, and it will be an unlikely thing if that someone else has sufficient experience or knowledge to deal with the matter, because men of experience and knowledge are back home trying to work at their own industries. The fellows who were here during the war cannot be got back here, so that as an administrative problem the thing is tremendous.
There is something else that I dislike. We have here a central bank, which I think is a good thing, and it has been well administered. But do not let us fool ourselves. It has taken away from the free expression of the chartered banks, for they are people subject to authority now. And we are going to do the same thing to industry in this country. How hon. members opposite can swallow this pill I do not know. Have they done it because they think it will be only for a matter of months? The minister says that months may be many months. Well, if my hon. friends think it is only a matter of months or of a few years, they had better forget it. Unless we get manna from heaven in the shape of the Marshall plan, or something of the kind, this will not be merely for a few months or a few years. This kind of power grows. It has grown, a colleague of mine says. Of course it grows. I read a book describing similar powers in the United States and there was in that book one phrase which I shall never forget. It is this, "Coercion is insatiable". I should like hon. members to remember'that.
I was glad to see a socialist friend of mine, Professor Underhill of the University of Toronto, writing the other day that we need vision, energy, enterprise and initiative in this country. Does anyone think this will conduce to that sort of thing? Does anyone think people who will be shackled, as this measure shackles them, will have vision and energy?
As a matter of fact, what I fear is that with this tied economy here and a free economy over the line, some able people will be constrained to leave this country and go elsewhere, where there is a chance for their energies.
Let us ask ourselves this question:	What
is possible under this measure? I have tried to look at that question because, after all, we are in a mess and must do something about it. That brings me back to the question of money or currency. As I said, I think there is an extraordinary measure of agreement in this country that what was done in July, 1946, was wrong. 1 am not saying that everyone who thinks that necessarily shares my view as to what should be done now, but I think there is an extraordinary measure of agreement that our present troubles flow from what was done then. For the life of me I cannot see why it it is not so; because, as I repeat again, in July, 1946, we had a kind of rough equilibrium which the government rudely disturbed.
I now want to make this point. I believe that these remedies will be seriously retarded unless we have a sound currency condition. If one looks at our background, as I said a few minutes ago, one realizes-quite properly in my opinion-that we have relied to a considerable extent on United States investment here; and it is the cutting off of that which is largely responsible for what is happening now. We have reached a kind of impasse, in my opinion, and we have now three courses open to us in the matter of currency.
The first is to stay as we are, and the minister assures us again that the government is adamant on that point. It is an unfortunate thing that our dollar and the United States dollar have the same name. They are not necessarily the same thing. The fact that they have the same name I think often deludes us into having a kind of false pride that they should have the same value. The French franc and the Italian lira at one time had the same value, but it was a fortunate thing they did not have the same name, because there was never any worship of the sacred cow in the matter of keeping them at the same level. I would say that the government as well as the Department of Finance have become the prisoner of their own ideas and are in great danger of relying on the doctrines of the textbook, instead of coming out into the clear, open air of reality, facing conditions as they are and dealing with them in a common-sense manner.
I want to read from something the minister said in his speech on December 9, and this will be found on page 91 of Hansard.'.
Currency depreciation is a device which may be resorted to, and which it may be desirable to resort to. if the value, either internal or external, of one's currency is below its real purchasing power; but that is not the case with respect to the Canadian dollar. We are not handicapped in a single export market of the world because our dollar is at par with the

Foreign Exchange Conservation
United States dollar. We are not losing a single sale in that market because our prices are too high.
I confess that when I read that statement it puzzled me a great deal. I do not set myself up to be an expert on exchange. However, I discussed it with a couple of experts or a couple of people whom I thought to be experts. One of them said it was so confused that he did not know whether it meant anything at all; and the other said that it meant exactly the opposite of what the minister said. Therefore, when I reached that stage I decided I would lay off it and not try' to be an expert at all.

Just this I will say on it. I think the ordinary man in the street in July', 1946, thought that when we appreciated our dollar to parity, one of the reasons was that at ninety cents it was considered to be below its true purchasing value.
But I am not going to bandy words on that. I want to appeal to the verdict of facts, because I think facts are stubborn things. It is on that ground that I venture to say' what I am going to say. It is an appeal to reality because I think at the present time we are living in an ivory tower and are trying to pretend things exist which do not exist. The Canadian dollar is valued today in New York at 12$ per cent discount which is approximately two cents less than when the minister's speech was made in November. That is not good. I know it is said by the foreign exchange control board that that really does not mean anything, because those dollars are not dealt with in the ordinary way. But I say this: Let anyone laugh off the test of value which comes from transactions between willing purchasers and willing sellers in very substantial amounts. If that is not a verdict of value, I should like to know what is. I know the difficulties. The minister has pointed them out. I know the fact that we did not get hard money from Europe has contributed to this question. I know that very well. But on the other hand, for the government here in Canada to say that the Canadian dollar is worth 100 United States cents seems to me rather laughable, because I can well imagine an American saying, "Come over here and see for yourself that it is not worth 100 United States cents. We are dealing with it at eighty-eight cents". The government seems to be like a man in a boat with the tiller in his hands, trying to steer the boat when the rudder is out of the water. Therefore he has no control. Whether we can compare the

government to King Canute I do not know; I will leave that. At any rate the results of what has been done are clear: excessive purchases of United States commodities; confusion worse confounded-embargoes and taxes; people put out of business, and the whole turmoil we are in, which the minister described very well.

Whether that is because we have been trying to dictate our ideas there, I do not know; but I suggest that also is not a good thing for Canadian credit.
I have spoken about the dollar and keeping it as it is; and I refer now to the second alternative, which is to let the dollar go free. That, I am sure, is the objective of most people in this house. I do not think it is an immediate objective. Personally I feel that we have to go by degrees; nevertheless I believe that is the only real objective we can have. I hate controls, but if I thought they would work I would stomach my dislike of them. The reason I am against them is that all history shows that in the end they bring their own retribution. There is another reason for not letting the dollar go free, and that is that we have obligations under Bretton Woods. I will say quite frankly that I think the world is too unsettled at the present time for us to take that risk. I will point out also in aid of the minister that when it was done after the first war-and incidentally there has been a great disposition to pretend that everything done after the first war was stupid, but I am not so sure it was stupid-in letting the dollar go free they had Europe on its feet and not on its back, as it is now. *
Then I come to the third suggestion, which has been made already by my leader and which- I repeat, of the dollar at ninety cents. Of course there are a great many unpleasant things about it. Tire minister has outlined them very well, and I agree with much of what he said. I do not suggest it because it is nice; I suggest it because I think it may help us to avoid worse things. When the minister 'says it would do no good that does not convince me at all. The minister said a little while ago that an additional ten per
cent in the price would not deter purchases in the United States. To me that is a most unconvincing argument. Rising prices are always a deterrent, and the last ten per cent is like half an inch on the end of your nose; it makes quite a difference.
Mr. ABBOTT; It all depends on your nose.
Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario); Furthermore you may as well say that if a company is not making a profit the addition of ten per cent to its gross would not help; but everyone knows that the last ten per cent of the gross usually makes the difference between a profit and a loss. I am sure the minister will not contradict that. We do not want to expect too much from this. I am not suggesting that it is going to work any miracle; no fear. The damage has been done. If you go to a doctor after disregarding the rules of health for eighteen months he cannot cure you over-night; he can only set you back on the road to recovery. I am not suggesting that anything can be quickly done. But when people say it will not do anything I reply, first of all, that when we were at ninety before, we appeared to be in a condition of very considerable financial health and stability. To give them every credit, the department were beginning to ease the restrictions. Business was getting rid of a few of the shackles, but of course when this happened they were put on again. We have a shackled economy now, and the minister will make it worse. Even at the present time we have all kinds of financial restrictions. In Germany they used to have travel marks, this kind of marks and that kind of marks. If you inquire into the regulations of the foreign exchange control board it will make you dizzy. They have all kinds of different rates at which money can be had for this purpose and that purpose and the other purpose, according to the judgment of the board as to the relative desirability of the transaction that is to take place. In other words, they are supposed to have all the wisdom of Solomon.
Another point I wish to make clear is this. I have spoken a good deal about American investment in this country. I do not want anyone to think I believe that going to ninety will suddenly bring about a rush of American investment, or anything of the kind. As a matter of fact, that action would be only recognizing facts, because at the present time they do not value our dollar at more than ninety, so that we will not have a rush of investment. What I do think, however, is that a movement toward reality will win respect from American businessmen. I think they

doO

will regard it as as sign of realism. I do not think they will regard it as a sign of weakness but as a sign of strength; and, furthermore, I think it can be maintained that it is not depreciation in the ordinary sense. It is going back to where we were. However, I do not press that.
It will, I believe, do three salutary things. In the first place, it will deter purchases from the United States. Second, it will stimulate sales. Third, it will tend-and I only say "tend"-in the long run to bring back American investment, which in my opinion we shall need for many years in this country.
I know the difficulties that are there. It will send up some prices, and there may be a tendency to exaggerate that. It will make our coal cost more, but it will not be as bad as some of the things we have now, as a result of which many other articles, some of them in great need, particularly for domestic use by young people setting up housekeeping, are going to cost twenty-five per cent more, which is bad enough. Of course some of those things may be included in the changes the minister has made.

The second thing it will do, and I do not minimize this at all, is make it more difficult for Britain to sell here. I would not willingly add one featherweight to Britain's burden; but my answer to that is if we are over-valued, Britain is over-valued; and my feeling is that there has to be a recognition of reality, not only by us, but by other people. At the p- sent time I believe part of our troubles, and no small part, is due to the over-valuation of currencies, and in that connection I want to read a short extract from a book I have in my hand, which seems to me to put the matter very well indeed. I think the point is of such importance that I am going to ask .the house to let me read this quotation. This book is by one Henry Hazlitt, a writer of standing, I believe, and is called, "Will Dollars Save the World?" I am reading from page 18:
When a currency is over-valued ... it produces a chronic surplus of imports over exports. The over-valuation of a nation's currency makes imports cheaper than they would otherwise be in the terms of that currency. This naturally encourages people in that nation to increase their purchases of imports. The over-valuation of the currency tends, on the other hand, to make the prices of that nation's exports high in terms of other currencies. This discourages other countries from buying.
I wish to interject here a remark about Bretton Woods, because I may forget to say

it later. I have no apology to make for having voted for Bretton Woods, because I thought two years ago we were entitled to believe that recovery might proceed at a different pace from what it did. I would point this out, that at the time we voted for Bretton Woods what we feared was everywhere competition in depreciation. But what have we got? We have not got that at all. We have competition in appreciation, because nations have been so keen to have goods from the United States they have appreciated their currency and, in some cases I believe, very unwisely.
Then, to continue my quotation:
Suppose, for example, that a French brandy sells in Paris for 1,200 francs a bottle. The black-market rate for the franc is about 280 to the dollar as this is being written. Let us assume that in a free market the franc would sell a little higher-say about 240 to the dollar. At such a rate the brandy could be bought for $5 a bottle in American money. But the official rate for the French franc, which the American importer is now forced to pay, is 119 to the dollar. This means that the brandy must cost him more than $10 a bottle. The arbitrary exchange rate enforced by the French police raises the price as much as would a 100 per cent American import duty (on top of the duty that we actually impose). And this applies to every French import to this country. Is it surprising, apart from any other factor, that France is exporting so relatively little to us?
I said at the beginning that this measure of control is complete, final and absolute. We shall continue to have the forms of freedom in business, just as they had it in nazi Germany under Schacht, but we shall increasingly lose the realities.
It is obvious, of course, that this is a socialist measure. They are entitled to believe in a completely planned economy. Once started, it will be terribly hard to control it. There is a tendency for it to go on. In my opinion there is no reason whatever to believe that it will end in any near future.
Having regard to this socialist aspect, I should like to read a brief extract I ran across in a socialist paper, the New Statesman. The article by Mr. Vallance was headed "Plans for the Planners." Here is a man who has the courage of his convictions in a big way. He says:
With every step which the government is compelled to take in the direction of operational planning, it will become progressively more advisable, indeed imperative, to extend the sector of nationalized industry. This is the inescapable consequence of the sort of planning which as a nation we cannot avoid taking and which cannot be halted half way.
Then there is this closing sentence which I think everyone should consider and ruminate upon:
Who rides a tiger must never dismount.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS, AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) discussing one of the most important bills that have been placed before this house for many a long day, a bill which, with all its powers, is perhaps necessary in some respects in order to protect the Canadian people at the present time.
If I may make a first criticism of what has been done I would say that the steps taken by the government to protect the Canadian economy in the present adverse exchange situation were taken too late. Had the government taken some steps earlier-and I shall have more to say on this later on-we might have avoided the necessity of seeking a credit of S300 million in the United States.
May I at once associate myself with what the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario said this afternoon about the impropriety of attacking in this house the permanent officials of Canada. Both hon. gentlemen quite properly warned the house that this should not be done because the men so attacked are not responsible for
government policy. Their advice would be tendered to any government, and the government itself must decide whether to accept or reject that advice. Consequently the officials should not be criticized in the manner in which they have been for tendering the advice which the government seeks.
The bill, as I said a moment ago, is a very important and drastic measure for peacetime. Yet if we look back to 1943 and 1944 it was obvious that many of the steps we took then to protect Canada's economy in wartime would have to be taken in order to protect our economy in the post-war period. I think the government was ill advised to remove controls as rapidly as they were removed.
We have a number of prohibitions in this bill. I do not want to labour the point, but in my opinion those prohibitions and quotas should have been accompanied by measures of control, control not only of the goods imported under quota into our country but of goods of the like class or kind produced in Canada, whether prohibited entry or coming in under quota. .
The bill was attacked by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario this afternoon on the ground that it conferred arbitrary powers on the government. It does confer quite arbitrary powers. But may I point out to the hon. gentleman and to the house that his whole speech this afternoon was, in my opinion, a request for the continuation of arbitrary powers in the hands of irresponsible and private persons, in the sense that they are not responsible to the people of Canada? I would much prefer, if we are to have arbitrary and emergency powers conferred at all, to have them placed in the responsible hands of the ministers of the crown, who are in turn responsible to parliament, as parliament is responsible to the people of this country. Consequently I cannot agree with the criticisms that were made of the measure from that point of view by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario.
As far as the devaluation of the dollar is concerned, I think our views are well known. Right from the outset we took the position that the devaluation of the dollar at this time would involve an added burden upon the mass of consumers in this country, and I think the hon. gentleman who spoke this afternoon recognized that when he said that a 90-cent dollar would cause a lot of unpleasant things. These unpleasant things, Mr. Speaker, would have been felt mainly by the consumers of Canada through still higher prices for many of the goods they must use.
There can be no question to my mind that the prohibition of the importation of luxury
Foreign Exchange Conservation

goods under the circumstances which this country faces and the curtailment or even the prohibition of luxury travel are two necessary steps to protect the Canadian dollar position at this time. But whatever may have been necessary, it should not have involved the prohibition of what we consider to be essential health foods or essential household commodities. Many of the goods prohibited or placed under quota are goods to which we have become accustomed in our homes as necessities rather than as luxuries, and to my mind the prohibitions in that field are much too wide.
Again, may I say that in spite of what the minister said this afternoon I think it was a mistake that we invoked the non-discriminatory clause of the Geneva treaty before we had to bring it into effect in 1948. Indeed, even then we do not have to bring it into effect because, if the conditions we face today in Canada continue, we can, with the consent of the other signatories to the treaty, extend the time further before we need to put that clause into effect. So the principal criticism that one is inclined to level immediately against the policy of the government in regard to these prohibitions and the use of this clause of the treaty is that it was invoked when it was unnecessary, in the second instance, and that the prohibitions and quotas were not accompanied by any attempt to control prices.
A further weakness with which I shall deal later is this. We quite overlook the fact, if we are going to place power in the hands of a minister to develop and plan the Canadian economy, that we must consider the effect upon our economy of those great monopolies and cartels which play such an important part in the economic life of all countries and to which Mr. McGregor, commissioner in charge of the Combines Investigation Act, referred in the report he submitted to parliament some time ago. Canadian Industries .Limited, for example, controlled as it is by two powerful international cartels, du Pont de Nemours and Imperial Chemical Industries, can do a great deal to prevent the minister and the government and parliament from putting into effect policies which are essential to the welfare of Canada at this time.
When the speech from the throne was read by His Excellency the Governor General I had hoped that in it there might have been, in view of the McGregor report, some reference to legislation that might be brought down to meet the needs of this country and to prevent the exploitation of our people by some of these great monopolies and international cartels. Until we are prepared to deal with that problem, and deal with it quite thoroughly, many

of the powers placed in the hands of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) to develop the economy of this country may be nullified by the activities of such organizations as I have mentioned.
Bill No. 3 clearly envisages the integration of our economy more closely with that of the United States. That, I believe, may prove, on a short-term plan, beneficial to a number of our producers, and we welcome some of the tariff cuts which will benefit some of the primary producers of our country; but in spite of the short-term advantages, I am wondering whether in the long run the integration of our economy with that of the United States will prove beneficial to Canada.
As I said a week ago, our economy is largely competitive with that of the United States, and we have been in the habit of trading as a member of the Atlantic triangle. It is true that Great Britain is no longer able to trade as she was before the war. But may I point out to hon. gentlemen that in integrating our economy with an economy which is competitive with ours, we are running grave dangers, and in spite of all that may be said with regard to the difficulties which our best long-term customer has been faced with over the last two years, nonetheless there are signs that the economy of Great Britain is rapidly reaching the stage where I do not think the people who are critical of what has happened there will be .inclined, if I may put it in a slang phrase, to sell Great Britain short.
In the last few weeks I have noticed in the papers some very interesting statistics and statements. If we look, for example, at the New York Times of a week ago, and at the graphs which accompany the article dealing with the British recovery up to that point we find the following:
An indication of the strides made in the iron and steel industry is conveyed by a comparison of the current rate of production with that in 1938. Using the 1938 level as 100, the current output of pig-iron stands at 115, that of steel ingots and castings at 135, cold rolled strip at 307, light rolled products at 142 and steel castings at 159.
And if we look at the figures which probably are more symptomatic of the recovery we find that the figures for coal are very impressive indeed. I am quoting from The Nation:
Since the national coal board took over the mines on January 1, 1947, the total output has been some five million tons greater than in the comparable period of 1946. In the week ending November 8, production was 97 per cent of the 1938 average, though the available working force

Foreign Exchange Conservation
was considerably lower. Since the five-day week was introduced last May, absenteeism has declined and over-all output per man-shift risen.
There we have an indication that perchance our long-term and best customer is rapidly reaching the point where she may turn the corner definitely, and in a few years may be able to resume the trading relationships, not perhaps in the same way, but be able to resume the trading relationships upon which our prosperity has so largely depended.
We sometimes overlook the fact that prior to the war something like twenty per cent of all the goods offered for sale on the markets of the world were bought by the United Kingdom, some of them consumed in her own country, some in fabrication to export and some for re-export, and we were a beneficiary of that system. Yet we find that today the British manufacturers are pointing out to the government of the country that that recovery and that move toward normal trade relationships is being impeded by policies very similar to those which we are putting into effect in our country at the present time.
In the Montreal Gazette of today, December 16, appears a report dated London, December 15, as follows:
British manufacturers, trying to boost Britain's export trade, are suffering from an underlying sense of frustration and increasing uncertainty, a delegation from the National Union of Manufacturers today told Harold Wilson, board of trade president. The delegation showed him the analysis of 1,146 replies to a questionnaire submitted to its membership of 50 trade associations and 4,000 manufacturers in many branches of industry. Most serious problems facing exporters, the report said, were restrictions imposed by foreign, dominion and colonial governments.
Import restrictions in the British commonwealth showed an almost complete embargo in India and Pakistan, and there were long lists of widely varied goods which could not be sent to Australia, New Zealand, Canada and South West and East Africa.
Except for restricted classes of goods, similar difficulties were being encountered in Belgium. Denmark, France, Greece, Holland, Norway. Portugal, Spain and Sweden.
Manufacturers were also finding difficulties in exporting to the United States and South America. Middle East. Egypt and Turkey all were reported difficult or impossible for a long list of goods.
Then this significant paragraph appears:
The National Union of Manufacturers recommended that "The government should regard as its most urgent task the conclusion of trade agreements with foreign countries, if necessary on a bilateral or barter basis, and the arrival at suitable understandings with the dominion and colonial governments, in order that British exporters may be assured of their markets and of their supplies of raw materials."
Then there appears one criticism of the government which I should also read. It is as follows:
The report criticized government bulk-buying of raw materials and recommended simplification of steel allocation to manufacturers.
There we have a statement regarding the trade relationships, and we find this powerful group, still powerful in Great Britain, urging that, if this condition continues, attempts be made to enter into bilateral trading relationships. That is a serious matter, because we realize that Canada in a peculiar way has depended upon a different sort of relationship. The very phrase I used a few moments ago, the "Atlantic triangle" indicates that we were once able to sell vast quantities of goods to Great Britain and buy vast quantities from the United States, and to have a deficit on our account in the United States and a credit in Great Britain, and the credit in Britain wiped out our deficit in the United States. Therefore, when we see our own country moving in the direction of restrictions, I say this is unnecessary at the moment because the non-discrimination clause of the Geneva trade agreements should not, in my opinion, have been put into effect until it was quite necessary to do so. Our dollar position gave us the right to forgo that until at least January 1. 1949. and even beyond that with the consent of the signatories to the treaty.
What I wanted to say particularly tonight was this. The whole program of the government can be made ineffective if we allow the powerful interests in our country-I call them irresponsible interests-who have an arbitrary power of which the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario complained, to continue to exercise that power. The McGregor report indicated how that power was exercised in Canada. I hope all hon. gentlemen have read the report. Just over four years ago, during the war, when we in this party pointed out how these powerful influences were being strengthened in our country, we were taken to task by various members of the house and were asked again and-again what proof there was of these statements. We used to go then for proof very largely to the United States, but today all we have to do is to read the official report submitted to the government by Mr. McGregor of the combines investigation organization to find that proof-reports submitted at the request of the government.
It seems to me that if we are going to achieve what the government hopes to achieve under the plans for the development of our economy there is one thing more that should be done, and that is there should be a thorough
Foreign Exchange Conservation

investigation into the control of powerful segments of the Canadian economy by monopolies and by international cartels. I would go as far as to say that it warrants the setting up of a royal commission before which witnesses could be called and the officials who are responsible for the enforcement of the Combines Investigation Act could appear.
In my opinion the organization enforcing the Combines Investigation Act is entirely inadequate to meet the task. When we have spoken of monopolies sometimes in this house we have heard the comment, as the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) interjected the other day, "Why don't you lay a charge in the courts against one of these monopolies or combines?" That sounds all right in the House of Commons; but, as hon. gentlemen know, no individual member of this house would stand very much chance of laying a charge against one of these powerful monopolies because it would ruin him financially and the monopoly could hire the best legal talent in the country in order to defeat the objective one had in view.
We are prohibiting, for example, the importation of radios into this country. I will give a personal experience of mine during the last few days. I happened to be in a large store in this city last Thursday, and on the counter I saw a portable radio similar to one which my wife has, which was given to her as a present last summer by a doctor friend in New York. I brought that radio back and when I was going to do so I had to ask what my friend had paid for it. He told me $96, so I declared that value, and last Thursday I saw in the local store in question a radio exactly like it, made by the General Electric Company. I went up to the counter and said, "That is a very nice radio; what is the price of it?" I was told the price was $197 plus the new excise tax, bringing it to over $240.
The radio industry in this country is a highly protected one, not highly protected merely by the tariff authorized by this parliament, but protected on account of the patent arrangements and the other factors that enter into the making of radios. The radio may be said to be a luxury. I do not regard it as such, especially in many homes where there is someone in the family unable to get out. Under those circumstances it is not a luxury. But if we regard it as a luxury, then I say there is a group of people who are controlling the patents in this country and who today are going to be still further protected because we cannot import radios from the United States.
It is quite probably true, as the Minister of. Finance said this afternoon, that the

number of importations during the past twelve months was very small in comparison with the number of radios manufactured and sold in this country, but there is a concrete example of exorbitant Canadian prices. Then we come to fertilizers, and very necessary drugs and medicines as well, and so on, manufactured by Canadian Industries Limited.
Canadian Industries Limited, as the McGregor report well points out, is under the control completely of two great international monopolies which have formed an international cartel. I refer, of course, to d>u Pont de Nemours and Imperial Chemical Industries. Mr. McGregor brings evidence to show that this cartel allowed Canadian Industries Limited to be set up, but set up for Canada only, and the company organized for Canada is forbidden, except under express permission from the parent companies, to export some of the commodities which it manufactures. Yet we find the government saying that this measure, Bill No. 3, is designed to increase our exports in order that we may get dollar exchange.
The same thing applies to electrical supplies. During the war we did develop a fairly substantial export trade in various electrical devices made in this country; but if we look at the figures over the last year and follow the speech made by the deputy minister of trade and commerce recently, we find that during the last year electrical equipment from Canada for export has fallen to a very low level indeed; that, again, because electrical supplies are largely under the control of a monopoly and are linked up with a great international cartel.
And so I say to the government tonight that if we are to benefit at all from prohibitions which involve great sacrifices on the part of the Canadian people, if the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) is to carry out the provisions of the bill which foreshadow the building of the Canadian economy along a new and perhaps stronger line, then we have to deal with the control of our economy by these monopolies and cartels. During the war the Minister of Munitions and Supply, now Minister of Reconstruction, in reply to me, said that he was engaged in fighting a war and that at that moment he was not interested in dealing with monopolies and cartels. Well, the war is over and here we have a bill before us ostensibly designed to foster the Canadian economy, to foster the building of various types of supplies and equipment in our country for export. And we find in the McGregor report-it is not a statement of mine but is found in the

Foreign Exchange Conservation
McGregor report-evidence to prove that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply may be checkmated in any efforts he makes along the line which the bill visualizes.
I say to the government that the time has come when there should be a thorough investigation into the operations of these large cartels and organizations within our own country. A cartel is, of course, an international organization; but we have parts of these cartels in the form of various nation-wide, monopolistic industries in our own country, and it is with those that we can deal. I quite agree with what Mr. McGregor says regarding international cartels, namely, that they will have to be dealt with probably by international action. Nevertheless we have the opportunity within our country to deal with some components of these organizations in our midst. So I say to the government that if the sacrifices of the Canadian people involved in this particular measure are to bring results to us, other action must be taken than that which is visualized in the bill.

Here we have the report to which I referred, "Canada and International Cartels, an Inquiry into the Nature and Effect of International Cartels and Trade Combinations." Everything I have said tonight can be found within the covers of this government publication to which I have referred. So I wanted particularly to emphasize this angle.
Before I conclude my remarks I want to say that, in my opinion, the government must do more than prohibit and must do more' than put Certain supplies under quota. In my opinion the government must see to it that the people of Canada who are denied access to goods are not exploited by groups, of arbitrary interests that operate within the borders of our own country.
We are up against these difficulties. This afternoon the minister spoke of the necessity, of getting steel. Why do we not develop, our steel industry to a greater extent in our own country? For example, we find that Canadian manufacturers have been held up and handicapped by a lack of steel. Yet what are we doing? We have a great development at Steep Rock where some of the finest iron ore on the continent has been mined. All that iron ore goes to the United States. Yet we are busily importing iron ore from the United States. We send iron ore over the border at one point and bring other ore back over the border at another point. Canada used the dollars which we obtained from Great Britain to pay our United States friends for their exports to us. This multilateral trade triangle worked quite satisfactorily for Canada.
But unfortunately the war came along, and with it came many dislocations. For one reason or another the British found they could no longer pay us in United States dollars; and for the past two years, to a large extent, the merchandise which we have sold to Britain and other western democracies, has been sold on credit. But we have had to continue buying from the United States in hard cash. Our purchases have increased rapidly. If my figures are correct I believe that since the first

We in the C.C.F. group, despite the tardiness of the government, despite the lack of planning, agree that some such bill as is before us is unavoidable at this time. But we thinik we see numerous weaknesses, numerous omissions and numerous dangers in it.
Our first criticism is, of course, the fact that, as we see it, it will nullify any trade advantages which might have accrued to Canada from the Geneva agreements. On Tuesday evening we listened to the Prime Minister eulogizing the great horizons the agreements were opening up for Can-adian trade. Yet every hon. member in this house knows that, as long as this bill is law, the Geneva agreements cannot mean a great deal to the people of Canada. As has been pointed out several times today the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) suggested that these restrictions-may last only a few months.
