The fourth feature of these restrictions which many members of this group are not keen about is the $300 million loan. In the past, Canada has made many loans, but usually those loans have been used to increase our wealth or to increase our productive capacity. It seems to us that this loan will be used simply to pay living expenses. In other words, Canada will be in a position something like that of a man who goes to a bank and borrows money to keep up a standard of living which he cannot afford. It seems to us that we should pay our way as we go, because this is only going to postpone the day of reckoning. It may be that we have to make the loan; but, if so, perhaps the minister would say why we
{Mr. Thatcher.]
cannot borrow from the international monetary fund, which was set up by Bretton Woods and from which I understand we could borrow up to $75,000,000 annually. I thought that was what it was for.
The fifth thing I do not care very much for in regard to 'these restrictions-and I am speaking personally-is this. Some people wonder why the government has not seen fit to remove the virtual embargo on the export of Canadian beef cattle and certain agricultural products. It has been estimated that about $100,000,000 could be realized in the United States from these sources. In this time of crisis, when we need United States dollars so badly and when the Americans are anxious to buy our cattle, I wonder why we are overlooking this source. There is the further point, as to how long Canadian farmers should be deprived of the benefits of the United States market, where I believe prices are anywhere from one and a half to two and a half times as high as Canadian prices. It is quite probable that if this virtual embargo were lifted or relaxed the British market would be affected. But I understand that at the moment a committee is in Ottawa negotiating for a market in Britain next year; and there is very great danger, I am told, that we may not have this market, or that it will be greatly reduced. In the newspapers of December 9 I read a Canadian Press dispatch which quoted food minister Strachey of Britain as having said:
It is too early to say whether Britain will be able to buy any bacon in Canada next year.
So I suggest that the day may soon come when we shall need that United States market. It might not be advisable to remove the embargo completely, but we could at least allow some of our cattle to go to that market and realize United States prices. I would be quite prepared to admit that if we took this action our domestic prices probably would be affected; but I do not think it is fair to remove price ceilings from, say, 998 items and leave them on only one or two. In other words, it is discrimination to take the ceilings off everything the farmer has to buy and leave them on the things he is producing. I believe the minister should at least give the house a statement as to the intention of the government in this regard. I suppose there is some good reason why we are overlooking that source of funds at the present time, but I hope that before the day is over, or at least before the debate is through, the minister will make a statement.
The sixth feature of this bill about which this group is not in agreement is the higher excise tax; in fact we strongly object to it.

When the war ended, the program was carried over into civilian life; a director was appointed, and the government gave the program considerable financial backing. Does it not seem strange, then, that now we should be undoing that good work, and taxing the very people we are trying to make fit? I think this tax is vicious and unfair. Mr. Speaker, I feel tonight it is necessary for me to say something on this measure for the reason that it is the one which forms the austerity program now facing the Canadian people. Just before leaving home to attend this session, I was met by a number of people registering grievances concerning the proposed austerity program. I was met by one or two small businessmen who despaired of their own businesses. I was met by others who, for years, had desired to purchase cars but who now find, either that they are unable to obtain those cars or, if they are obtainable, that they must pay excise taxes, of such proportions as to render them incapable of buying.
I was surprised to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) say, when he interrupted the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), that no one was under any legal obligation to pay the excise tax. I am willing to let the lawyers fight out the technicalities of that statement, but I would ask the minister to realize something of the practicality of the situation. If a man gees today to buy

a car and tells his dealer that he will take the car, but that he is under no legal obligation to pay the excise tax, does the minister tell me that the car will be delivered to the purchaser? Apparently he does not want to answer the question. It is all very well to say that there is no legal obligation to pay the excise tax; but no one gets the goods without paying it. I listened with a good deal of interest to the minister's speech this afternoon. It was a nice speech, in that it was an attempt to explain the situation in which Canada now finds itself and the manner in which the government is attempting to creep out from underneath the burden of administration. But let me say that, while the speech sounded nice, the voice of austerity will sound much louder than did the minister's speech, especially when the people realize that in Canada today, three years after we have passed through the austerity and severity of wartime economy, they are now being asked to go back to that period of austerity. That is the voice which will sound louder in their ears, especially when they cannot have, three years after the war, those things of which they were deprived during the war. And as my hon. friend the member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) adds, they were promised these things too.
What will be happening within the next few months? During the war years, we were told how the compulsory savings of the taxpayers would be a little nest-egg to be used when we reached the time of peace. They would (hen be able to spend it on goods that would be available. Now what is happening? Just at a time when the compulsory savings are to be returned to the people, a lot of excise taxation is slapped on the goods that the people will need; and in a period of uncontrolled consumer prices, in a period of inflation, how far will those same dollars go? That is the question which will face the people of Canada during the next few months. The war has been over for about three years and we should be looking towards a period of abundant prosperity, comfort, contentment, peace of heart and mind, and security. Now the people are being asked to go through a period of austerity. Something must have gone wrong somewhere, and it is the government's responsibility to tell us, not what has happened, not how things have gone wrong, but why they have permitted things to go wrong.
The leader of this party a little while ago mentioned the fact that not only is Canada being asked now to go through a period of
austerity, but that other countries seem to be facing austerity too. Great Britain was mentioned, also Australia; and even the United States, which seems to be wealthy in dollars, is facing difficulties. If all these nations now, almost three years after the war, are being asked to go through a period of austerity, somebody in the world somewhere must be prospering. You see, it just does not make sense that, three years after the war when our productive system has been geared to a peacetime economy and a peacetime production potential, all these nations should now be facing austerity. Something is wrong somewhere, and someone else somewhere or another must be benefiting. Just try to figure that out. If my logic is wrong I wish someone would say so.
It does seem to me that someone has bungled somewhere. So many policies that are adopted to me just do not make sense. I mention this one right now, three years after the war. It does not make sense to me. What are we told now? We must take our production, our real wealth, those things that are made by the workmanship and skill of our own workers and the technical brains of our scientists and send them out of the country. It does not make sense to me for a government to propose a policy and say that we are going to benefit by getting rid of our real wealth. It does not make sense to me for the government to tell us that we cannot enjoy our own national abundance because we have not got somebody else's dollars.	*
With respect to the monetary -technique of which this group have spoken here a good many times in past years, to say that we have to pay interest on money which is created by the stroke of a pen and which the government could create through its own bank, that does not make sense to me either. There is no question in my mind., Mr. Speaker, that our present difficulties have their roots, if not entirely, partly at least in that old Bretton Woods agreement which we fought here two years ago. How this group fought against being tied to that international monetary fundi Xt was drawing on towards Christmas, and how we were accused of trying to create a filibuster! How unpopular we were with people who did not know anything about the agreement. Yet we were told that it would be part of the solution of the world's post-war economic ills. It was passed as a sort of cure-all, although the minister admitted that perhaps it was not altogether perfect. I am quite convinced that the present austerity program is partly the result of our being tied hand and foot to the Bretton Woods agreement. We shall have something more to say on that when we discuss the Geneva trade agreements. It does seem to me to be a dangerous thing to tie our internal economy to some external legal monetary authority. I am certain of this, that we cannot manage our internal economy according to the will of our Canadian people, because we find ourselves tied to an external monetary power.
What has happened? The government tried to tell us that that agreement would bring peace, prosperity and enjoyment upon the earth. They have told us for years that their policy of free trade among nations would bring us to the verge of utopia. Anyone who talked in terms of economic nationalism was surely taboo in this house. Now what do we find our position to be? We find now that, through some sort of bungling, the present government has been forced to an economic nationalism, the severity of which no economic nationalist in his right mind would ever dream of. That, to my mind, is the truth.
I am not going to say any more except to register my severe objections to this bill. The leader of this group has suggested that it should go to the banking and commerce committee. I do not know whether it is the inten-

tion of the Minister of Finance to send it there. In his speech this afternoon he said that he did not think these experts who are sometimes called bureaucrats could be blamed, and that the government would have to stand or fall by the policy which it had adopted. But let us remember this, and I have nothing to say against the advisers of the government. They are good men in their places; they are capable men in their places, but when they give advice which is wrong I do not believe their right place is in that field any longer. That is my honest conviction. Let us remember that governments come and governments go, but the advisers stay on forever, and when they advise the government with respect to this or that policy and it proves to be wrong, even though it cost the life of the government, another government coming in would be subject to the same advice from the same people. That is what I call, not the strength of our parliamentary and democratic institution, but the weakness of it.
I say this, and this is where I believe the austerity program is going to be so severe. I believe we shall discover within the next few months, and perhaps within the next year-I do not know how long the program will last- that no end of small businesses will go on the rocks. There is no question about that. Big business is not always bad business. We hear a lot in this house from some quarters about big business. Well, I am not prepared to say that big business is always bad business, but I will say that big business perhaps will be able to weather the storm. Perhaps they have certain financial resources; perhaps they have certain connections and they will be able to weather the storm; but imagine a small business that is just starting. It may be an electrical shop, I do not know; it may be a variety of small businesses. Take the veterans who have come back and started up small businesses here and there. I know that times are good, and they should get better in these years of peace following the war. Some of these businesses are going on the rocks. Take small textile industries. I tell you that some of these are going on the rocks. We all know that a new business has a struggle to gain a hold, to gain momentum and to keep its head above water for a year or two until it gets on its feet. Small business always has that experience, and now just when it should have an opportunity of becoming permanent what is going to happen? They will not be able to get the raw material; they will not be able to get this or that, and the result will be that they will have to close down. That is perhaps one of the worst features of this austerity program.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before you is for the second reading of Bill No. 3 wherein the minister seeks certain powers that, in my opinion, are entirely dictatorial. Such vast and gigantic powers as are asked for in this bill have never before been conferred upon any minister of the crown. The minister who is now asking parliament to grant these powers to him did some good work in the war, and I therefore regret that he should now be asking for what amounts to a totalitarian dictatorship.
Let us look at cause and effect so far as this bill is concerned. To find the cause of it we must go back two years. All that was done at Ceneva is interlocked with the proposals of this bill and we can do nothing now but hold a post mortem. The government is simply asking us to allow it to establish a Hitler autocracy, because the bill proposes to make the minister absolute over the law courts and over the House of Commons. In the schedules to the bill we find the list of Canadian articles set out in the pamphlets issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce last February, March and April down to September. They are all linked together.
In this bill the government proposes to do two things. Two standards of living are being set up. One relates to imports and exports fMr. Knowles.]
and the other has to do with our mode of living. There is something more serious than the dollar situation and that is the principle of the bill, which relates to the standard of living we have had in this country, according to which the liberty of the subject has been guaranteed. The freedom of a man, freedom of body, mind and soul, is a priceless heritage and it is being taken away by this bill, under these Hitler autocracy powers, these totalitarian powers which the minister proposes to assume. What can it profit a man if he gain the whole world and lose his own soul? The government may succeed in the first principle of the bill regarding exports and imports, mode of living and all that kind of thing, including the dollar situation. They knew two years ago what they would do but kept the House of Commons in the dark, never telling us a word about it. I say, they may succeed with regard to imports and exports, with regard to the dollar situation and all that sort of thing, but they will not succeed in attaining their second objective, for what will it profit us if we win the first two and lose our souls?
As I said before, we must look to cause and effect. What about the empire? Where do we go from here in this bill? The limit of the bill should be March 31. That should not be exceeded. Then there is the austerity about which we hear so much. We never heard of it all last session until the end of Geneva. When did the government first start to talk about austerity? Did y.ou ever hear about it at the time of Lake Success, when certain people went down there and occupied a whole floor of the Biltmore hotel. Was there any austerity proposed there? A hundred thousand dollars for one whole carload of people to go down there for weeks and months. The government knew all about the Geneva pacts last spring. But when I asked the acting leader of the house, who is a fine gentleman, about this matter on February 10 and if he could tell us anything about his Geneva talks, he told us he could not tell us anything about them because they were going to meet some time later in the next few months.
As I say, we no longer have a in- freedom of body, mind or soul as a result of this bill.
If you look at the principle of expansion of world trade it is just a myth. All trade will now flow to the United States and little to empire countries. They will get all the trade and the empire and the dominions will get nothing. What has become of preferential trade? That is down and out by the Geneva route. It is mentioned in the schedules, and what do you find? You find this if you make a close study of this bill. We should be close friends and allies for ever of the United

States. That should be our policy. But we should keep to the great principle of being economically independent of them. That is the chief requisite. That is what we lose now by Geneva. For that reason I supported preferential trade and opposed Brett-on Woods and the Geneva pacts. We should stick to empire preference and lessen our trade dependence on the United States by developing empire preferential trade along the lines I have indicated. We need that- policy today.
What is my policy? What do I propose? I would apply protection by way of bonuses, subventions and subsidies to Canada's natural resources, resources of grain, bacon, eggs and food, which should all go to our best customer, Britain and be within the empire. I would apply the national policy program of bonuses, subventions and subsidies and all that kind of thing to develop preferential trade within the empire family. My chief complaint with regard to this Bill No. 3 is that it has been used to make it appear that we are surrendering everything we have to please Washington. There will be no more future success for empire trade, and that preferential trade is out if this bill passes. The bill is political. It is not economic. Britain will be ruined beyond any hope of .recovery and so will Canada, because we are going to lose empire trade. As I say, we need to get back to the vision of those men who founded that particular doctrine, gave it to us and made a success of it. By this Geneva pact scheme, that is being eliminated.
If what is set, out- in this bill is supposed to be the best that can be done in this economic emergency situation then I say no to it. I say, further, that the bill should be limited ' to March 31. It should not be on forever because we do not know what kind of austerity will follow from this bill. It may be a huge austerity. In other words, by this bill, we are going to place control under one minister and his officials, totalitarian Hitler autocracy, over the head of the law courts and over the head of the House of Commons, until next March.
What is to become of Bill No. 3 based on the Geneva charter which ruins empire trade? See what we pledged to United States by that. By Geneva we pledged ourselves to the United States to accept the principle of non-discrimination as a right and proper principle in world trade. That is what I object to principally, namely, that we have adopted a wrong principle and a doctrine which was proposed by the United States many years ago when they fought tooth and nail against these preferences. They fought right along against them. Not only is that principle contained in this particular Bill No. 3, but we find the same
principle which the government are adopting now in lease-lend, also in the United States loan and now, in this farce of all-American trade, the Geneva agreement. Those three principles are still in the two schedules in the bill here. We are going to agree to what . the United States asked for at Geneva, namely the abrogation of these preferential trade doctrines, as set out in the schedules, by what is known as the non-discrimination clauses. That is, we agree to grant no favours to empire countries under these schedules, but agree religiously to avoid that, to let America grab all trade. That is a dangerous doctrine.
A large part of this bill is called a charter.
It is the Geneva charter. It is in the book here. You have the same system applying to Canada which Canada accepted. This particular charter is called the Geneva charter. Bill No. 3 is the local end of it and it is the only end of it we are dealing with now. In this Bill No. 3, in its present form, I say the government is making the same mistake as it made before. The bill is based on white paper 27 and 27A made at Geneva. As I say, Mr. Speaker. I am opposed to the doctrine set out. My complaint is that at Geneva we pleased Washington and ruined any hope of empire trade to put Britain on her feet again. We agreed to this principle and thereby gave up all hope of success in ever getting our empire trade back. The government at Ottawa has no mandate for this Bill No. 3. The government has shown by Bill No. 3 that it lacks any evidence of vision, and "where there is no vision, the people perish." The government has adopted this internationalism found in Bill No. 3. I am absolutely opposed to the dictatorship set up over the people of Canada by Ottawa and the creation, by this Bill No. 3 proposed by the present government, of a vaster bureaucracy than has ever before been attempted here over the lives and liberties of individuals. I clearly saw in December, 1945, the coming of this tragedy when I strongly opposed the Bretton Woods agreement and the American loan which have been -the cause and effect of this dollar situation set out in this bill, the awful result of which two agencies has led at Geneva to attempts to liquidate and dissolve the British empire and end British preferences.
I would use the national policy under this bill for capital and labour, both of them to harmonize industry in Canada and not nationalize it-a national policy brought up to date to meet after-the-war conditions, for grain, food, bacon and all farm products. I would use the national policy by giving bonuses, subventions and subsidies instead of

this Bill No. 3. We would have accomplished it, because the British empire today is, in natural resources, much stronger than either Russia or the United States. For that reason I have taken a stand on it. I believe New Zealand and Australia are with the mother country, and are opposed to much of this regimentation. It is going to be on nearly three years after the war. It will be on until next Easter. This will be good anyway until next March. I would amend the bill until March 31. That is as far as I would go.
Among other things, this bill has become an absurdity at Christmas time. We have over one million Canadians who have gone to the United States, many of them in poor circumstances. How are you going to give them this Christmas grant of the usual $25 under this bill? We used to be able to send $25. They are poor people over there who left Canada; some of them are students. They have gone over there to seek a living. They have been driven out of Canada by such measures as this; they did not get a chance. They are left over there under this bill, at Christmas time, without any notice. We cancel, by foreign exchange, any hope of sending money over. You used to be able to send them over some benevolent grant, money now limited to $25 a month. Some of them are out on the street or will be if they do not get this. This is done over the head of parliament and of the law courts. Why was not this whole matter referred to the supreme court in the last six months to find out if the government of the day had any power to extend the Foreign Exchange Control Act in the way they are doing?
What are we here for? We might as well go home if the executive can do that. It is getting worse than in the days of the family compact of 1837, when the government can pass measures like this over the head of the commons and over the head of the law courts. This is the high court of parliament; yet one man has power to do all this. I want to be fair to the minister. He did a lot of good work during the war, and I am sorry he has taken this new job.
I have consistently supported the system of preferential trade, but by this measure we are eliminating it for all time to come. Where is Britain to get the food, if she cannot get it from this empire source? Last session the government knew all about this Geneva pact. Look at the schedule. Last session the government knew about it, but they told us they did not know. Why did they not tell us something about this when parliament was
TMr. Church.]
sitting last July? They were taking United States dollars from Britain to pay for some of the food they gave Britain then. Parliament knew nothing about it. I did not know anything about it, nor did the press, nor the radio, nor the public; yet they were proceeding in the manner indicated.
As I say, I have been a great admirer of the American people, but here we go farther than in any other bill we ever had. We have surrendered too much initiative, economically, politically and financially to Washington all along, and the American people do not want that. Nor do our people. The Americans want to know the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. They want to know all about our exports and imports, and our economic problems, but the people in the constituencies do not know. Why were we called here? We are to be sent home on Friday, and we might as well not have come at all. What was the need for this session, if the government has all these powers? The dictators in Europe have seen their day, but the government here are adopting measures such as Hitler imposed. In Bill No. 3 we are just trying to imitate the Hitler autocracy by removing these things from the jurisdiction of the House of Commons and the law courts. Well, it is good-bye to law and order. It will take a small standing army all along the border to enforce these regulations, asking everybody at the border: "Are 3'ou sane or insane? What have you in your pocket? Have you an American dollar?" In the -end they are going to cause widespread dislocation of business and great unemployment. We should have stood by the people of Britain, our best customer, who stood by us during the seven dark years of the war. We should have enabled them to get on their feet again. What are we doing? With all the standing army we had down in Washington, with all the officials we had down there, they knew nothing about this Geneva bill until it was proposed in the House of Commons.
I do not want to talk the bill out. I would be quite capable of doing so, but I have some respect for the young minister, whom I have known for a great many years. I am surprised that he did not let the people know long ago about this policy of wait and see what Washington does. The Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe), who will carry out this measure, does not look like a dictator. He is a sportsman, anyway; but I can tell him that he is adopting totalitarian powers, along with his deputy, Mr. Berry. I do not know Mr. Berry personally, and I have never
